News.title: Trump blitzes Iran just hours before midterm election as ‘secret bombing campaign’ is revealed
News.content:
DON'S FURY Trump blitzes Iran just hours before midterm election as ‘secret bombing campaign’ is revealed







Next

THE US has blitzed a key island in the Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Explosions rocked Qeshem, a large island off Iran on Monday, as Donald Trump played down the idea of resuming major blitzes on the country.



As blasts hit the island, Trump told reporters: “We had a war with Iran. We won.”

“I don’t know if you even call it a war because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”



But officials told the Wall Street Journal the US has been engaged in smaller-scale hits against Iran for weeks.

The paper reported that Washington has carried our a series of secret strikes on Iran in recent weeks, while talking up the chance of a peace deal.

Monday’s strikes on Qeshem were just the latest in a string of similar assaults.

Some officials, it said, called the secret strikes “defensive”, arguing that they were to block Iran from attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

The blitzes have been kept quiet, unlike earlier blasts in the war, to avoid suggesting that it is ready to relaunch major combat operations, one official reportedly said.

After a speech yesterday evening, asked if he was mulling more strikes on Iran, Trump replied “no”, shaking his head.



Explosions had been reported on and around Qeshem hours earlier.

Sources told NewsNation that the US has bombed radar detectors and missile launchers “as a continuation of the strikes in Iran”.

The strategic island hosts an underground missile site, a naval base and a sprawling desalination plant.

It was blitzed five months ago during a testy ceasefire between the US and Iran.

Around six blasts were said to have rocked the island on Monday, as the IRGC claimed it had “intercepted and warded off” a hostile fighter jet.



Witnesses heard explosions and saw suspected projectiles light up the sky, with sources telling Iranian state media that air defence systems on the island had been activated.

A US official said it was addressing threats to American forces in the region.

News.title: Britain faces an attack on infrastructure that could wipe out food supplies & energy in 2years, warns cyber chief
News.content:
Next

THE UK faces an attack on its critical infrastructure that could wipe out food supplies and the electric grid in two years, the country’s top cyber chief warns.

Dr Richard Horne, CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, will say in a speech today there is a real prospect of “when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under” amid an “unprecedented” rise in hacking.



A new NCSC report warns Russia, China and Iran will routinely use artificial intelligence to achieve their political goals.

And Dr Horne will say that, by 2028, hostile actors’ adoption of AI is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their attacks.



That, he will claim, is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable”.

He will call for urgent investment, saying: “For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency.

“And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.”

Security minister Dan Jarvis said: “In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber front line.

“NCSC’s latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated.



“We’re using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new National Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.”

News.title: Andy Burnham to discuss ‘formal apology’ to countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery during his Caribbean trip
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham is set to use his trip to the Caribbean to discuss issuing a formal apology for Britain’s role in slavery.

The PM will meet fellow Commonwealth leaders and begin talks on whether the UK should say sorry for the 17th and 18th century trade.



He revealed at the weekend he is open to calls for a formal state apology, but Downing Street has refused to entertain financial compensation.

Mr Burnham will now set out plans to enter a “structured dialogue” recognising Britain’s role.



It would be the first time a PM has issued such an apology.

No10 said: “We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than deciding unilaterally what form it should take.



“An apology of this ­significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected as they ask for it.

“Acknowledging the horror of the slave trade and considering a formal apology for Britain’s role does not accept present day financial liability.”

The King and Queen acknowledged slavery while in Antigua and Barbuda yesterday.

They toured a museum where slavery artefacts include shackles. The King also had a surprise meeting with British actor Sir Idris Elba, who told him: “Sorry about the Prime Minister.”



It is thought he was talking about Gaston Browne, the PM of Antigua and Barbuda, who is demanding Britain pays reparations for slavery.

Buckingham Palace said the King will not shy away from the “darkest days of our past”. His speech to the Commonwealth heads of government today is set to be “unflinchingly honest”.

In St John’s, Mr Burnham fell playing cricket with one of the game’s greats, Sir Viv Richards.

He joked: “My running between the wickets needs a bit of work.”

News.title: Burnham claims he’s different from other politicians but when it comes to his own travel, he’s a high-flying hypocrite
News.content:
PM’s high life







Next

ANDY Burnham loves to tell us how different he is from all other politicians.

But when it comes to his own travel, he’s a high-flying hypocrite.



Yesterday morning, a taxpayer-funded VIP jet took off at Stansted Airport to fly a government delegation to a Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean.

But it was forced to make a sharp turn and head North to pick up the Prime Minister and his wife.



Why? Because he’d spent the weekend in his beloved Manchester and couldn’t be bothered to catch a train to London.

So he treated an Airbus A321 like an expensive taxi service to collect him on his own doorstep — landing taxpayers with an estimated £20,000 bill.

Labour spent years in Opposition screaming about Tory ministers using private jets and they are forever lecturing us about the need for Net Zero.

But while families struggle with green taxes, Burnham is burning jet fuel so he can spend more time up North.

It seems like it isn’t enough to fritter money on his “Number 10 North” vanity project in Manchester and he now wants a “Heathrow North” to go with it.

Or perhaps he’s working on his next election slogan: I’m Andy, fly me.



No10 white flag

SHABANA Mahmood was hailed as the “tough cookie” with the tenacity to drive through controls on mass immigration.

Her flagship reforms were welcomed by millions but met with whingeing from open borders left-wingers.

Eight months on, her proposals have gone the same way as most other radical policies under Andy Burnham.

The PM has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and at least 100 MPs and told the Home Secretary to dilute plans to restrict settlement rights for lower-skilled migrants.

Once again the bleeding heart backbenchers have got their way, ignoring the wishes of the country.



It has taken just 12 weeks for Burnham to show his true colours.

He promised to tackle the big issues.

But at the first sign of a scrap with his own backbenchers, he’s proved he doesn’t have the stomach for tough choices.

Trivial pursuits

LABOUR continues to spend its time on trivial fluff while kicking Britain’s biggest dangers into the long grass.

The Budget last week provided no extra cash to grapple with the threats we face from hostile foreign powers.



The Prime Minister should be rallying Commonwealth leaders in Antigua instead of apologising for things that happened 200 years ago.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch points out that the PM is more concerned about pleasing his own party than making difficult decisions.

Britain can’t afford another three years of treading water.

News.title: Tourist, 26, and instructor killed in hang gliding crash after smashing into wall & falling during landing
News.content:
Next

A TOURIST and his instructor have been killed in a horror hang gliding crash in front of horrified holidaymakers.

The pair smashed into a wall and fell while attempting to land at a popular beach in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.



Argentinian tourist Adrián Guillermo Arismendi, 26, died in the freak accident at São Conrado beach on Monday.

It was the holidaymaker’s first hang gliding flight – he had travelled to Rio with a group of fellow thrill seekers.



Adrián’s Brazilian instructor Luiz Eduardo Rodrigues dos Santos, 45, was also killed in the crash.

He had a decade of flying experience.



The pair had taken off from the Pedra Bonita ramp, a 1,706ft jumping-off point on a nearby mountain known for incredible views across Rio.

They had planned to land at a sandbar airstrip in São Conrado.

But horrified onlookers reported seeing them suddenly lose height.

The duo then smashed into an eight-foot wall separating the boardwalk from the beach and fell to their deaths.



Paramedics rushed to treat both men at the beach.

They were airlifted to hospital in critical condition, but could not be saved.

Witnesses said the hang glider appeared to malfunction as it flew towards the coast.



Investigators have yet to determine the cause of the fatal accident.

Beachgoer Ana Clara Goulart told O Globo: “Those of us on the sand thought it was strange because they were flying very low.

“They were too close to us, and it was already quite windy. We didn’t imagine they were falling.

“At one point, the hang glider started spinning in the air. That’s when I realised something was wrong.”

Another witness called the crash “devastating”.



He said: “They were enjoying themselves, having an adventure, and they couldn’t even imagine that that would be their last breath.”

All hang gliding flights in the area were suspended while a probe was launched into the deadly crash.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Vice president of the São Conrado Free Flight Club José Bruno Batalha Menescal Filho said instructor Luiz had worked as a pilot for around ten years.

He had become an instructor a year ago after completing his training, the club vice president added.

News.title: Minute-by-minute timeline of doomed Learjet’s final moments before tech tycoon & family among 9 killed in fireball crash
News.content:
Next

NEW details have been revealed following a private Learjet flight crash that left nine dead.

The passengers onboard the private flight have since been identified.



The private Learjet 60 descended quickly into a fireball crash on Sunday in Palm Beach County, Florida.

In roughly one minute, the flight plunged over 25,000ft into the ground, crashing into a residential area of the county.





The flight first departed from the Austin-Bergstrom International in Texas at around 10:37am, heading towards Freeport, Bahamas.

Roughly two hours later at 12:47pm, the co-pilot, identified as Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20, reports that the flight is experiencing “light, clear ice that is manageable.”

read more plane disasters HORROR DIVE Hidden clues in bone-chilling audio may reveal cause of nosedive plane crash

At 12:48pm, Filgueiras is heard on audio from the cockpit asking the air traffic controller permission to climb to 37,000 feet.

The co-pilot also said the flight was experiencing precipitation.



Within the same minute, the co-pilot is heard saying that the plane is rapidly descending.

“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday, – we’re descending 10,000ft per minute,” the co-pilot said.

During a press conference on Monday, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said that the private jet “announced the descent followed by a mayday call,” roughly 30 seconds after requesting to climb to 37,000 feet.

Before 12:49pm, the co-pilot is once again heard on the cockpit radio saying that the flight was “descending 20,000 feet per minute.”

“We’re going to crash into the ground.”



At 12:49pm, Filgueiras can be heard saying that the plane was actually plunging at a rate of 22,000 feet per minute.



“Holy f**k we’re out of time,” the co-pilot said within the 12:49pm minute.

The audio from the jet then went silent and at 12:50pm, the flight crashed directly into the ground, leaving the pilot and eight others dead.

Videos from bystanders show the plane speeding into the ground before it disintegrated into a fireball on impact.

“It looked like a missile going down. It left a big crater,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said about the crash.

The other victims on the plane have been identified as tech tycoon Adam Robinson, 45, his wife Helen Sharp, 40, and their two children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2.



Two friends of the family, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, as well as the family’s nanny, Anita Maria Apellido Cetina, were also identified as victims on the deadly flight.

The captain of the flight has been identified as Jeff Gregory, 55.

All seven passengers, along with Filgueiras and Gregory, died in the crash.

“Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives,” Robinson’s relatives said in a statement.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.”



Timothy Monville, the NTSB investigator in charge of the incident said that “the biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway.”

News.title: Tories paid heavy political price for failing to deliver on immigration & Burnham should be wary of making same mistake
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Tories paid heavy political price for failing to deliver on immigration & Burnham should be wary of making same mistake







Next

SHABANA Mahmood has spent months promising to get tough on immigration but when push came to shove, it was Labour’s Left that got its way.

More than 100 Labour MPs had made clear they would not stomach forcing foreign care workers to wait 15 years to settle in Britain.



And opposition was not confined to the backbenches, with Cabinet figures including Angela Rayner, Lucy Powell and Miatta Fahnbulleh also raising concerns.

The pressure paid off, with the Home Secretary watering down one of the toughest parts of her crackdown.



That is not to say the reforms have been abandoned – with the standard wait for permanent residency still doubling from five to ten years.

But for Andy Burnham, the bigger problem is what all this says about who is calling the shots in his Government.

Sir Keir Starmer knows only too well what happens when Labour MPs discover they can force a Prime Minister into retreat.

The timing is also not ideal, with the PM preparing for a major EU summit later this month after reopening the debate about Britain’s future relationship with Brussels, including freedom of movement.

And yesterday, Burnham refused to say whether legal migration was too high, insisting it was “difficult to say” because it depended on the needs of the economy.

While his comments might please some Labour MPs, it it is a harder message to sell in places like his own constituency of Makerfield, where Reform won more than a third of the vote in June.



Farage’s party may have slipped back in the polls but Labour has handed it a ready-made attack line against both major parties.

Having watched the Tories pay a heavy political price for failing to deliver on immigration, Burnham should be wary of making the same mistake.

News.title: Needles & pins discovered in kids’ Halloween treats in Donegal as Gardai confirm investigation into ‘alarming’ incident
News.content:
SICK TRICK Needles & pins discovered in kids’ Halloween treats in Donegal as Gardai confirm investigation into ‘alarming’ incident







Next

GARDAI have launched an investigation after needles and pins were found concealed inside children’s Halloween treats.

Donegal mums Savannah McDaid and Philippa Falls made the grim discoveries inside their children’s candy cache after trick-or-treating on Saturday.



Savannah, who lives in Stranorlar, found small metal pins inside four different sweets and Philippa’s son, Joshua, found a possibly-fatal pin embedded in a bar.

Savannah’s little son, Arló, 3, collected a large amount of goodies when trick-or-treating in Srath Aoibhinn and Ard Greine.



Savannah shared a pic of Arló’s treats, which were spread across the sofa, with her own mother.

Savannah told Donegal Daily: “Mum had seen photos or videos before and told me to check them.

“I got a fridge magnet and four of the sweets – two chocolate bars and two chewy bars – stuck to the magnet. I just ripped them open and I was shocked at what I found.”

The small pins appeared to have been carefully pierced through the wrapping paper and into the various bars.



Savannah said: “I just thought I would check them and they’ll be grand. I got such a shock when I took the wrappers off.

“Never in a million years did I think we would find something like this happening here in Donegal.

“It is just crazy and it ruins the fun for the kids. I’ve had to chuck most of the stuff in the bin. Some of the stuff was inside wee bags and they’re all fine.

“The scary thing is that one of the pins was inside a wee Milky Way bar and you’d give that to younger kids because it’s soft inside.”

A social media post by Savannah sparked Philippa into action.



Philippa, who lives in Ballybofey, told Donegal Daily: “I have heard of these types of incidents before, but not here.

“The pin that was inside Joshua’s bar didn’t even show up with a magnet.

“Never in my wildest dreams did I think we would have something like this here in Ballybofey.

“I don’t know Savannah, but I know her mum and when I saw the post I told Joshua not to eat any more of the sweets.”

Intrepid Joshua investigated for himself, checking a range of confectionery with a fridge magnet.



He was going to attempt to eat the offending bar when the kitchen light reflected back from the sweet.

Joshua explained: “I just got a glimpse of the needle part when I was going to eat it.”

Joshua and his friends were trick-or-treating in the Blue Cedars, The Cedars and Glenwaters estates.

Philippa said: “When I saw that pin, I was nearly shaking and I just thought how could people be so sadistic? It was like an embroidery or sewing machine needle that was in the chocolate.

“It is just awful to think that this is happening here in Donegal. My son and two of his friends were out for a bit of craic and harmless fun and people were so welcoming. It is horrifying and frightening. How many more are out there? These are potentially fatal.



“Someone has set out with the intention of causing a fatal injury or severely hurting a child. It is just beyond belief that this has happened. God knows what else could be in sweets.”

Local Sinn Fein Councillor Dakota Nic Mheanman hit out at the disturbing acts.

Cllr Nic Mheanman said: “It’s very worrying and alarming that parents have found the pins in their children’s sweets.

“Parents should never have to worry that taking their children trick-or-treating would pose such dangers.”

Gardai are now investigating after shocking reports of pins embedded in the sweets on Halloween night.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A spokesperson for the force said: “Gardai received a report of an incident which occurred on 31st October 2026 in the Ballybofey / Stranorlar area in Co Donegal.

“Enquiries are ongoing.”

News.title: Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has scrapped plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for permanent settlement.

Mahmood had proposed doubling the wait for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait.

But following a backlash from several Labour MPs, Mahmood revised the policy and care workers who earn at least Â£25,000 a year and arrived in the UK before May 2025 would continue to qualify after five years.

The Conservatives said Mahmood's "U-turn" would cost taxpayers billions of pounds.

ILR, also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.

Last November, Mahmood announced plans to delay settlements in response to concerns over the number of people approaching eligibility, in the wake of record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Conservative government, nicknamed the "Boriswave".

Asked by the BBC whether she had u-turned on her earlier promises, she replied "I don't accept that", adding that some 500,000 people in the UK "will not now settle at five years".

"They will have to wait longer before they can achieve settlement in this country, and I've come to a fair resolution for care workers," she said.

The Home Office has said its figures show net migration - the difference between those entering and leaving the country - added 2.6m people to the UK population between 2021 and 2024.

The department estimates that between 2026 and 2030 between 1.3m and 2.2m people will settle in the UK, adding its central estimate has increased to 1.9m.

The home secretary faced criticism for proposing to apply the changes to migrant workers already in the UK, with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner previously saying this would "change the goalposts".

Several Labour MPs also described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.

Making a statement to the House of Commons, Mahmood said settlement "should not be automatic, it should be earned".

News.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
News.content:
UK exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes will also be able to resume.

The agreement will also allow for passports for UK pets taken into the EU.

Under the agreement the UK will commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards. This process is called "dynamic alignment".

While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.

The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.

The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.

The BBC understands that the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence cooperation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans.

While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.

The British Chamber of Commerce released a new analysis of its members' views on Monday suggesting options for a closer relationship.

The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

It also pointed to economic analysis of more fundamental changes to the UK-EU relationship, suggesting the largest long-term economic boosts from rejoining the single market or the EU itself. The BCC called on government to analyse and publish options, as it consults its members.

The BCC is calling for an exploration of what a new relationship could look like, and offers nine options, including a customs union, a "Swiss-style" Single Market relationship, and a "Canada model" associate membership.

"The evidence from businesses suggests that the prime minister is right to have initiated a conversation on our future relationship with Europe, and he deserves real credit for having done so.

"Government needs to examine all of the options, remain clear-headed about the trade-offs each involves, and involve business in the decision-making process from the start," Shevaun Havilland, director general of the BCC, said.

More than half (56%) of exporting businesses in a BCC survey said they wanted EU customs paperwork and delays removed so they can grow. That rose to 58% of manufacturers.

The prime minister has said he wants to use this month's summit to launch a conversation on a longer term path for the UK's relationship with the EU, including "going all the way", meaning rejoining the bloc.

News.title: PM plans debt re-set for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
News.content:
The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.

As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.

The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.

"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.

The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting that reparations were not on the agenda, but other leaders insisted they should be.

This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.

"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery, external. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.

Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.

They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.

"A formal apology," Miliband said in a social media video, external, is something "the British government are open to".

He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right of feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."

News.title: Jewellery sold as sterling silver on Amazon and Temu found to contain toxic chemicals
News.content:
Jewellery advertised as sterling silver on popular online marketplaces was found to contain toxic chemicals, following a BBC investigation.

Some 25 items - bought from Amazon, eBay, Temu, Etsy and OnBuy - were examined by experts for BBC Watchdog on The One Show.

Laboratory analysis found eight contained illegal levels of cadmium - a chemical that can cause cancer. Only two items could be classified as sterling silver.

Amazon, eBay, Temu and OnBuy said misleading listings were prohibited and that it had removed the jewellery identified by Watchdog. Etsy did not respond.

News.title: 'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?
News.content:
"Mogging", a word used playfully to mean outshining, outperforming or upstaging someone or something, has been named as word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary.

A fast-growing slang word among members of Generations Z and Alpha - both online and in everyday conversation - mogging went mainstream in 2026 with a 210% increase in its usage.

Collins' managing director Alex Beecroft said its lexicographers look at "how often words are used" and also "analyse patterns of usage" that reveal the latest linguistic trends.

The selection of mogging as word of the year, he said, "shows how each generation leaves its mark on language".

News.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
News.content:
The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.

John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.

While the costly phone, which sells for Â£1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack.

The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.

"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.

Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.

Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.

During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.

Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.

Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.

Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.

However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.

Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."

Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.

Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.

Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.

Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.

As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.

Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."

It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

News.title: Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
News.content:
Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity.

The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland.

The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men.

This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp.

Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail.

She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added.

The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity.

The first Christmas stamp collection came out in December 1966 after a children's art competition was announced by the then-postmaster Tony Benn.

David Gold, of Royal Mail, said: "We hope this year's Christmas stamps will add an extra touch of festive magic to the millions of greetings sent to family and friends at home and around the world."

News.title: A simple guide to the midterms
News.content:
Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.

A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.

The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.

The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.

News.title: Two boys arrested after Halloween party stabbings
News.content:
Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.

Officers said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.

Police said two boys remain in hospital having suffered serious injuries, with one 17-year-old victim in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.

A 17-year-old and 16-year-old, both from Southampton, have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and remain in police custody.

Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.

One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.

"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."

Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.

Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie said: "Whilst the two arrests are a significant development in our investigation, which has moved at pace since the incident was first reported to us, we still urge our communities to contact us with any information, no matter how small it may seem."

She added: "If you were at the party and have not spoken with officers yet, or you have any CCTV, mobile phone, dash cam or doorbell camera footage covering Park Road and the surrounding area, then please get in touch."

News.title: Dry and chilly start to November after wet but sunny October
News.content:
High pressure has seized control of the UK weather meaning largely dry, settled but chilly autumn conditions will continue this week.

Days will bring a mix of patchy cloud, sunny spells and a few showers, with frost and fog expected to form at night - especially in northern and western areas.

Temperatures will generally be around or a little below the seasonal norm and it will feel particularly chilly in southern England and south Wales where there will be a brisk easterly breeze.

The relatively quiet start to November follows a decidedly mixed October which - according to Met Office data just released was wetter, warmer and sunnier than average.

News.title: Train attacker said 'I am the baddest', trial hears
News.content:
A man accused of a mass train stabbing was heard saying "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me", on a different train the day before the attack, a court has heard.

Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder 10 people on a London-bound train which had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire on 1 November last year.

A passenger texted the British Transport Police reporting a male behaving erratically the night before, Cambridge Crown Court heard.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder over events on the train, and beforehand in Peterborough and London.

He is accused of trying to kill three people in Peterborough during the evening of 31 October. Later that night he boarded a train from the city's railway station, headed towards London.

In a statement read to jurors, another passenger, Keirah Lee-Oakman, said a male entered the train, sat down and "appeared to be talking and mumbling to himself".

She said he began walking up and down the carriages stating "boom and power", repeatedly saying things like "I haven't got it" as well as referencing the devil, jurors were told.

Lee-Oakman said he was "acting in an aggressive and intimidating manner... I felt unsafe" and while on the train she sent a text to the British Transport Police.

Jurors heard police officers attended Stevenage station but the male dropped down on to the tracks and officers eventually deemed it unsafe to continue following him.

News.title: MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row
News.content:
Carla Lockhart has quit the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in a row over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute.

The MP for Upper Bann had been calling for the party to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.

Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.

The fall-out comes after unionist anger over Sinn FÃ©in's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road, which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn FÃ©in figures have been interviewed by police investigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn FÃ©in in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.

The Sinn FÃ©in vice-president has defended her involvement in the protests, saying it was the "right thing to do".

DUP leader Gavin Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.

In an open letter to colleagues last week, Lockhart said it was the "only one credible option" and any kind of "graduated response" would be "insulting to those who have trusted us".

In a statement posted on her Facebook page on Monday, the MP said: "My first responsibility remains to the people of Upper Bann.

"You placed your trust in me, and I will continue to work every bit as hard for you, your family and our community."

News.title: Mother told to book appointment to give birth to baby who had died
News.content:
Warning: This article contains themes and images some readers may find upsetting.

A seven-month pregnant woman whose unborn baby died after she was discharged from hospital while suffering from a life-threatening condition was told by staff to make an appointment to give birth.

Danielle Brown, 31, from North Tyneside, said she was devastated to have to return home knowing the baby she was carrying was no longer alive.

She said no family should be put through the same experience and wants hospitals to offer alternatives for those grieving.

After she was discharged from hospital suffering with pre-eclampsia, Danielle insisted on returning to the maternity unit as she felt so unwell and was seen by doctors.

She was told her daughter had died but, instead of delivering the baby, the hospital sent her home and told her to ring to book a slot to give birth.

Her partner Anthony Miller, 34, described it as "horrible... lying in bed and holding that belly" knowing their baby was not alive.

The Newcastle Hospitals NHS Trust said it fully accepted "aspects of the care we provided fell short" and offered a "heartfelt apology".

News.title: Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
News.content:
The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.

Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it â at any level of government."

Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from it's local councils".

In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.

The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.

Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided. Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.

Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.

Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.

Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.

The areas are:

Arun District Council

Derbyshire Dales District Council

Havant Borough Council

Lewes District Council (The Green Party announced last week it was "mutually" ending its alliance with Labour)

Runnymede Borough Council (Labour says local co-operation had already ceased)

Sheffield City Council

Stafford Borough Council

Warwick District Council

Wealden District Council

West Devon Borough Council

West Suffolk Council

Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.

It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise, arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".

The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.

Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.

In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".

News.title: Teen had leg amputated after stabbing on beach on bank holiday, court hears
News.content:
In the moment after the attack, the 17-year-old fell to the ground and looked pale, saying: "I am going, I feel myself going."

Ahmed then fled the scene and discarded the knife close to a nearby building, an act seen by an eyewitness who later identified the 19-year-old in an identity parade.

Before he threw the object Ahmed was heard saying: "I need to dash this."

He was also captured fleeing the scene by a woman who was taking selfies on the beach with her partner.

The court heard the 17-year-old was taken by air ambulance to the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, and had sustained an injury to the main blood vessel in his right leg, with one artery completely blocked.

Despite several transfusions, oxygen was not flowing properly to the leg and a decision was reached that an amputation was necessary.

The court heard the teenager had a through knee amputation - removing the lower half of the leg.

Ahmed was questioned by police shortly after the incident and responded "no comment" to most of the questions, but the court heard he denied stabbing anyone and said he knew nothing about the incident and was released.

Gobir said it was the prosecution's case that the defendant was the person responsible for stabbing the victim and "that he must have intended to cause him really serious harm by stabbing him to a vital part of his body with such a dangerous weapon".

The court was then shown CCTV from various cameras around Barry Island Pleasure Park area showing the groups of teenagers on the day of the incident.

On Tuesday afternoon, the jury were played a police interview with the victim where he explained more about the incident.

He said that some of his female friends had started talking to a large group of boys as they sat on the rocks.

He said that a male friend had started to get nervous, believing he "might have had a problem with these boys" but the teenager tried to calm the situation with the other group.

He said he did not know the reason why he was attacked, describing the sensation of being stabbed as "like a punch", adding "I knew straight away I had been stabbed".

He said it was a "sharp pain" but it "didn't really sting how you'd expect it to".

He described how he was in and out of consciousness as he was taken to the hospital but remembered seeing his friend being attacked by another man with a plastic shovel. He said in total he had to have four surgeries on his leg.

The trial continues.

News.title: Parents' concerns to trigger urgent checks in A&E
News.content:
A similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital wards.

More than 90 hospitals across England have been using the alert system in children's wards, with different age-appropriate assessments available for babies through to teenagers.

The NHS has already said it will expand Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England. The rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review if they are worried that a patient's condition is getting worse and their concerns are not being responded to.

The initiative is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis, in hospital following a bike accident.

A coroner ruled that her family's concerns about her worsening condition were not listened to and she would probably have survived had she been moved to intensive care earlier.

Martha's parents Merope and Paul came up with the idea of the rule in a bid to change the culture that contributed to her death.

A&E units will have a dedicated phone number that can be called to trigger an urgent review of a patient's care.

Duncan Burton, chief nursing officer for England, said the new early warning system for children in emergency departments was an "important next step in improving care for children and young people across England for this winter - and beyond".

He added: "In fast-paced emergency departments, staff need to spot quickly when a child's condition is deteriorating.

"This standardised approach will help them recognise the warning signs, communicate concerns, and make timely decisions when every moment matters."

The early warning system for children, PEWS, is a collaboration between NHS England and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and the Royal College of Nursing.

News.title: 1-year-old killed after crawling onto highway while his family was doing yard work
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A 1-year-old boy died on Friday afternoon after wandering onto a road in Jonesville, Florida, where he was struck by a vehicle, state authorities said.

Florida Highway Patrol troopers reported that the child’s parents were doing yard work at their residence when the toddler walked away unnoticed.

According to officials, the parents searched for the boy in locations he typically frequented, but he managed to reach the nearby roadway before they could locate him.

The driver of the vehicle was unable to see the toddler prior to the collision, authorities said. The child was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Investigators stated that charges are not expected to be filed against either the driver or the parents, as reported by ABC affiliate WCJB.

open image in gallery State troopers in Florida are investigating a Friday afternoon collision in Jonesville that left a 1-year-old boy dead after he walked onto a nearby roadway and was struck by a vehicle ( Getty Images )

On social media, reaction to the incident reflected sympathy and debate over supervision.

While many expressed condolences for the family and support for the driver, others noted how quickly young children can wander off outdoors or raised questions about early reports from the scene.

News.title: Bodycam video shows aftermath of fatal shooting by National Guard in Memphis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on a man as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows.

A Memphis police officer can be heard in the footage from an officer's body camera calling for an ambulance and then asking the troops, “Hey, you guys got a medical kit or anything?”

The Shelby County District Attorney’s Office released the videos, which also include footage from stationary cameras and a cellphone from a bystander, as the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation continues its investigation into the July 5 shooting of Tyrin Johnson.

Johnson, 20, who had been armed, died at the scene from a single gunshot wound, according to investigators. An autopsy report shared by Johnson’s family found that he was shot in the back, contradicting police and National Guard accounts that said he was facing the guard members with a gun when they fired at him.

The footage did not show Johnson's initial encounter with the guard members or them firing at him.

The guard members were part of a federal task force created by President Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democrat-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. Tennessee's Republican Gov. Bill Lee had deployed the Guard to support the effort. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

District Attorney Steve Mulroy said he has not yet decided whether to file charges in connection with the death.

A spokesperson for the Tennessee National Guard did not immediately respond to email and phone messages seeking comment. Ed Yarbrough, an attorney for the two guard members, said they have no comment at this time.

Authorities said the troops were responding with local police to reports of gunshots around 4 a.m. when they began pursuing an armed man fleeing on foot.

Footage from stationary street cameras shows a person in dark clothing firing shots through an empty parking lot at three people walking on a sidewalk. Two Memphis police officers hear gunshots nearby and start walking and then running in that direction, a body camera worn by one of the officers shows. The officers say on their radio that they are pursuing a man who is running and armed with a gun.

The video, which is blurry from the officer’s movement, captures yelling and the sound of a single gunshot, followed by several additional gunshot noises.

A Tennessee National Guard report obtained by The Associated Press via a public records request said two guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who “rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them.” Both guard members fired their service weapons — M17 handguns — and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the report stated.

Police body camera footage shows guard members at the scene shouting “Hands!” and “Turn over!” as they point their handguns at a man lying on his back on the sidewalk.

André C. Wharton, an attorney for Johnson’s family, noted that the videos do not show the moments immediately before the shooting, or the shooting itself.

“This investigation must stay focused on the moment the guardsman fired the fatal shot and whether that action was reasonable,” Wharton said.

Johnson was the father of a young child and was preparing to help lead the family construction business, his grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said.

At least six guard members were on the scene immediately after the shooting, the body camera video shows. One can be seen moving a handgun that is on the ground until a police officer tells him to leave it alone. An officer calls for an ambulance over the radio, and a guard member begins to cut off the man's shirt just before the video ends.

___

Schoenbaum reported from Salt Lake City.

News.title: A surprisingly high number of measles cases are misdiagnosed, study finds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nearly 7 percent of U.S. measles cases are misdiagnosed at least once in the two weeks before a doctor’s diagnosis, an alarming new study has found.

Of 4,651 cases reported between 2001 and 2023, 381 were misdiagnosed, the University of Iowa assessment of private and federal insurance databases revealed.

The findings suggest the “not uncommon” delays could be helping to facilitate transmission of the world’s most contagious virus amid a historic national resurgence - especially in outpatient clinics and hospital waiting rooms.

“Delays occurred most frequently in outpatient settings” at 81 percent, the researchers wrote, noting that the virus can remain airborne for hours.

Some groups are more affected than others, too, including patients who received respiratory antibiotic prescriptions and those who were under 2 years old who may not be able to discuss their symptoms with doctors.

open image in gallery New research reveals hundreds of measles cases have been misdiagnosed since 2001 ( AP )

Doctors who have never seen a case of the measles - previously eliminated in the U.S. in 2000 - may not initially incorporate measles in diagnoses they consider, the researchers also noted.

A growing problem

Measles is continuing to spread in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Florida.

There have been 4,852 confirmed cases nationally this year, according to federal data, though Pennsylvania updated its own case tally to a total of 1,433 on Monday. That’s more than double the 2,289 cases recorded in 2025.

The spread has been tied to outbreaks in under-vaccinated communities, and all of the year’s deaths have been reported in the state of Pennsylvania - and in people who were unvaccinated.

open image in gallery There have been 4,852 confirmed cases nationally this year. Pennsylvania makes up more than 1,400 cases, according to new state data ( AP )

Two doses of the vaccine against measles, which also targets the mumps and rubella viruses, are 97 percent effective against infection, offering lifelong protection.

Without the shots, infections - which are also transmitted from person to person - can lead to life-threatening brain swelling, pneumonia and fever, as well as ear infections and a rash.

Unfortunately, MMR vaccinations have fallen, according to both state and federal data.

Vaccine coverage among kindergarten-aged children decreased in more than half of states between the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 school years, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

“Idaho - where one-quarter of all children are unprotected against measles, mumps and rubella - reported the largest drop: more than 3 percentage points (from 78.5 percent to 75.2 percent). Louisiana and Virginia each saw decreases of about 2 percentage points,” the school said.

News.title: Haley tries to explain her backing of Mike Rogers and suggests he can be another centrist Republican
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

House Representative Haley Stevens defended her decision to cross party lines and back Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan’s crucial U.S. Senate race.

Hours after making a surprise Sunday public appearance with Rogers, the centrist Democrat addressed the fallout from her endorsement on CNN.

“I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart, and that's that,” Stevens said in an interview with Anderson Cooper.

When questioned about her specific reasoning for breaking ranks just two days before Tuesday’s midterm elections, Stevens offered a simple rationale for her last-minute reversal.

“I changed my mind,” she said. “(El-Sayed) said, ‘Hey, I don’t need your endorsement.’ That's fine. Why the anger? Why the frustration?”

open image in gallery Democrat Haley Stevens has defended her choice to support Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan’s US Senate election ( AP )

Stevens insisted that “nothing with me changed,” telling CNN she was now “rock solid” in her choice to support Rogers.

“I still love my party a whole lot,” Stevens said.

The move marks a dramatic shift in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate contests. Michigan’s open seat is currently held by Democrats, and analysts consider a victory here essential for the party’s effort to gain control of the U.S. Senate and counter President Donald Trump in his final two years.

Stevens, who lost a closely fought Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed in August, initially conceded and endorsed him. As recently as Saturday night, she was sticking with her fellow Democrat and denying rumors of a party switch, according to CNN.

However, on Sunday morning, Stevens posted a video to X explaining her decision to endorse Rogers after appearing at an event with the Republican.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in the video. “Who we are as Michiganders is not hate. ... That’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers.”

Stevens noted that although she was initially scheduled to attend an event with El-Sayed on Sunday, he had asked her not to come earlier in the weekend.

“This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn’t want me there,” Stevens said on Sunday.

open image in gallery Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed brushed off the late-turnaround endorsement on Sunday, saying he remained focused on voters ( Reuters )

Democratic leaders quickly condemned the move. Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the U.S. Senate, called the move a “despicable betrayal,” and multiple staffers for Stevens reportedly resigned immediately following the announcement.

Debbie Dingell, who represents Michigan in the House with Stevens, called her colleague’s network interview performance “painful.”

Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens was “not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”

Republicans were quick to welcome the endorsement. Rogers praised Stevens for showing “courage,” and Trump stated that she had been “very brave.”

Stevens and El-Sayed have clashed over foreign policy since the primary. El-Sayed’s strong criticism of Israel divided state Democrats, leading to a recent dispute over a political ad from an outside liberal group that linked U.S. support for Israel to rising prices in the U.S.

Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn the ad. El-Sayed said he had nothing to do with the spot and disagreed with its contents, a response Stevens welcomed.

Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed — who would become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate — has faced sharp attacks from both Rogers and Trump. The president invoked 9/11 and called him a “jihadist” without citing evidence, drawing accusations of Islamophobia and widespread criticism.

Asked about the late endorsement on Sunday, El-Sayed dismissed the political fallout and stated he was focusing on issues affecting Michigan voters.

“At the end of the day, I don’t think about Haley Stevens,” El-Sayed said on Sunday. “None of this matters.”

News.title: Apple posts stronger-than-expected Q4 revenue in first earnings report for new CEO John Ternus
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Apple Inc. posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal fourth quarter, giving new CEO John Ternus an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech giants this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results.

The Cupertino, California-based company earned $30.71 billion, or $2.10 per share, in the July-September period. That's up 12% from $27.47 billion, or $1.85 per share, in the same period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included 5 cents per share from tariff refunds.

Revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion from $102.5 billion.

Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 per share on revenue of $113.4 billion, according to a poll by FactSet.

“Apple’s strong earnings come in the wake of a recent tech sell-off, as investors question the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom driven by Apple’s Big Tech counterparts," said Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne, adding that record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrate the resilience of Apple's business.

While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over massive investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple's “tepid approach" to AI infrastructure spending helps preserve its cash flow — while partnerships with companies like Alphabet could help Apple to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.

Despite the solid quarterly numbers, Apple said its closely watched gross margin, which was 47.9% during the fourth quarter, will be lower in the December quarter — between 45% and 46% — primarily due to higher memory costs and expenses related to its release of Siri AI.

While Apple's stock was flat after the earnings numbers came out, it declined 2.6% to $329.60 during the earnings call. The stock had closed down 1.8% at $338.32 in regular trading.

News.title: A West Point cadet drugged his girlfriend to force an unwanted abortion. Then he went to grad school
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A onetime West Point cadet drugged his then-girlfriend in her barracks room, administered abortion pills to her against her will and caused a miscarriage. Then he went on to study at two Ivy League universities, starting at one of them after he pleaded guilty to assault, according to court records and a new lawsuit.

The man, Caleb Suh, graduated from Cornell University this year and was a public health graduate student at Columbia University as of Oct. 28, when the woman sued in a New York court. His current status at Columbia is unclear.

The suit drew attention to a case that had played out quietly at West Point and in federal court, where Suh pleaded guilty this past June to the March 2022 assault on a cadet in the class below him. She was 19 and in her second year at the U.S. Military Academy, according to prosecutors.

She wanted to have the baby. Suh didn't. Instead, he told the judge, he impersonated the woman to open an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion medications, got Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative, and duped his girlfriend into drinking what she thought was just a prenatal protein shake. After waiting until she fell asleep, he administered the abortion pills orally and vaginally.

According to the woman's lawsuit, Suh left her alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to contact him after she woke and realized she was bleeding. She called 911 and was hospitalized.

Lawyer: ‘She’s suffered a life-changing event’

While she was being treated, Suh went back to the online pharmacy's website to post questions about whether doctors might detect the pills, according to the lawsuit, first reported by The New York Times.

“She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life,” her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, said by phone Monday. Her suit against Suh seeks unspecified damages.

Suh, who is awaiting sentencing, told the court in June that he was “deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused.”

His lawyer, Thomas Kenniff, declined to comment Monday.

The lawsuit, which the woman filed under the alias Jane Doe, comes amid national scrutiny of how universities handle student misconduct complaints. Cornell, in particular, has faced criticism since a former student's lawsuit alleged that several men raped her at a fraternity house in 2024 and that the university did too little after she reported the accusation.

Woman made report to West Point

In Suh's case, it's unclear what discipline, if any, he may have faced at West Point. The woman reported him to the Army Criminal Investigation Division there in May 2022, according to her lawsuit. Assistant U.S. Attorney Marcia Cohen said in court in June that Suh had told a West Point investigator the woman’s miscarriage was accidental, denying that he’d ordered abortion medication.

The military academy didn't provide information Monday on the probe's findings or outcome.

Suh was criminally charged in a Manhattan-based federal court in June, court records show.

What Cornell says it was told

In the meantime, he transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The Ithaca, New York-based university said in a statement Monday that he answered “no” to an application question asking whether he'd been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous educational institution. West Point reported that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return, Cornell said.

Cornell websites indicate he was recognized for his writing in spring 2024 and got involved with the Cornell Center for Health Equity, a research group. He wrote on its site that he was interested in “the intersection of emergency medicine, addiction and public health” and aimed to become a physician.

Suh also briefly worked at Cornell's medical school, leaving several months ago, the university said. He's credited among authors of a medical journal report summarizing a 2025 conference on cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

This September, Suh started a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health in New York City, his lawyer wrote to the judge in Suh's federal case.

Sentencing set to let Suh finish semester

Columbia declined to comment Monday, citing educational privacy laws.

A person familiar with the matter but not authorized to comment about it publicly said Mailman applicants aren’t asked about their criminal records but are asked whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance. Suh’s application never mentioned any disciplinary proceedings, the person said.

At the request of Suh's lawyer, his sentencing recently was put off until January for him to complete his semester at Columbia. He also has been taking a three-month life skills course for people charged with federal crimes, Kenniff told the court in a letter last month.

Prosecutors didn't oppose the postponement. They declined to comment Monday.

The woman's lawyer declined to say whether she ultimately graduated from West Point or what she is doing now.

“We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else,” Kornblith said.

___

Associated Press writer Larry Neumeister contributed.

News.title: Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns
News.content:
Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

News.title: US dairy worker dies from bird flu as outbreak rages in cattle
News.content:
“People at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. Transmission of avian influenza between humans is extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States. Public health officials are continuing to monitor individuals who had close contact with the patient for symptoms,” the health district said in a statement.

Experts say the US bird flu outbreak is not only costing the dairy industry millions of dollars but also raises the risk that the virus could mutate to spread more easily between mammals. They are also concerned that authorities are doing little to check the spread.

Marc Johnson, a virologist at the University of Missouri, told the Telegraph last week that the outbreak in dairy cattle was “completely preventable”.

“Cattle infections last only a few weeks before the animals recover. If infected herds were simply isolated until the outbreak fizzled out, it would stop.

“But cattle keep being moved around, spreading it into new states,” said Dr Johnson, referring to the way the US dairy industry operates, in which cows are routinely transported across state lines, whether to join new herds, for breeding, or to replace animals at large milk-producing operations.

A bird flu outbreak has also been raging on a mink farm in Utah for the last couple of months, according to news outlet ProPublica.

Jonathan Ball, professor of molecular virology at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, said allowing a virus to rage unchecked raises the risk of it mutating.

“Viruses like influenza are constantly exploring new hosts, and more often than not, it burns out. It’s not quite got the right combination of genetic changes to allow it to efficiently infect, efficiently replicate, and then efficiently transmit to the new host. But the longer these steps - adaptive changes, so genetic changes - are happening in these sporadic outbreaks, the more likelihood you’ve got of it mutating. It’s a bit like a one-armed bandit machine - if you keep pulling that handle, eventually you’re going to get three cherries,” he said.

News.title: First ever trial of long-acting injection against malaria to launch in Africa
News.content:
Dr Cristina Donini, executive vice-president of research and development at MMV, said the compound would be “complementary” to existing tools, rather than replacing them.

“The vaccine is doing a fantastic job in infants but if you could add onto that another tool that can cover a broader population with a longer regimen then we would be in a very good position to eliminate the disease,” she said.

Children in malaria-endemic regions are already given prophylactic drugs during the malaria season and studies have shown that these combined with the vaccine are highly effective. However, resistance has developed to these drugs and they have to be given monthly.

The malaria season in Africa varies by region but usually peaks after periods of rainfall. If the season lasts longer than three to four months it’s likely that people would need two injections. However, Dr Donini and her colleagues are working on a second generation LAI which they hope would provide year-long coverage.

Full costs have not yet been worked out but Dr Donini said affordability was an important factor in assessing the LAI’s suitability.

“It’s too early to say whether it will be cheaper than an injection - hopefully, yes. The beauty of it is that if you simplify it and decrease the number of injections needed you decrease the cost,” she said.

LAIs are gaining traction in the fight against infectious diseases - Lenacapavir, now being rolled out after being approved in 2025, provides almost 100% protection against infection from HIV and many believe it could help end the HIV pandemic. There are also LAI candidates in development for the prevention of tuberculosis, treatment and prevention of which usually relies on daily pills being taken over many months.

Lottie Renwick, global campaign director at Malaria No More UK, welcomed the launch of the trial.

“Thanks to sustained investment in malaria science including here in the UK, we are now on the brink of a number of breakthroughs which could turn the tide on the fight against the disease. And the long-acting injectable, specifically, could be a valuable addition to this toolbox as it has the potential to provide sustained protection from a single shot, avoiding the need for repeat doses.

“This phase of the trial also builds on earlier research conducted in the UK, highlighting the importance of the UK’s ongoing role as a malaria science superpower and the value of continued investment in malaria R&D. We look forward to the trial progressing further and eagerly await the results.”

News.title: Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.
