News.title: Tears flow for Antonelli after becoming youngest champion in F1 history
News.content:
Welcome to our coverage for the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix from the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez. Today could be the day for Kimi Antonelli, the day he becomes a Formula One world champion. In fact it is very likely. All he needs to confirm the drivers’ championship is to finish ninth or higher. If George Russell or Lewis Hamilton do not claim victory then he is champion whatever happens. Given his season so far, it is difficult to see the title fight going to Brazil next week.

What chance of a decent race here today? The first few laps are often entertaining as the pack bunches up and there are plenty of chances to overtake early on. Generally the top four teams have been close together (last week in Austin excluded) and it is possible to overtake here, though it is not exactly easy.

Qualifying yesterday as an intriguing and close session. Hamilton secured his first grand prix pole for Ferrari, by just 0.009sec from the Mercedes of George Russell, with Charles Leclerc of Ferrari a little behind him in third. Then came Max Verstappen, Antonelli, Norris, Hadjar and Lindblad. Liam Lawson was disqualified on a technicality.

Ferrari have been an up-and-down team this season but have been strong without really delivering on it fully in the last few rounds. Could they secure a third victory of the season today? They do not really need to worry about losing second in the constructors to Red Bull or McLaren and Mercedes are too far out of reach in any case.

In any case, the biggest story is likely to be Antonelli’s coronation in Mexico. Hamilton has won titles here before for Mercedes, will the Italian give the Silver Arrows another fiesta in Mexico City? The race starts at 8pm GMT and we will be here for all the build-up, live updates and reaction from it.

News.title: Lewis Hamilton becomes oldest driver to claim pole position in 44 years
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for qualifying for the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix from the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in Mexico City, obviously. The big story this weekend is that Jimi Antonelli is almost certain to become the youngest world champion in Formula One history. To guarantee it he needs just two points, but if George Russell or Lewis Hamilton fail to win here then the title is his whatever he does. It has been a superb, strong and consistent season from the man who began the year as a teenager. He has not quite been faultless, but he has not been far away.

There are other stories floating around the paddock, too. Notably, Esteban Ocon has been dropped by Haas today for final practice, qualifying and the race, to be replaced by reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa for the weekend. Whether Ocon will continue in any other races has yet to be confirmed but you have to say that it seems extremely unlikely. More on that later.

Another line is the ongoing tension between Liam Lawson and Max Verstappen after their crash in FP2 yesterday. It was certainly a strange one in which neither driver backed down, which resulted in contact, debris being strewn across the track and a red flag. Both drivers seemed unrepentant, though admitted it was clumsy. Lawson and Verstappen each receive a one-place grid penalty for the incident, which feels about right given how silly and unnecessary it all was.

But what about the competitive order on track? Since the summer break, and a little before in fairness, things have been unpredictable at the top. Mercedes have still, on average, been the best team but Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren have all had their moments.

What happened in final practice? It was Lando Norris who topped the timesheets by just 0.001sec ahead of Mercedes’ Antonelli. Charles Leclerc was a further tenth or so back for Ferrari followed by Oscar Piastri in the other McLaren, who was 0.195sec off his team-mate’s pace. Then came Verstappen, Hamilton, Russell, Isack Hadjar, Lawson and Arvid Lindblad. All drivers were within 0.6sec off Norris, which promises a close qualifying session. Let’s hope we get it.

News.title: Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points
News.content:
Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

News.title: Alex Mitchell injury blow for England but Northampton dig deep to win
News.content:
England were dealt a fresh blow ahead of their Nations Championship opener with Australia after scrum-half Alex Mitchell was forced off early in Northampton’s victory over Gloucester.

Mitchell left the field gingerly 20 minutes into the action after picking up a suspected hamstring injury following an innocuous coming-together with Gloucester winger Will Joseph.

The Saints scrum-half has suffered a series of hamstring issues this year – this would be a fourth time he has picked up a problem – and he looked visibly disappointed as he limped off.

He suffered a left leg hamstring tear during England’s Six Nations defeat to Ireland which left him sidelined for two months and, in a cruel twist of fate, sustained another on his right leg during an England three-day training camp in Bagshot last May. He suffered the injury for a third time in England’s 73-8 rout of Fiji in July.

With Mitchell’s club-mate, Archie McParland, nursing an unspecified knock that forced him to miss Saints’ high-stakes clash with Gloucester, Jack van Poortvliet is likely to start at nine against the Wallabies next Sunday. McParland was the third-choice scrum-half in England’s Nations Championship squad, but Steve Borthwick may be forced to look elsewhere if Mitchell’s prognosis is serious.

Grealish’s absence from the squad comes after he missed the club’s League Cup clash with the Toon on Thursday.

David Moyes had banished the star from the squad following a breach of discipline.

It came after Grealish spent two boozy nights in pubs and karaoke bars.

As a result, Everton took disciplinary measures due to his unauthorised absence from training.

The club stated the reason he was dropped for the first game was due to a “breach of club discipline”.

Grealish had also missed Everton’s 2-0 defeat to Arsenal the weekend before but that absence was explained as illness.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The Sun exclusively revealed how Grealish had spent two nights boozing in London and Cheshire days before he was axed.

He first hit a London karaoke bar until late on Monday night before following that up by joining pals for a late-night session at The Mucky Pup pub in the North West.

A visit to a ten-pin bowling alley in Altrincham near his £6million pad was also included on his AWOL adventure on October 19 and 20, which had all started when he attended the Pride of Britain Awards at London’s Grosvenor House hotel.

He spent last season on loan at Everton and had impressed before an injury in January curtailed his season.

The blow ruled out any chance that the former Aston Villa ace had of playing at the World Cup in the summer under Thomas Tuchel.



Grealish rejoined Everton on loan for the current season on September 1.

He has so far played five games in the Premier League and not scored or assisted a single goal.

Sports.title: Carragher: Boring Newcastle face a tough season ahead
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher described Newcastle as flat and boring following their defeat to Everton on Monday Night Football and reckons Matthias Jaissle's side faces a difficult season.

Thierno Barry's second-half goal earned Everton a 1-0 win at St James' Park and their first away victory in the Premier League this season, as Newcastle were booed off at half-time and full-time following their fourth defeat in five games across all competitions.

Newcastle have slipped to 13th and are now four points above the bottom three, with a trip to lowly Fulham to come on Saturday.

"I think it is going to be a tough season for them," said Sky Sports' Carragher. "I felt tonight [Monday] was actually more important for Newcastle than the cup game [Carabao Cup loss at Everton last week], and it was the other way round for Everton, who are desperate for a trophy.

"But I fear a little bit for Newcastle, I think it could be a long, tough season."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Premier League match between Newcastle and Everton.

Jaissle was appointed in August, replacing Eddie Howe, and made a promising start by earning entertaining draws against Liverpool and Bournemouth, with a win at Tottenham sandwiched in between, but that has quickly faded as their home form has continued to be an issue.

No Premier League side has lost more home games in 2026 than Newcastle (7) and they have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their last 14 games at St James' Park, the longest run in their league history.

Carragher added: "Watching them of late, especially at home, it feels flat and a little bit boring, and that was one thing I didn't think I'd ever be describing Jaissle's Newcastle as.

"You think of the system he's come from, the Red Bull model, how they like to play. At times, those types of teams and managers can leave themselves open at the back, but it's front-footed, it's aggressive, it's getting the crowd involved, and we've just never seen any of that at all tonight. I'm a little bit flummoxed watching it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Did Thierno Barry foul Fabian Schar in the build-up before the game's only goal?

"I was really impressed with him, how he came across. They were very impressive at Spurs, a great result for them early on, and the results in the main have been okay, but I think there's always been a worry about the performances and their underlying numbers, even early on.

"I watched Fulham at Villa over the weekend, they were really good, and that'll be a tough game, and you look at some of the games they've got coming.

"I think it's going to be a tough season for Newcastle. They've got a lot of young players, they've got a young manager in there. The crowd are expecting a lot more."

Jaissle: Our plan didn't work - I understand boos

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Newcastle United boss Matthias Jaissle understands the fans’ frustrations after boos were heard at half-time and full-time, and takes responsibility for his side’s poor performance.

Jaissle opted for a different approach from their defeat against Everton four days earlier, but his tactical changes failed to pay off, with Newcastle not managing a shot on target until the 85th minute.

"Unfortunately we couldn't deliver our style of play across the whole 90 minutes," Jaissle told Sky Sports.

"That's something we are frustrated about. We had a different approach. It looked so good during the week, I have to say the lads were committed to what we were doing and today we can just look back and wonder why we couldn't bring it on the pitch. If you can't deliver when it counts, you don't deserve to win.

"We were not brave enough in possession. Too many long balls. We did not use our double six in possession where I think we were quite good against Everton a couple days ago. Then it was more of a wide game, back and forth, collecting second balls. That's something that we wanted to avoid to be more dominant.

"It feels at the moment that there's not too much confidence. Not only with the young lads, but also with the more experienced ones. We have to overcome that as a unit. It is expected when you are in transition. Only together we can come out of it.

"After a performance like that, I can understand that [fans booing]. That's a reality and I am responsible for that. We need to work again and again on the things we need to improve. After today, that's a lot."

Sports.title: Harmer urges England to recall Leach - and stop 'isolating' spinners
Sports.content:
South Africa's Simon Harmer said England should take Jack Leach on the Test tour of his homeland this winter as he suggested a lack of spin coaches in county cricket is leaving slow bowlers "isolated".

Since Ben Stokes' international retirement in June, England have rejigged the balance of their side with Dan Lawrence's part-time off-spin now supporting four fast bowlers - a policy they could maintain when they play South Africa in three Tests from December 17.

However, Proteas frontline off-spinner Harmer, a county-cricket stalwart with Essex, bagged 14 wickets in three games in the just-completed 2-1 series win at home to Australia, including a 10-wicket match haul in the deciding Test at Cape Town.

Image: Jack Leach has not played for his country since the tour of Pakistan in October 2024

Somerset left-arm spinner Leach last played for England two years ago - he does not have a central contract - and national selector Marcus North recently told the Wisden Cricket Weekly podcast that the team were moving in a "different direction."

Harmer, though, told the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast Leach, who has 142 wickets in 39 Tests to date an an average of 34.07, "would be his guy" as England prepare to tackle South Africa in Johannesburg, Centurion and Cape Town, live on Sky Sports.

"If you are going to play a spinner at those venues, you need, in the first innings, somebody who can hold an end so that your seamers can rotate, attack and bowl four overs of aggressive, fast bowling.

Image: Leach has taken 142 wickets in 39 Tests at an average of 34.07 for England

"If you don't have that control, it makes it very difficult to find 90 overs in a day and how that stacks up with your seamers. So, for me, Leach is still the guy for England.

"I know Marcus North was on a podcast saying that they're moving away from him, but I just don't understand [that].

"I'm sure the chats are, 'well, he doesn't bowl teams out on day five', but the amount of control that he gives you, I just think at the venues that South Africa will be hosting England, if you are going to take a spinner, he is probably your guy."

'England need to be proactive improving spin bowling'

Harmer also namechecked Shoaib Bashir - who is on an England central contract - Yorkshire's Dom Bess and Sussex's Jack Carson as players good enough for international cricket, but says they need more guidance at domestic level.

England recently appointed former Glamorgan coach and ex-Yorkshire spinner Richard Dawson as elite national spin bowling lead in an attempt to boost that element of the game.

Image: Richard Dawson was recently appointed England's elite national spin bowling lead

Harmer said: "I worked with [former Leicestershire spinner] Carl Crowe for the first time at the SA20 with Durban's Super Giants and he is an absolute genius when it comes to spin bowling. He understands the game and the biomechanics of spin bowling.

"How he isn't being utilised more within the county system, I don't understand.

"It's not a lack of resources, it's just a lack of want to get [spin] structures into the county game.

"I think as a result of that, a lot of spinners feel isolated, feel alone, like they don't have the means in order for them to take their game to the next level.

"I think it's something that needs to be looked at. How are guys being developed when they are not with the England national team?

"You've got [England assistant coach] Jeetan Patel working with the spinners there, but I haven't seen him working with spinners at a county game or coming to watch.

"What happens is that England will wait until they don't have any spinners and then they will start to try and problem solve instead of being proactive. There are plenty of good spinners in England but they just don't have the tools necessary to upskill."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from day five of the series-deciding third Test as Simon Harmer's wickets helped South Africa beat Australia and go top of the rankings.

Sky Sports Cricket pundit Michael Atherton said after listening to Harmer's comments about spin on the podcast: "I agree with him.

"When I was bowling leg-spin as a very young first-class cricketer, the absence of knowledge was a big thing, particularly around leg-spin.

"When I went on my first Ashes tour to Australia, I was taken speaking to people who know about leg-spin intimately for the first time, whereas in England it was all a bit of a mystery.

There is a sense of that still."

Sports.title: Russell posts statement to 'speak from the heart'
Sports.content:
George Russell has posted a statement on social media to "speak from the heart" after his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli secured the F1 Drivers' Championship on Sunday.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff revealed Russell was "distraught" in Mexico and went home after congratulating Antonelli on becoming world champion.

The FIA gave Mercedes a €5,000 (£4,173) fine as Russell missed his mandatory media duties post-race, but the British driver has made his own first public comments on Monday.

"Now feels like a pretty suitable moment to speak from the heart," he wrote on Instagram.

"This season started off exactly how I had hoped but it very quickly unravelled with tough luck and poor performances.

"It's been the first proper season of my career where I've had more bad days than good. Has it been tough to deal with? Yes, very. Has it been tough to pick myself up week in, week out? Yes, very. Confusion at times? Often. All I know is that I've given it my all and 2026 was not meant to be my year."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell said last week he wants to be more consistent as the Mercedes driver turns his attention to challenging for the world title next year

Russell began the season as the clear title favourite but has been comprehensively outperformed by Antonelli, who became F1's youngest ever world champion at the age of 20, with four rounds remaining.

Antonelli has won nine races compared to Russell's three and the latter has dropped to fourth in the Drivers' Championship after a power unit issue left him with sub-optimal power on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Russell continued: "I want to sincerely congratulate Kimi on what has been an absolutely incredible season. You truly deserve the Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player How Kimi Antonelli's championship-winning moment sounded with Italian commentary

"Thank you to the team for producing the best car and power unit this season; it's been inspiring to see everyone coming together over four tough years to bring Mercedes back to the top.

"Now, all I can promise is that for the rest of this season, and into the next one, I will be giving my absolute all to rediscover the performance I have been capable of producing for the majority of my career and fingers crossed a little bit of luck returns.

"Thanks for all the support."

Sports.title: Australia's Maxwell announces retirement from international cricket
Sports.content:
Australia all-rounder Glenn Maxwell has announced his retirement from international cricket but will continue to play T20 for Melbourne Stars in the Big Bash League.

The 38-year-old's final appearance for his country came against Oman in the T20 World Cup earlier this year, when he recorded figures of 2-13 from three overs with his off-spin and was not required to bat.

Maxwell scored five T20 international hundreds, a record he shares with India's Rohit Sharma, while he is one of only five Australian men, alongside Shane Watson, David Warner, Josh Inglis and Mitchell Marsh, to score a ton in all three international formats.

Image: Maxwell scored the fastest 50-over World Cup century back in 2023, from 40 balls

Speaking on the Final Word podcast, Maxwell said: "I suppose [I had] a small hope that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the MCG. But I can completely understand the direction they're going with this [T20] squad.

"There's going to be a lot of change over the next 12 to 24 months with the Olympics coming up [in 2028], and they've got to make sure they get their eyeballs on a few young guys coming through, making sure they're getting exposed to international pressure."

Maxwell - who said he had considered trying to get ready for Australia's T20 series at home to England in late November, which includes a match in Melbourne - quit one-day international cricket in June of last year, the format in which he put in his most memorable performance during the 2023 World Cup.

He plundered a match-winning 201 not out from 128 balls against Afghanistan while battling injury as Australia recovered from 91-7 to reach a target of 292.

Maxwell's 128-ball double hundred was the-then second-fastest in all ODIs, behind India star Ishan Kishan's 126-ball effort versus Bangladesh in 2022, but is now fourth.

England white-ball captain Harry Brook smoked the quickest ODI double ton from 114 balls against Sri Lanka in October, after India's Shubman Gill had done so from 117 deliveries versus West Indies less than a month earlier.

Image: Maxwell will continue to play T20 cricket for Melbourne Stars in the Big Bash League

Maxwell's heroics against Afghanistan three years ago came in a tournament in which he also hit the fastest 50-over World Cup century, from 40 deliveries against the Netherlands.

The right-hander won the 2023 and 2015 50-over World Cups with Australia, while he also hit the winning runs as his nation claimed the T20 World Cup title in 2021.

Across 286 international matches (149 ODIs, 130 T20Is and seven Tests), Maxwell scored over 7,000 runs and took 136 wickets.

Sports.title: Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache
Sports.content:
Jack Grealish will do well to get back into the Everton starting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.

Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against 10 men at St James’ Park after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.

And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.

Moyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game following a breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”

Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”

Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”

Newcastle fans had made their feelings about the 3-1 Carabao Cup defeat away to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.

Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.

View image in fullscreen Matthias Jaissle struggles to get his message across to his Newcastle players. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

Frustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.

Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.

Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.

Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Jacob Ramsey sees red in stoppage time after coming on as a substitute for Newcastle. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

By now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.

Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.

Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.

The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.

“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.

Sports.title: Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family
Sports.content:
Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.

Exciting, right?

Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.

As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the first Superclásico without away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press area Moores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.

View image in fullscreen Fans of Boca cheer from beneath their umbrellas. Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images

Over the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known as La Doce leads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.

Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.

The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in by La Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.

Barritta was the infamous leader of La Doce decades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with two River Plate fans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.

My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.

View image in fullscreen River Plate fans clash with riot police outside the Monumental prior the final of the Copa Libertadores against Boca Juniors in 2018. The match was rescheduled after the bus carrying Boca players was attacked, injuring several players. Photograph: Sebastian Pani/AP

Death at the Superclásico was not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm of La Doce in 1981, by which time the rupture was total.

In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle the Superclásico might be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of the Superclásico has remained, if it hadn’t been sucked out already.

Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.

“I’ve seen better Superclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.

View image in fullscreen Leonel Flores of Boca celebrates with teammates following the team’s victory in the Superclásico. Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images

That must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).

I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.

Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch the Superclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.

View image in fullscreen River Plate’s Gonzalo Montiel leaves the pitch under police protection against Boca. Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty Images

Maybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all this Superclásico nonsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”

Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to a Superclásico with my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.

Sports.title: Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.

Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.

If there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. In Arsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.

They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.

It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficient to get them past Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.

There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.

But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.

Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.

Sunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.

Sports.title: Stumbling block: Wirtz's and Liverpool’s costly struggles against tight defences | Andrew Beasley
Sports.content:
Liverpool did not have a shot on target in their 1-0 defeat by Arsenal on Sunday, according to Opta, the first time they have drawn this type of blank in a Premier League game at Anfield since records began in 2003-04. They did not find the target in a goalless draw at the Emirates Stadium this year either, though in both games they struck the woodwork. The margins tend to be fine when recording statistical outliers.

If Alexis Mac Allister’s floated ball from distance into David Raya’s waiting arms had actually counted as a shot, would Andoni Iraola’s side have delivered a markedly better attacking performance? Far more concerning for the Spaniard will be that his team had 52 touches in the Arsenal penalty area (which is good) to create only one Opta‑defined big chance (which is bad). The Premier League average this season is five times more efficient; 10.3 box touches per big chance.

Credit to Arsenal for restricting the quality of Liverpool’s chances despite them getting repeatedly within range of their goal. Most teams have been able to do this, though. While 12 teams have had fewer touches in opposition penalty boxes than Liverpool, only Coventry with 11 have generated fewer big chances this season than Liverpool’s 12. Everton’s Thierno Barry alone has had 15, while Manchester City’s Erling Haaland has also had more than Liverpool with 14.

Liverpool have not had this issue in Europe. They have 12 big chances in the Champions League in just three games. As two of their opponents, Lask and Villarreal, are rated by Opta as being of lower standard than any side in the Premier League, this is little surprise. The relatively low stakes of a given match in the league- phase of the Champions League encourages those matches to be more open, too.

This has not been the case in the 2026-27 Premier League for Liverpool, who have spent more time building up against low defensive blocks than any other team. This is, in part, a problem of their own making as they have conceded first in five of their eight matches. Only against Ipswich and Brighton have they held two‑goal leads, meaning opponents have rarely had compelling need to significantly loosen their defensive grip.

In his first Liverpool press conference, head coach Iraola spoke of embracing the challenge set by deep-lying defences. “I prefer to face low blocks in terms of: ‘OK, we will be in control of the game, probably we will concede less chances, we will spend a lot of time in the opposition half and those are the scenarios that we have to find,’” he said. Only four teams have had more touches in the opposition half or attempted more final‑third passes than Liverpool this season, but such dominance has not led to higher value chances.

This is where Florian Wirtz should be making an impression. He has the ability to unpick the tightest of backlines. Yet he has not created a big chance in the league this season. If his low total of five in his debut campaign was understandable with the problems Liverpool faced on-and-off the pitch, he trailed distantly behind Dominik Szoboszlai (14), Mohamed Salah (11) and Cody Gakpo (10). Wirtz is frequently involved in dangerous areas, as his ranking of ninth in the division for final-third passes completed will attest. His contributions have been far more geared towards ball retention and circulation rather than incision, however.

Iraola will want Liverpool to make more productive use of their high press. Most of their big chances in the league have come via corners or open-play crosses. Bradley Barcola has had moments; he recovered possession to go clean through on goal at Brentford, before pouncing on an opposition mistake to assist Alexander Isak against Brighton. But Liverpool have produced shots from only 16.7% of their ball recoveries in the final 40 yards of the pitch, which is below average (18.4%) and the seventh-worst rate in the Premier League. Improvement here will help significantly.

Big chances account for 18.1% of shots in the Premier League this season but 59.5% of the goals. They are vitally important. Liverpool’s ambitions for Iraola’s first campaign will be severely limited unless they start fashioning them far more easily.

Sports.title: Fifa to share documents on World Cup sell-off plans with council members
Sports.content:
Fifa will grant its council members access to documents regarding the doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme but has not responded directly to more than 50 questions from Uefa about its governance and recent scandals.

In a letter sent to the Fifa Council by Mattias Grafström, the governing body’s secretary general, members were told material relating to FFE will be released for them to view in person at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich. They will be allowed only to view the documents, of which the exact nature and scope are unclear, under strict confidentiality protocols. A deadline of 16 November has been set to apply for such visits; eyebrows may be raised in some quarters about the fact this is two days before candidates for the Fifa election next year are required to declare their hand.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Uefa had written to Grafström on 19 October giving Fifa a fortnight to answer a series of questions about FFE, the Folarin Balogun affair, the Fifa peace prize, the organisation’s relations with Donald Trump and other major decisions that have caused controversy in the past 12 months. It had asked for all documents regarding FFE to be made accessible, saying refusal to comply with any of its demands should be “justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon”.

The deadline imposed by Uefa expired on Monday night, although Fifa Council members are understood to have been told a response is being worked upon and will be shared with them. Fifa’s stance is that Uefa’s questions, posed after Gianni Infantino told delegates at the Fifa Council meeting last month to submit questions in writing before they next convened in December, were too substantial in number for the two-week turnaround.

It remains to be seen whether those Fifa Council members who travel for the document inspection will depart with the answers they require. In August Uefa made an application to four courts in the US for the release of documents pertaining to FFE, with a view to lodging a criminal complaint in Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement. Preliminary rulings are yet to be handed down and the amount of information available to view may be affected. Fifa has accused Uefa of “harassment” and “misinformation” and denied wrongdoing by Infantino.

As reported last week Uefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate who could stand against Infantino in March, with movement possible early this month.

Sports.title: Carrick not concerned about Martínez’s attitude as United prepare for Roma visit
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has insisted he is not concerned about Lisandro Martínez’s attitude despite the defender’s recent outburst aimed at the Manchester United hierarchy which was then followed by his reckless sending off in the defeat against Chelsea at the weekend.

Martínez, who was fined for his comments about United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, is expected to keep his place for the visit of Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday as United aim to end their worst run in 38 years, having failed to win any of their past nine matches.

“I’ve got no concerns about commitment at all,” Carrick said of the Argentina World Cup winner. “Things happen in football, sometimes you do things, sometimes you make a decision, sometimes you make mistakes, sometimes it goes well for you, but the commitment is not an issue.”

Away defeats against Atlético Madrid and Como have left United’s 21st in the Champions League league phase, with it felt that Carrick needs a positive result against Roma, as well as against Aston Villa in the Premier League on Sunday, to keep his job. Martínez is suspended for the visit of Unai Emery’s men following his red card at Stamford Bridge.

“I can’t look into the future, I don’t know what’s going to happen,” Carrick insisted. “That doesn’t change the way I feel, that’s how we’re preparing for the game tomorrow and I’m really looking forward to the game.

“You might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had and what’s going on, but I genuinely can’t wait for the game tomorrow and that’s all I’m focused on. Whatever happens is going to happen after that, in whatever direction it goes in.”

United’s most recent home game was the 3-0 defeat against Bournemouth, which concluded with the players being booed by the Stretford End. “In these tough times you can’t expect the fans 100,000% of the time to be happy and cheering when we’re not putting out results,” Kobbie Mainoo said. “We owe it to them to put the results out there for them to cheer again.

“I feel like our way to repay that [the manager’s support] is to also be behind the manager on the pitch and off it and fight for us and fight for us as a team.”

Carrick will be without Luke Shaw, Marcus Rashford and Benjamin Sesko for the visit of Roma, while Patrick Dorgu has returned to training but is not fit enough to take part.

Sports.title: Dazn secures exclusive deal on global streaming rights for 2029 Club World Cup
Sports.content:
Dazn has secured an exclusive option for global streaming rights for the next men’s Club World Cup in 2029 in a development that deepens its partnership with Fifa.

The Saudi Arabia-backed ­streaming company came to Fifa’s aid before the inaugural 32-team Club World Cup in the US last year by agreeing to pay $1bn (£745m) for global rights for the tournament after many ­linear broadcasters and other streamers had declined to bid.

Apple TV had held talks with Fifa over a global streaming deal for 2025, but withdrew owing to a disagreement over valuation, and Fifa’s subsequent attempt to sell the rights on a regional basis foundered.

Dazn’s surprise late bid, facilitated by the purchase of a 10% stake in the company by Saudi’s Surj Sports Investment group, in effect bankrolled Fifa’s $1bn prize fund, with the winners, Chelsea, taking home about $114m (£85m).

Dazn is a loss-making business despite having more than 300 ­million registered users, with its 2025 accounts showing its operating losses increased from $772.9m to $939.8m over the previous 12 months, but appears content to continue to invest heavily in rights.

Quick Guide How do I 

The value of its Club World Cup rights deal, or the point at which the option must be triggered, is not known but will give Fifa breathing space before the second edition of its expanded competition that has been designed as a major money ­spinner but remains fraught with political problems.

Planning for the 2029 tournament has proved difficult, with no decisions made on venues, format or size despite longstanding discussions between Fifa and the clubs about expanding to 48 teams, first reported by the Guardian two years ago.

Club World Cup progress has been a casualty of the fallout from Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off proposal, which led the lobby group European Football Clubs to threaten to withdraw its support. In a letter to Fifa obtained by the Guardian, EFC also expressed “serious concern and disappointment” at the delays in paying $250m in solidarity money owed to clubs from 2025 more than a year after the first competition had concluded.

Relations between EFC and Fifa are understood to have improved since the withdrawal of Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise plan, but they have yet to agree the finer details of a proposed joint venture to manage the Club World Cup’s commercial operations, which may be put on hold until after the Fifa presidential election in March.
