World.title: Kawambwa residents urged to improve on waste management
World.content:
Kawambwa Town Council Secretary, George Biemba has urged residents to improve waste management practices ahead of the rainy season to prevent environmental pollution and the spread of waterborne diseases.

Mr Biemba noted that proper waste disposal is important in maintaining a clean and healthy environment, especially during the rainy season when poor sanitation could increase the risk of disease outbreaks.

He said this in a press release issued to the media by Kawambwa Town Council Public Relations Officer, Mwango Kapalaula,

Mr Biemba said poorly managed waste could block drainage systems and contaminate water sources, increasing the risk of diseases such as Cholera and Diarrhea.

He has since urged residents to avoid dumping garbage on roadsides, in drainage channels and in open spaces.

And Ms Kapalaula has also encouraged households to ensure that waste is properly collected, stored and disposed of at selected disposal points.

She said poor waste management could create breeding grounds for disease causing organisms and pests, posing a public health risk to communities.

She said keeping Kawambwa clean is a shared responsibility that requires the active participation of every resident.

World.title: A 10 year old boy drowns in Solwezi River
World.content:
A 10 year old boy from the Kyawama area has drowned in Solwezi River after he went swimming with his friends.

Northwestern Province Police Commanding officer, Brighton Siwale confirmed the incident in a statement to the media in Solwezi today identifying the deceased as Ignitious Mwendelema aged 10.

Mr Siwale said the incident occurred on November 1, 2026 at around 17:00 hours at Kafwaya Bridge in Kimasala area of Solwezi District.

He said the incident was reported on November 1, 2026 at 18:30 hours by the boy’s father, Muluku Mwendelema, aged 40 of Kimasala area that his son, Ignitious aged 10 of the same residence drowned in Solwezi River and that his body was still missing despite concerted efforts by the fire brigade team, the Police and members of the general public that conducted the search.

He said the brief facts of the matter are that Ignitious Mwendelema, now believed to be dead, was last seen on November 1, 2026 at around 15:00 hours in the company of his friends going to the river to swim.

Mr Siwale said a few hours later, around 17:00 hours, he was reported missing by his friends who called his parents and the matter was officially reported to the Police.

“Upon receipt of the report, the Police officers called in the fire brigade emergency response team and moved to the scene at Kafwaya bridge,” he said.

He said a search was conducted on the river until it was dark but could not find the body.

“The mission was called off for safety reasons since it was dark. However, this morning, a search continued, and the body was retrieved from the river, and physical inspection by officers reviewed no injuries, hence no foul play suspected,” he said.

Mr Siwale said the body has since been deposited into Solwezi General Hospital Mortuary awaiting postmortem examination and burial.

In a related development another 34 year old man of Kasempa District of Northwestern Province has drowned in Lwamadamba stream.

North-Western Province commanding officer, Brighton Siwale confirmed the incident to ZANIS in a statement in Solwezi district today and identified the deceased as Mulyata Lumuna of Lwamadamba area.

Mr Siwale said the incident happened between 28th October, 2026 at 10:00 hours and October 1st 2026 at 08:50 hours in the Lwamandamba area situated four kilometers away from Kasempa Police Station.

He said the matter was reported on 1st October, 2026 at 09:20 hours at Kasempa police station by Timothy Mushili aged 52, a village headman of Lwamandamba that his nephew Mulyanta Lumuna aged 34 drowned in the nearby stream and his body was discovered floating in Lwamandamba stream.

Mr Siwale said the brief facts of the matter are that the deceased was last seen on 28th October, 2026 at 10:00 hours, and his body was discovered floating in a stream running down the village area.

“His disappearance was not reported to the Police by the relatives as he had a habitual tendency of going out to stay with friends for a few days before returning back home,” he said.

Mr Siwale said after disappearing from the village, villagers who were at the stream came across his body floating in the stream and informed others who identified it as that of Mulyanta Lumuna.

He added that it was at that point that the deceased’s uncle took up the responsibility and made the report to the Police.

“Upon receipt of the report, the officers visited the scene where they confirmed the incident, and the body was retrieved from the water with the help of the family and neighbors. Further, the officers conducted a physical inspection, and no visible marks of injuries were found,” Mr Siwale said.

He said police suspect no foul play and that the body was deposited into Mukinge Mission Hospital mortuary awaiting postmortem examination and burial.

World.title: Stakeholders laud ZRA’s Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme
World.content:
Kabwe Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) president, Kapai Banda has commended the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) for supporting the growth of the informal sector through provision of an amnesty facility to taxpayers.

Mr Banda said in an interview with the media that the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme, which is being implemented by ZRA across the country, has provided relief to eligible taxpayers in Central Province.

The scheme allows businesses and individuals to disclose previously declared liabilities and settle principal tax obligations with relief from qualifying penalties and interests.

“As KCCI, we are happy with the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme that has been offered to the business community by ZRA. It is a good tax relief to the business community,” he said.

ZANIS reports that Mr Banda said the initiative has motivated eligible taxpayers to regularise their tax affairs on favorable terms to avoid penalties.

He said the organisation will always support initiatives aimed at supporting the growth of the informal sector.

Mr Banda said the business community in Kabwe will continue supporting such government initiatives by fulfilling their tax obligations as a way of contributing to the country’s economic development.

He called for fair, transparent and collaborative tax administration ahead of this Friday’s National Budget presentation by Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane.

Mr Banda urged eligible taxpayers to take advantage of the amnesty to settle their tax obligations to avoid penalties.

Under the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme, taxpayers who disclose undeclared liabilities and settle their principal tax obligation receive a proportionate waiver of qualifying penalties and interest of up to100 percent.

ZRA is targeting to raise K185 million this year.

World.title: Governance Expert condemns dictatorship remarks by Khama
World.content:
Governance Expert and Human Rights Advocate, Wesley Miyanda, has condemned remarks attributed to the former Botswana President Ian Khama, that are describing the current democratic elected government under President Hakainde Hichilema as the newest African state under dictatorship.

Mr Miyanda says the remarks are not only unfortunate and enormously misplaced, but a threat to political, social and economic ties the two countries share from time immemorial.

In a statement made available to the media ,Mr Miyanda said Zambia stands out as the only African country which has maintained its status as a democratic and peaceful nation with a clean record of conducting credible, peaceful, free and fair elections which have seen peaceful transition of power from one government to the other without any bloodshed.

“Unlike other African countries that have largely continued suffering at the hands of either personalists, military, one-party or totalitarian dictatorships, the European Union rated Zambia as a democratic and peaceful nation in the just ended August 2026 general election”, he explained.

He added that anything that concerns about Zambia’s democratic governance should be addressed through constitutional and constructive engagement and established diplomatic channels by all stakeholders within the country, foreign diplomats and other African leaders.

ZANIS reports that Mr Miyanda further explained that Zambia remains a constitutional, multiparty democracy with full autonomy of all institutions of governance such as legislature, judiciary, electoral Commission of Zambia, Human Rights Commission, and the executive.

“As an African Icon, and especially as former President under a democratically elected Government of Botswana, Dr Ian Khama is fully entitled to express his views on democracy, but serious allegations such as these against a democratically elected Head of State should be supported by credible evidence”, he emphasised.

He said Zambia would not have secured a seat on the United Nations Human Rights Council if the country’s democratic status was questionable or condemned by the Human Rights Council.

Mr Miyanda said the recent securing of a seat is a milestone which stands unchallenged, especially after amassing 171 votes out of the total votes of 188 in the UN General Assembly.

He said Zambia has demonstrated to other countries in Africa and at a global level that the country still believes in democratic governance as a beacon of peace 62 years after liberation from colonial masters in 1964.

World.title: President Hichilema, AFC confer on Lobito corridor project
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has reaffirmed government’s commitment to the Lobito corridor project, describing it as a strategic investment that will strengthen regional trade, stimulate industrialisation and unlock economic opportunities across the three countries.

Mr Hichilema says the project was critical to Zambia’s economic transformation agenda and aligned with the government’s ambition to grow the economy through increased production, value addition and regional economic integration.

Speaking at State House in Lusaka today when he received a delegation from the African Finance Corporation (AFC), which is providing leadership on the corridor project, Mr Hichilema said the initiative would also strengthen trade among African countries.

He said Africa currently conducts limited trade within the continent and that the corridor would help address the challenge by improving connectivity and facilitating the movement of goods between countries.

“This project is extremely important to us in Zambia as it fits into the global and Grow Zambia Agenda,” Mr Hichilema said.

He pointed out that the initiative was equally important to Angola and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), adding that its benefits would extend beyond the three participating countries to the wider African continent.

Mr Hichilema said the corridor would improve the ability of African countries to conduct business with one another and contribute to the realisation of the continent’s economic integration aspirations.

He cited the need to connect food-producing areas with markets where demand existed, saying the project would improve the movement of agricultural produce and other goods.

The President further stressed that the corridor should not be viewed merely as a railway line but as a broader economic development initiative involving infrastructure, industries, primary production and processing.

Meanwhile, African Finance Corporation Chief Executive Officer, Samaila Zubainu, said the corporation and the Zambian government were aligned on the need to deliver the project.

Mr Zubainu said discussions with President Hichilema had addressed key issues surrounding the initiative and expressed confidence that the two sides would work together to ensure its delivery.

“We have covered most areas. We are aligned that we will deliver this project together,” Mr Zubainu said.

World.title: Govt. welcomes Moody’s Ratings’ to upgrade Zambia’s independent rating from Caa2 to Caa1
World.content:
The Ministry of Finance and National Planning has welcomed Moody’s Ratings’ decision to upgrade Zambia’s sovereign rating from Caa2 to Caa1, noting that it comes after Zambia reached a staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund for a proposed 36-month Extended Credit Facility arrangement worth US$1.472 billion.

Moody’s rating from Caa2 to Caa1 indicates a significant improvement in the creditworthiness of an obligation, reflecting substantial and sustained improvements in the obligation’s credit trajectory, moving away from the speculative grade classification.

The Ministry says the staff level agreement, reached on October 9th, 2026, is aimed at safeguarding macroeconomic stability, strengthening debt sustainability, and supporting inclusive, private-sector-led growth.

In a statement issued to the media in Lusaka, the Ministry indicated that the proposed arrangement, however, remains subject to IMF Executive Board approval.

It described Moody’s Ratings’ decision to upgrade Zambia’s sovereign rating from Caa2 to Caa1 as another step in the country’s recovery from the debt distress that culminated in its 2020 default, while maintaining a positive outlook.

According to the Ministry, the upgrade also strengthens Zambia’s international credit standing and signals, improving perceptions of sovereign creditworthiness, following progress in debt restructuring, fiscal consolidation, and macroeconomic stabilisation.

The Ministry considers the Moody’s upgrade an important endorsement of the progress made by the Government in restoring fiscal credibility and improving the country’s debt position.

It noted that the positive outlook also offers an encouraging assessment of the country’s prospects for further improvement anchored on sustained fiscal and economic reforms.

The Ministry stressed that the upgrade strengthens Zambia’s international creditworthiness and investor confidence, potentially lowering borrowing costs for the Government and businesses, attracting foreign direct investment, supporting exchange-rate stability, and easing inflationary pressures.

The Ministry further stated that these gains offer opportunities to accelerate productive investment, infrastructure development, export growth, job creation, and improved household incomes under the broader Grow Zambia Agenda.

“Thankfully, the rating action comes in the week leading to the presentation of the 2027 National Budget by the Minister of Finance and National Planning, Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane, MP, on Friday, 6 November 2026.

“The Government views this timing as particularly important as the 2027 Budget is being prepared to consolidate Zambia’s stabilisation gains while strengthening the foundations for higher production, investment, employment, and household incomes,” the Ministry explained.

The Ministry further reaffirmed its commitment to fiscal discipline, prudent debt management, and growth-oriented economic policies, calling upon public institutions, the private sector, cooperating partners, and citizens to continue working together and turn the country’s economic stability into measurable development results for the benefits of ordinary Zambians.

World.title: Solwezi resident seeks cash payment model
World.content:
A resident of Kamatete area in Solwezi District Kayamba Mobela, a beneficiary of the social cash transfer program, has appealed to the Government to consider paying cash to Social Cash Transfer beneficiaries.

Speaking during a community meeting recently, Mobela stated that the previous cash payments were better, as it was easy for the aged to access their money.

He explained that some elderly people are not accessing their money, which is sent through mobile money, because they are struggling to operate phones.

“Because of old age some elderly people are being duped by the people they trust to withdraw money for them,” Mr Mobela said.

He added that because some vulnerable people do not have people they can trust with their money some elderly people are not directly benefiting from the group.

“We understand that government started paying us through mobile money for safety reasons, our appeal is for them to find ways of paying us cash instead of using mobile money,” he said

Mr Mobela has further attributed the poor communication network in the area to some of the challenges hindering people from accessing their money in good time.

Meanwhile, Mr Mobela has thanked the government for implementing the Social Cash Transfer programme adding that it has helped to uplift the livelihoods of vulnerable people in the community.

World.title: Africa: Six in Seven Journalist Murders Go Unpunished, Unesco Reports
World.content:
Global impunity for journalist killings has risen for the first time in more than a decade, while the growing use of drones is an emerging threat for reporters in conflict zones, according to the latest report from UN cultural organization UNESCO.

"Journalists are increasingly paying with their lives for reporting from the frontlines of war and far too often those responsible for their killings are not held accountable," said Director-General Khaled El-Enany.

UNESCO first began measuring the proportion of journalist killings that go unpunished in 2012. The rate reached 86 per cent in 2024-2025, up one per cent from the previous two-year period.

A confirmed total of 189 journalists and other media workers lost their lives in 2024-2025, or 20 per cent more than during the previous biennium and the highest number since 2014-2015.



More than two thirds, 127, were killed in conflict zones, accounting for 67 per cent of the death toll.

Paying the ultimate price

The findings come in the Director-General's Report on the Safety of Journalists and the Danger of Impunity, which is published every two years to mark the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed on 2 November.

"Over the past year, at least 34 journalists paid the ultimate price. Six of every seven such killings go unpunished. In conflict settings, the rate of impunity is close to 100 per cent," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in his message for the Day.

"This is a heinous affront to the victims and their loved ones, as well as all of us who depend on journalists to remain informed and engaged."

'A global scourge'

Killings were recorded across all regions of the world during the 2024-2025 biennium, representing "a global scourge", the report said.

The highest number of verified cases were in the Arab States (97) followed by Latin American and the Caribbean (37), Asia-Pacific (34), Central and Eastern Europe (14), Africa (6) and Western Europe and North America (1).

The State of Palestine had the highest number of killings in both years, at 30 and 32, respectively.

New technologies, growing risks

The report also identified what UNESCO called "a disturbing new threat" - the growing use of drones to kill journalists. During 2024-2025, drone strikes killed 50 journalists, or 40 per cent of all those killed in conflict zones.

It documented seven incidents in which several journalists were targeted and killed in a single attack, including strikes on media workplaces and temporary reporting centres. Fifteen journalists were reportedly killed while wearing press vests or in vehicles clearly marked 'Press'.

"I reiterate my call for the respect of UN Security Council Resolution 2222 unanimously adopted in 2015 on the protection of journalists, media professionals and associated personnel as civilians in situations of conflict, a status reaffirmed in the Pact for the Future," said Mr. El-Enany.

Progress is possible

The report also highlighted progress, as impunity in non-conflict countries has continued to decline. The rate has fallen from 94 per cent in 2012 to 77 per cent in 2026, or one percentage point per year.

The number of journalist killings in non-conflict zones, 85, is also the lowest in 18 years.

"This demonstrates that when governments invest in investigations, prosecutions and protections for journalists, progress is possible," UNESCO said.

Close 

Women journalists under fire

The agency noted, however, that women journalists continue to face particular risks, both in war zones and online. Thirteen out of the 14 women killed in 2024-2035 were in countries experiencing armed conflict.

Furthermore, a 2025 study by UN Women and the International Center for Journalists found that 75 per cent of women journalists had experienced online or offline abuse and harassment. More than 40 per cent reported offline violence linked to online attacks, up from 20 per cent in a 2020 UNESCO survey.

"Across the world, journalists continue to pay an outrageous price for telling the truth," the UN Secretary-General said.

"On this International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, we demand justice. When journalists are targeted and their reporting is extinguished, it makes victims of us all."

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Congolese Refugees Caught Between War and Closing Doors
World.content:
Refugee women from the Democratic Republic of the Congo walk towards the market in Mantapala Settlement, Zambia (file photo).

analysis

As fighting continues in eastern DRC, shrinking aid and tighter security in host countries undermine the rights of refugees.

In June, the governments of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reaffirmed their commitment to the voluntary, safe and dignified return of refugees between the two countries.

This builds on provisions in the 2025 Washington peace accords and the provisional agreement between the DRC government and the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC)/M23, now Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN)/M23, under the Doha Process.

Previous peace deals failed to secure lasting solutions for refugees or reflect evolving realities on the ground. Continued insecurity, renewed displacement and worsening conditions in host countries have aggravated the plight of refugees.



War in eastern DRC has turned a protracted refugee situation into a regional emergency, particularly after M23 captured Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. In June 2026, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) counted 1.25 million Congolese refugees and asylum seekers, 80% of whom are hosted in DRC's neighbouring countries. Over 245 000 new arrivals were registered between January 2025 and April 2026.

Burundi has been particularly affected, with about 142 000 new arrivals, including some returning Burundians. Most entered following the capture of Bukavu in February 2025 and Uvira in December 2025, straining an already overburdened reception system. Uganda hosts 53% of the Congolese refugee population. It registered over 236 000 arrivals between 2022 and 2025, on top of an additional 139 500 South Sudanese refugees since 2022.

International funding cuts have decimated humanitarian response capacities. In February, the UNHCR reported that only 20% of the US$35 million required for its 2026 lifesaving assistance in Burundi had been received. In January, the International Rescue Committee warned that Uganda's refugee health response had secured only 6% of the funding required for 2026, forcing it to cut health services for over one million refugees.

These conditions shape returns. Within a month of the Burundi-DRC border reopening in February 2026, following M23's retreat from Uvira, 33 000 Congolese refugees spontaneously returned to the DRC, despite the fragile situation in South Kivu.

Continued fighting and rebel occupation create an unsustainable environment for returns. The UNHCR maintains a non-return advisory for South and North Kivu, while facilitated returns to M23-held areas are not possible. Over 80% of Congolese refugees in Rwanda have indicated their willingness to return to the DRC but await the right conditions.

While M23 encourages spontaneous returns to areas it holds, which it considers 'post-conflict', its actions threaten the rights of refugees and displaced people. When it captured Goma, it dismantled internally displaced persons camps, forcing hundreds of thousands of civilians to leave.

M23 is responsible for widespread violence against civilians, including Rwandan refugees. Many are targeted on suspicion of ties to the Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda (FDLR) or Wazalendo, a network of community-based militias fighting M23. Several Rwandan refugees have been forcibly transferred to Rwanda, including through interference with the UNHCR screening process.

M23's encouragement of Congolese refugee returns fuels suspicion of a broader strategy to consolidate rebel control and Rwandan influence in eastern DRC, complicating refugees' reintegration. Due to longstanding disputes over the citizenship of Congolese Tutsi, their (perceived) association with M23 and Rwanda risks deepening community tensions.

In the Great Lakes Region, protracted displacement has profoundly shaped conflict dynamics. The fallout of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, the DRC's regional wars and domestic conflicts in Burundi uprooted communities, forcing many into prolonged exile in neighbouring countries.

Armed groups including M23, the FDLR and Burundian rebels use the unresolved refugee situation to justify their fight and mobilise support. The UN Group of Experts reports that these militants recruit among refugee populations, including in camps in Rwanda and Uganda. This heightens fears of armed infiltration in host countries, creating regional security dilemmas that hamper political solutions to the refugee situation.

Land border closures between Burundi and Rwanda from 2015-2023 and since 2024 have brought repatriation to a halt. Burundi's position has even hardened. In October, Interior Minister Léonidas Ndaruzaniye announced that people coming from or transiting through M23-controlled areas would not be allowed to enter Burundi.

Uganda has also tightened restrictions on cross-border movement over Ebola concerns. Measures announced last month require Congolese travellers deemed non-essential to be returned to DRC. This could prevent refugees from accessing protection and goes against Uganda's 'open-door' refugee policy.

Regional tensions fuel host country suspicion towards foreign nationals, including refugees. In Burundi, Congolese refugees face tighter encampment policies, restricting work and movement. In some cases, police and ruling party youth, Imbonerakure, reportedly detain refugees before sending them back to official sites in remote areas.

Heightened surveillance is reported, particularly of Banyamulenge refugees suspected by authorities of collaborating with M23. While Congolese refugees are generally granted access to national services in Rwanda, many remain dependent on humanitarian assistance and have been subjected to excessive force when protesting against their conditions.

There is a gap between repatriation commitments in peace processes and the realities of forced and spontaneous returns. At the same time, refugee protection needs extend beyond the DRC and Rwanda to the wider region.

Close 

Three sets of measures can close this gap. First, peace efforts should focus not only on repatriation but on respect for refugees' rights and protection, including through diplomatic engagement and independent monitoring of conditions of displacement and return.

Second, integrated regional solutions are needed to address the situations of Congolese, Burundian and Rwandan refugees, and linkages with armed groups. Refugees should be involved in developing these processes - not only the states that are often responsible for their exile.

Third, donors and host states must keep protection in place, including sustained funding, so that return is voluntary and not driven by deprivation.

Tatien Nkeshimana, Research Officer, Conflict Prevention, Management and Peacebuilding in the Great Lakes Region, ISS

Veronica Chepseba, Research Intern, Conflict Prevention, Management and Peacebuilding in the Great Lakes Region, ISS Nairobi

World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Threatens to Leave Kenya for U.S. If Opposition Loses 2027 Election
World.content:
Nairobi — Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has suggested that he could move permanently to the United States with his family should the Opposition fail to unseat President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua, who leads the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), linked his possible departure to the political direction of the Mt Kenya region, warning that a divided electorate could undermine the Opposition's prospects of taking power.

Speaking during a Sunday night interview with a vernacular television station, the former Deputy President maintained that the Opposition had sufficient political support to defeat Ruto but cautioned that internal rivalries could hand the incumbent an advantage.



He expressed optimism about the Opposition's chances, arguing that victory would be achievable if its leaders resisted attempts to fragment their political support.

"I am convinced that the Opposition will win, if it does not allow itself to be divided," he said.

However, Gachagua appeared to place part of his political future in the hands of Mt Kenya voters, urging them to resist competing political interests and rally behind one presidential candidate.

He warned that he would have no reason to continue living in Kenya if the region ignored his calls for political unity and allowed its support to be split among rival camps.

"If our people allow themselves to be divided, I will just board a plane and go to the US. I have a home there," he said.

Gachagua further indicated that he could make the decision before the 2027 polls if he became convinced that political leaders from the region were misleading voters and frustrating efforts to build a united political front.

"If I see that our people have been misled and divided through their own leaders, because I will be woke, I will not be here in Kenya," he added.

The DCP leader maintained that he had done his part in attempting to bring together Mt Kenya's political leadership and would not accept blame should the region fail to heed his appeals.

He reiterated that he had the option of relocating to America alongside his family, insisting that he had already established a home there.

"I have tried to unite the region, so no one will ask me any question. No one will ask me the reason for fleeing. I will just go to America with my people because I have a home there," he said.

The remarks come weeks after Gachagua returned to Kenya from an extended visit to the United States, where he reportedly met Kenyans living abroad and spent time at his American residence.

He departed Kenya on August 26 and made a low-key return on October 20, following nearly two months away.

Close 

His latest comments also come against the backdrop of growing political manoeuvring within Mt Kenya as leaders position themselves ahead of the 2027 elections.

The region, which commands a significant share of the national electorate, is expected to play a decisive role in determining the outcome of the presidential contest.

Gachagua has been seeking to consolidate his influence in the region and secure its backing for a common Opposition candidate as political parties work towards building an alternative coalition to challenge Ruto.

World.title: Liberia: Civil Servants Rank As Liberia's Third-Biggest Taxpayer
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberia's third-biggest taxpayer this year is its own payroll office.

The Civil Service Agency is credited with US$41.1 million from January through October on the Liberia Revenue Authority's list of top revenue contributors. Only two mining companies paid more. The government's own wage bill outranks Orange Liberia, every bank, every fuel importer and every private business in the country.

The figure almost certainly reflects income tax withheld from public employees' pay and handed to the LRA. That is how a payroll office ends up on a list of taxpayers. Money the government pays its workers comes back to it as tax. The revenue is real, and it counts toward the record collections the government has celebrated this year.

A record built on a few pillars

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Collections have risen fast. The LRA said it collected about US$818 million in 2025, beating its target of US$804.6 million and up from US$699 million in 2024. For 2026, it set a target of US$1.176 billion. Collections passed US$1 billion by mid-September.

The LRA's year-to-date figures through Oct. 31 show where much of that money comes from. The 10 biggest contributors paid US$570.7 million. ArcelorMittal Liberia accounted for US$276 million and Bea Mountain Mining Company for US$125 million, together 70% of the top 10.

ArcelorMittal's total is inflated by a single transaction. In March, the company paid a one-time US$200 million fee to extend its mining rights to 2050 and reserve capacity on the Tokadeh-Buchanan railway, a payment the International Monetary Fund has confirmed. Strip out that fee and ArcelorMittal's contribution this year falls to about US$76 million. The fee also explains the company's uneven monthly payments: it paid just US$2.7 million in October, a fraction of its average.

Without the one-time fee, the top 10 paid about US$370.7 million. Even on that basis, the two miners account for more than half. Bea Mountain has grown into one of the state's most important payers. Its US$125 million in 10 months is more than three times the US$37.6 million the Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative recorded from the gold miner for all of 2023, though the two sources count payments differently. In October alone, Bea Mountain paid US$16.6 million, more than any other contributor and six times ArcelorMittal's payment for the month.

The payroll, the pump and the bottle

Once the miners and the government's own payroll are set aside, much of the rest of the list is also less than it appears.

Fuel importers form the next largest block. Aminata & Sons paid US$21.8 million, Conex Petroleum Services US$16.3 million and West Oil Investment Liberia US$12.3 million, together more than US$50 million. Most of what fuel importers pay is import duty and petroleum petroleumtax, built into the price at the pump. The companies write the checks. Drivers, commercial transport operators, generator users and, through them, nearly every household bear the cost. The same is likely true of much of the US$14 million paid by Monrovia Breweries, which is largely excise on beer and drinks.

On the adjusted figures, the two miners, the government's payroll, the fuel importers and the brewery account for about US$306.5 million of the US$370.7 million paid by the top 10. That leaves about US$64 million, roughly 17%, from the remaining three:

Orange Liberia, US$35.7 million

APM Terminals Liberia, US$16.6 million

The LISCR Trust Company, which administers Liberia's shipping registry, US$12 million

What emerges is a revenue base resting on commodity exports, consumption taxes and the government's own wage bill. Comparatively little comes from profitable private Liberian businesses paying tax on what they earn.

The names that are missing

The absences are as telling as the names on the list.

Lonestar Cell MTN, Orange's main competitor in mobile telephony, does not appear among the top 10, which means it paid less than the US$12 million that marks the cutoff. No bank appears. Neither does Firestone Liberia. The rubber company paid US$11.6 million in 2023, according to the LEITI's most recent report, making it the third-largest extractive payer that year, but it does not reach the top 10 this year. Nor does any palm oil concession or other agricultural company.

The list does not say why. Lower profits, tax holidays and incentives in concession agreements, losses carried forward and arrears could each explain part of it. But the gaps show how narrow the taxpaying base remains outside two mines, and how little the sectors that employ most Liberians, agriculture and small trade, contribute directly to the treasury.

The IMF said tax revenue rose to 15.9% of gross domestic product in 2025, from 14.5% in 2024. It has pointed to a planned value-added tax in 2027 and mining tax reforms as critical to sustaining the gains. A World Bank review of Liberia's public finances put the country's tax compliance gap at about 3% of GDP, money owed under existing laws that goes uncollected.

New money, old tensions

The October figures also show where some newer money is coming from, and the questions that come with it.

APM Terminals paid US$2.6 million in October, well above its monthly average of US$1.66 million this year. That came the same month Gbarpolu County Sen. Amara M. Konneh asked the Senate to summon the port operator and others over container delays and what he called "a multiplicity of opaque transaction costs and fees" passed on to consumers.

Close 

October's top 10 also includes a new name, "LTMI Collection," with US$1.4 million. That appears to be revenue collected through Liberia Traffic Management Inc., the private operator that took over vehicle registration and driver licensing from the Ministry of Transport on March 1. That followed a February directive from Boakai activating a 25-year concession first signed in 2018. The concession has been challenged in both houses of the Legislature.

What it means

The LRA is collecting more, its systems are expanding, and some sources, Bea Mountain above all, are growing quickly. But the figures suggest the record year rests on a few pillars, and each carries a risk.

Mining revenue depends on world gold and iron ore prices and on operations at two companies. A drop in either, or a stoppage at either mine, would hit the treasury directly. ArcelorMittal's US$200 million fee was a one-time payment, and the government cannot count on it again to fund recurring spending. Revenue from fuel and drink falls hardest on ordinary households. And the tax withheld from civil servants' pay grows only as fast as the government's own wage bill, which the same revenue must pay for.

World.title: South Africa: Rigging Claims, Xenophobia Raise Fears of Polling Station Tensions
World.content:
Cape Town — Days before South Africans vote in the local government elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026, social media is carrying unverified claims of election rigging alongside posts that blame foreign nationals. This has raised concerns about the potential for online hostility to spill into real-world tensions.

The Centre for Analytics and Behavioural Change (CABC), through its High-Risk Events Monitoring programme, logged 79 potentially harmful posts between 22 and 29 October. This included allegations of electoral fraud, hate speech and calls that could incite violence.

One post urged people to gather at voting stations to stop foreign nationals from voting. Of the 79 posts, 51 were tagged as misinformation or disinformation, 33 as hate speech and 12 as incitement to violence. The categories overlap, so a single post can fall into more than one. The posts attracted approximately 546,600 views, 29,600 likes, 4,100 shares and 1,350 comments across platforms.

According to CABC, the wider conversation was much larger.



Over the eight days to 29 October, the CABC recorded more than 15,310 mentions of the elections from 6,426 unique authors, with volumes rising steadily from 25 October.

Illegal immigration was the leading topic.

The organisation found that conversations about illegal immigration were largely driven by frustration with government immigration policies and perceptions among some users that protests against immigration were being silenced. Elements of collective blame directed at foreign nationals were also identified. Users were angry about the government's immigration policy and what they saw as an attempt to silence protests on the issue.

The monitoring also reported on the mobilization of foreign nationals to campaign for political parties, with concerns that immigration related grievances could fuel tensions around the electoral process.

Most of the South African conversations were critical of the ruling political parties, with users expressing concern over the ongoing struggles facing citizens. Other posts criticised governing parties or focused on the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) and its preparations.

Election-related discussions increased steadily from 25 October, with a spike of approximately 1,000 additional mentions on 26 October.

The quietest day was 24 October, with 1,253 mentions, which the CABC said coincided with Economic Freedom Fighters ( EFF) leader Julius Malema's campaigning in Mpumalanga, where he put "unemployment and poor service delivery at the centre of his party's election campaign."

The highest volume of mentions was recorded on 27 October, reaching 2,615. According to the CABC, this increase was driven partly by debates between the African National Congress (ANC) and the Democratic Alliance (DA) over housing delivery in Cape Town.

The ANC's mayoral candidate argued that the party had a stronger housing delivery record, claiming it had "delivered more housing in that period than the DA has in 20 years".

According to CABC, the log records approximately 546,600 views, 29,600 likes, 4,100 shares and 1,350 comments across entries with available metrics.

Three narratives driving online hostility

The CABC identified three recurring narratives in the online conversation: allegations of election rigging, xenophobic claims linking foreign nationals to electoral manipulation, and calls that could translate online hostility into confrontation at polling stations.

The first centres on distrust in the IEC and the credibility of the electoral process.

Several users cast doubt on the IEC and the credibility of results before voting took place. One post claimed the ANC had already voted on behalf of citizens and offered what it presented as proof of ANC–IEC collusion. The CABC logged 95,500 views for it. Another user suggested that a delay in announcing results would allow them to be doctored. Other posts alleged the IEC was compromised or asked whether an ANC or DA victory could occur without rigging.

The CABC said these posts show how suspicion of election administration is being expressed "as specific, but unverified, allegations". It stressed that criticism or distrust alone is not necessarily misinformation.

"Distrusting an institution is not misinformation. Posting specific accusations with nothing behind them is," said CABC. "Claims that the count is rigged hand people a ready-made explanation for any result they dislike. When those claims are tied to foreign nationals, they can send people to a polling station looking for someone to blame."

CABC warned that unsubstantiated rigging allegations could undermine confidence in election results, particularly when used to explain outcomes that political supporters or voters may dislike.

The second narrative links foreign nationals to alleged electoral manipulation and political advantage.

One user claimed the ANC was replacing South Africans with foreign nationals, using a derogatory term for migrants. Another alleged that Home Affairs was issuing identity documents to foreign nationals in Cape Town, a post with 35,000 logged views. A third claimed migrants would be used to dilute South Africans' votes and rig elections.

The CABC said the common thread is "an unsubstantiated suggestion that immigration and documentation are tools for manipulating the electorate". It warned that this framing risks confusing immigration status with eligibility to vote and reinforcing hostility towards migrant communities.

Close 

The third narrative raised concerns about the possibility of online allegations translating into confrontation at voting stations.

Some posts went beyond claims of unfairness to calls for direct action. One user urged South Africans to gather at voting stations on 4 November to prevent foreign nationals from voting for the ANC and the EFF, a post with 3,366 logged views. Another warned that foreign nationals were allegedly being mobilised to campaign for a political party.

The CABC said these examples "do not establish organised intimidation or impending violence". However, they illustrate how unverified claims about migrant participation might be translated into confrontational activity near polling stations. Lawful observation and political mobilisation, it said, must be distinguished from threats, discriminatory targeting and interference with voters.

In its conclusion, the organisation warned that allegations of electoral fraud and xenophobic narratives could reinforce one another.

"The clearest risk is not proof of widespread manipulation, but the possibility that unverified claims weaken confidence in electoral processes and encourage hostility towards perceived foreign voters," reported the CABC.

World.title: Ex-West Point cadet sued for secretly drugging pregnant girlfriend with abortion pills
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A former West Point cadet who admitted to secretly drugging his pregnant girlfriend and administering abortion medication to her without her knowledge or consent is now being sued over the 2022 incident.

The woman, identified as "Jane Doe" in court documents, sued Caleb T. Suh in New York Supreme Court on Oct. 28, accusing him of assault and battery and seeking damages.

Doe and Suh were cadets at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point when Doe learned she was pregnant in January 2022, according to the complaint.

The lawsuit alleges Suh repeatedly pressured Doe to have an abortion, while she told him she intended to keep the baby. Suh later appeared to support her decision but allegedly used her identification to create an online pharmacy account in her name and obtain abortion medication without her knowledge.

WOMAN HELD DOWN, FORCE-FED ABORTION PILLS AT HEART OF ‘HELL ON EARTH’ FIGHT OVER BIDEN-ERA POLICY

On Feb. 4, 2022, Suh brought a drink he described as a pregnancy protein shake to Doe's barracks room, according to the complaint. She became sick and drifted in and out of consciousness after drinking it.

Suh later admitted in federal court that he administered abortion medication to Doe without her knowledge or consent. Hours later, Doe became seriously ill and was taken to a hospital, where doctors confirmed she was suffering a miscarriage.

Doe reported the incident to the Army Criminal Investigation Division at West Point in May 2022.

Suh was charged in federal court in June 2026 and pleaded guilty June 30 to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner.

Suh admitted creating an online pharmacy account using his girlfriend's identity to obtain abortion medication without her knowledge or consent. He also admitted to obtaining Xanax to sedate her before administering the abortion pills.

"My intent was use the Xanax to unwittingly sedate my girlfriend so that I could then administer the abortion pills, which I had obtained via the online pharmacy," Suh said, according to the complaint.

EX-DEMOCRAT SHARES ABORTION PILL EXPERIENCE THAT LEFT HER 'HEMORRHAGING IN THE BATH'

Suh also admitted deceiving his girlfriend into believing he supported the pregnancy before giving her the medication. He acknowledged that she later miscarried "as a result of the abortion pills that I had administered without her knowledge and consent."

After leaving West Point, Suh attended Cornell University, graduating in May 2026, before enrolling in a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health.

A spokesperson for Cornell told Fox News Digital that when Suh was admitted as a transfer student, he answered "No" when asked whether he had been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at a previous school. Cornell said his previous university had reported he was in good academic standing and eligible to return.

A person with knowledge of the matter told Fox News Digital that Columbia was unaware of Suh's status until the New York Times contacted the university Friday and that the school took swift action. Applications to the school do not require applicants to disclose prior criminal convictions, the person said.

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

Suh asked a federal judge in October to postpone his sentencing until January 2027, in part to complete his semester at Columbia. Federal prosecutors did not oppose the request, and U.S. District Judge Philip M. Halpern granted it.

Doe is seeking compensatory and punitive damages.

"Our complaint sets out that our client was forced to endure an unimaginable trauma and was robbed of a pregnancy she wanted, while Mr. Suh has since managed to attend not one, but two ivy league schools. We are outraged on her behalf and plan to aggressively pursue justice," Russell Kornblith, partner at Wigdor LLP, said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

World.title: Four states vote Tuesday on ballot measures that could reshape girls' and women's sports nationwide
World.content:
Four states have measures on Tuesday's ballot that could change who gets to compete in girls' and women's sports — and, in some cases, who gets to use their locker rooms.

Arizona and Nebraska already have laws restricting biological males from competing in female sports. A "yes" vote in either state would expand or strengthen those existing restrictions.

Washington and Colorado are different. Neither currently has the statewide sex-based restrictions proposed by these measures. If voters approve them, both states would establish statewide sex-based restrictions for school sports — a significant change in two traditionally Democratic states.

WHERE TOP DEMOCRAT SENATE CANDIDATES AND THEIR GOP OPPONENTS STAND ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

So what's at stake Tuesday? Here's a state-by-state breakdown of what the measures would do, what opponents are saying, how supporters are responding and what the betting markets are predicting.

Washington: Initiative 638

What a yes vote would do: Prohibit students defined as biologically male from competing in girls' K-12 interscholastic sports. Girls seeking to participate would have to provide documentation from a healthcare professional verifying biological sex based on "reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels."

As it stands, K-12 athletes in Washington can compete based on their gender identity under current eligibility rules, which allowed a boy in Camas, WA, to switch to the girls' team mid-season earlier this year.

What a no vote would do: Keep the current eligibility rules in place, without adding the initiative's new sex-verification requirements.

What opponents say: Organizations such as No Hate in Washington State argue that the initiative would discriminate against transgender students and could subject girls to invasive genital examinations.

NEW POLL SHOWS WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS ARE READY TO END BOYS COMPETING IN GIRLS' SPORTS

Proponents call the "invasive exam" argument fearmongering, saying that biological sex can be verified as part of a routine sports physical — something high school athletes have been undergoing for years. They also point to a simple cheek swab, which collects DNA from inside the mouth, as another possible way to verify biological sex.

Polymarket prediction at the time of writing: 64% market-implied probability of I-638 passing.

What a yes vote would do: Establish statewide sex-based participation requirements for school sports from K-12 through the college level. Athletes would generally compete on teams matching their biological sex, with exceptions for coed sports and girls joining boys' teams when no equivalent girls' team exists.

The measure covers public, charter and private schools, as well as colleges and universities. It applies to interscholastic and intramural athletics, including school-sponsored club sports.

Proposition 134 defines females as "a person whose biological reproductive system is organized around the production of ova" and males as "a person whose biological reproductive system is organized around the production of sperm."

Unlike Washington's initiative, Colorado's measure doesn't specifically require a doctor's note or medical examination to verify biological sex. Instead, schools would have to establish their own eligibility policies, with no verification method specified in the measure. The state education commissioner could take action against school districts that intentionally refuse to comply.

What a no vote would do: Maintain the existing eligibility system, allowing schools, districts and athletic associations to continue setting their own participation policies, subject to state and federal law.

What opponents say: Planned Parenthood and other opponents echo the concerns raised in Washington, arguing that Proposition 134 amounts to government overreach and "risks invasive gender checks for girls."

But as XX-XY Athletics founder Jennifer Sey — who chairs the campaign supporting Proposition 134 — has pointed out, 27 states already have restrictions on biological males competing in girls' sports. Sey argues that the invasive examinations opponents warn about aren't happening in those states.

Polymarket prediction at the time of writing: 55% market-implied probability of Proposition 134 passing.

Arizona: Proposition 318

What a yes vote would do: Build on Arizona's existing public school sports rules by expanding restrictions to private schools and athletic associations, including those overseeing youth and college sports. It would also require schools and athletic associations to restrict access to restrooms, locker rooms and other private spaces connected to athletics based on biological sex as recorded on an original birth certificate.

The measure would also allow athletes to sue schools and athletic associations that knowingly violate the law. It would retain protections for athletes competing on coed teams and would not categorically prohibit girls from participating on boys' teams.

What a no vote would do: Leave existing laws in place, keeping Arizona's current public school sports restrictions without expanding them to additional institutions or adding the measure's new requirements for private spaces.

What opponents say: Civil rights groups such as the ACLU argue that Proposition 318 singles out transgender students, could subject girls to intrusive questioning about their biological sex and opens schools up to expensive lawsuits.

Supporters counter that the measure closes loopholes in existing law, protects privacy and safety in locker rooms and bathrooms, and establishes consistent rules for fair athletic competition across the state.

Polymarket prediction at the time of writing: 82% market-implied probability of Proposition 318 passing.

SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Nebraska: Initiative 442

What a yes vote would do: Amend Nebraska's Constitution to prohibit biological males from competing in girls' and women's school sports, from K-12 through college. Schools would have to designate teams as male, female or coed, with female teams reserved for biological females.

The measure would apply to public schools and colleges, as well as private institutions whose teams compete against public schools.

Unlike Washington and Colorado, Nebraska already has a law restricting biological males from competing in girls' and women's sports. Gov. Jim Pillen signed the Stand With Women Act in June 2025. Arizona also has an existing law, but Nebraska's ballot measure would go a step further by putting its restrictions into the state constitution, making them harder for future lawmakers to overturn.

What a no vote would do: Leave Nebraska's Constitution unchanged. The existing law restricting biological males from competing in girls' and women's sports would remain in effect.

What opponents say: Groups such as OutNebraska and the Fairness for All campaign argue that the amendment would discriminate against transgender students and unnecessarily write restrictions into the state constitution when a law already exists. Opponents also point out that transgender athletes make up a tiny percentage of the state's population.

Supporters counter that putting the restrictions into the constitution would protect female athletes from future changes to state law. The Fairness for Girls campaign argues that allowing biological males to compete against girls creates safety concerns and can cost female athletes medals, advancement opportunities and scholarships.

Polymarket prediction at the time of writing: No Polymarket prediction found.

World.title: How a midterm tie gets settled in the case of the Senate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In the World Cup, they play overtime, then rely on penalty kicks to settle ties.

The National Hockey League plays a short overtime, followed by a shootout. NHL games used to end in ties. In the playoffs, the teams keep going – until there’s a winner. In the 2020 playoffs, the Tampa Bay Lightning finally topped the Columbus Blue Jackets 3-2 after a staggering five overtimes. In other words. They played nearly THREE total games. That’s the equivalent of 26 innings in baseball.

Speaking of Major League Baseball, teams play extra innings. And keep playing until one team is ahead and the home team has completed an at-bat in the bottom of the inning. MLB modified its rules a few years ago, introducing a "ghost runner" on second base to start the 10th inning. That’s an effort to end the tie and finish the game sooner.

If only there were a method to settle a tie in the U.S. Senate.

THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND

Yes. In the case of a tie roll call vote, the vice president — who doubles as president of the Senate – can vote to break a tie vote. In fact, the VP doesn’t even have to cast a ballot if it’s a tie and the roll call vote is going the way he or she wants. By rule, tie votes go down to defeat in the Senate.

But what if we wake up Wednesday morning (if not Friday or Saturday morning or sometime in early December, depending on how hotly contested things are) to discover that the Senate is tied at 50-50?

There is nothing in the Senate’s 44 standing rules which serves as a tiebreaker. The Founders didn’t provide a system to bust up a tie and determine which side is in the majority or minority. And no, it’s not written down anywhere that the party of the President is automatically thrust into the majority.

Maybe soccer is on to something with penalty kicks. At least there’s a system. There’s nothing concrete to sort out which party controls the Senate if things are deadlocked at 50-50.

There was a tie was a Senate tie in 1881 after resignations and political maneuvering. The Senate was also tied for a period in 1954. Nearly ten percent of all senators died during the two-year Congress which stretched from early 1953 to early 1955.

However, the Senate featured two ties in recent Senate history. Both instances reflect what the Senate did to sort out which party captured the majority. One tie came after the 2000 election. The other in 2020. Both elections took a while to sort things out.

In 2026, Alaska, we’re looking at you.

It took until early December, 2000 to determine that Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., defeated then-Sen. Slade Gorton, R-Wash., establishing a 50-50 Senate.

In fact, the tie for the Senate from the 2020 election wasn’t even established until two days into the new Congress on January 6, 2021. Yes. That was the day of the Capitol riot. Sens. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., both won runoffs to set the 50-50 split.

In early December, 2000, the Supreme Court finally settled the Florida election dispute between President George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore. Republicans had held the Senate. But then Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Miss., and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, D-S.D., engineered a power-sharing agreement between the parties. This aligned with the election of Vice President Dick Cheney.

Lott would serve as the Majority Leader and the GOP technically had the "majority." But the bipartisan pact granted Daschle some special floor powers. Republicans chaired each committee. However, there was equal representation by both parties on each panel.

The full Senate had to ratify this agreement. And it did just that.

Such a process is subject to two filibusters requiring 60 yeas. One to bring up the proposal for debate. Another to terminate the debate. Then a simple majority to pass it. But none of that was a problem. The Senate greenlighted it with all 100 senators signing on.

Why such smooth sailing?

Republicans feared Democrats would stall the agenda of President George W. Bush. So they got on board. Democrats agreed because they knew they were kinda, sorta in the majority. Otherwise, they were relegated to an outright minority.

Former Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., was well aware of those same dynamics in 2001. He insisted that Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., propound – word-for-word – the same accord in 2021 which Lott and Daschle hammered out.

Which brings us to a potential tie in 2027. Is there the political will in the Senate – let alone the votes – to agree to such a compact? President Trump is still president. And Vice President JD Vance is still President of the Senate. What would they say about that? Unclear.

The Senate isn’t compelled to present a dedicated "majority" or "minority." The concept of a "Majority Leader" is relatively new – only dating back to the early 20th Century. The Senate is a body of "equals." Thus, the Founders didn’t expect one senator to wield operational control of the Senate. You won’t find the words "Majority Leader" anywhere in the Constitution. Just Speaker of the House and President of the Senate.

If there’s a 50-50 Senate and an impasse, could Vance suddenly have more power? Maybe. As President of the Senate, he can’t debate. He can only preside over the body and break ties. Moreover, would Vance even want to assert more authority? It’s unclear what that could be. And what would all of this do to his plans to run for president in 2028?

EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING

In fact, a deadlocked Senate with no power sharing agreement could potentially hamstring Vance. It wasn’t that long ago that the Vice President spent much of his time presiding over daily Senate debates. But not anymore. If there’s no set majority, those responsibilities either fall to Vance, current Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, or the possible Democratic Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash. The latter two are the most senior senators from their respective parties. The President Pro Tempore is third in line to the presidency, following the Vice President and House Speaker. A power sharing agreement is what helps determine who presides over the Senate. Otherwise, Vance may be moored in the Senate.

So there is precedent for settling a "tie" in the Senate. But it hinges on the political will of senators. And if there are disputes about seating Members – say the Alaska Senate race or another contest becomes a conflagration – one can anticipate a toxic climate on Capitol Hill. Few may be willing to sign on to anything.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Senate relies a lot on history and precedent to do things. But absent political will, senators may just resort to rock, paper, scissors.

Or maybe, penalty kicks.

World.title: Supreme Court quickly rejects Trump effort to target alleged noncitizen voters in California
World.content:
WASHINGTON — In a loss for President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court on Monday swiftly rejected the administration’s request that California separate out up to 20,000 mail-in ballots that officials allege could be submitted by noncitizens.

In a brief order without explanation, the court turned away an emergency request the Trump administration filed just hours earlier in an unusual last-minute flurry of election litigation. Lower courts had also ruled against the Trump administration.

The court acted so quickly that it did not even ask California for its views first, as it normally does of the opposing party in such cases.

“This latest decision should put an end to the administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement.

“But our work is not over. We will remain vigilant and keep fighting back against federal efforts to undermine our democracy,” he added.

The White House and Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests seeking comment.

California officials had resisted the Justice Department’s intervention, noting that it is already illegal under state law for noncitizens to vote and expressing skepticism about whether the federal government’s information is accurate.

Separately, the administration has warned California election officials they could face prosecution if they allow noncitizens to vote. A federal judge told the Justice Department on Saturday to stop making such threats.

Although elections are administered exclusively by local officials, the Trump administration says it has grounds to intervene because there is a federal law that prohibits voting by noncitizens.

Trump has long claimed, without evidence, that millions of noncitizens illegally vote in U.S. elections. Experts say it rarely happens.

That has not stopped the administration from putting pressure on states to check voters’ citizenship, including by using a federal database.

But the effort has faced multiple setbacks. When the federal government said it had confirmed 185 noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada, the state responded that all of them were, in fact, citizens.

Thousands of mail-in ballots have already been submitted and processed in California. Once election officials check whether a ballot is valid by checking the voter’s signature against voter registration records, the details identifying the voter are discarded before the vote is counted. As a result, it would be impossible to retroactively determine which votes may have been cast by the alleged noncitizens.

In rejecting the Trump administration’s claims, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said there was no evidence Congress intended the federal law that bars noncitizens from voting to pre-empt state election laws.

Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Washington University in St. Louis, said the Supreme Court’s decisive action rejecting the Trump administration was similar to how it turned away a series of Republican requests seeking to use a new congressional district map over the summer.

In both instances “the court acted quickly to show its displeasure for the underlying claims” as well as reinforcing longstanding precedent against federal courts intervening in elections when they are underway, Crum said.

World.title: How the Michigan and Alaska dramas shape the fight for the Senate: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains how a pair of controversies in Michigan and Alaska could impact the broader battle for Senate control. Plus, Rebecca Shabad examines President Donald Trump’s election eve message.

— Adam Wollner

How the Michigan and Alaska dramas shape the fight for the Senate

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

An “October surprise” and a “November surprise” have rocked the Senate races in Alaska and Michigan, which are critical chess pieces in the battle for the majority.

To understand why these contests are so important, consider two scenarios.

The “red wall” scenario: Picture this: Democrats are having a good night and hold every seat they are defending, including in Michigan. They flip North Carolina. And they accomplish their long-held goal of unseating GOP Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. That would leave Democrats with 49 seats.

Other targets would include five states that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. There’s a plausible scenario where Democratic candidates in those states overperform by 10 points compared to the 2024 presidential margin, and still lose all of them.

The “blue tsunami” scenario: Now consider this: Michigan and Maine tip into the Democratic column and, one by one, all five of the red states start to fall. The blue wave turns into a tsunami and breaches the walls of MAGA country.

Through some mix of depressed Republican turnout, swing-voter movement and high Democratic enthusiasm, Democrats win Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. That’s their dream scenario, and it’d result in a 54-46 Senate majority. And if South Carolina flips, that’s 55 seats.

The Michigan and Alaska scenarios: That brings us to two states that have sparked controversy lately.

In Michigan, Haley Stevens, the runner-up in the Democratic primary, defected from her party and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers two days before the election. It’s a race where Democrats already were experiencing anxiety over progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s prospects.

If Democrats lose Michigan, their path to the majority gets steeper: They would need to flip at least three double-digit Trump states, rather than two.

In Alaska, a New York Times report that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited a candidate with the same name as GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan jolted the race, and the saga is under state and federal investigation. Peltola has denied any involvement in the effort. (Over the weekend, a federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s effort to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher and first-time candidate.)

There’s a scenario where Senate control comes down to Alaska. And if the race is close, it may not be decided for a while.

Alaska law allows up to 15 days for absentee ballots to arrive, as long as they’re postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3. That means counting can continue through Nov. 18, and the target date to certify the election is Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving.

If it’s very close, a candidate could demand a recount. There could be a court fight. That would put the country into December without knowing which party will control the Senate.

🏃 Related read: ‘A genuine toss-up’: Senate battle comes down to red states and Republican voters, by Bridget Bowman

Ahead of Election Day, Trump sets the stage for potential Republican losses

By Rebecca Shabad

In an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, President Donald Trump said that Republicans “gave this a very strong shot,” while acknowledging that historically, the president’s party “doesn’t win the midterms.”

“This is the last day before the midterm elections — the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime,” Trump said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

Although a White House official had said in advance that the speech would represent Trump’s “closing message” before voters make their final trips to the polls, the president spent most of his remarks speaking about the Reflecting Pool.

Trump announced the Reflecting Pool will reopen after months of repairs, and talked about other renovation projects he has ordered around Washington, D.C., a key focus and fascination of his second term.

Speaking about the election, the president touted what he considered economic wins. But, he said, “it all doesn’t matter if we’re going to be foolish and let people that hate our country win an election.”

Trump’s speech today came after he held his final midterm rally in Kansas last night — one of 28 for him over the last month, Peter Nicholas notes.

“I’m closing the sucker down,” Trump told the crowd, standing in a chilly evening breeze. “I’m getting out of here. I got to get a little sleep. I’ve been doing a little too many of these.”

World.title: New York reports first measles death in more than 30 years
World.content:
New York health officials Monday reported the state’s first measles-associated death in more than 30 years.

A child in a rural county in northern New York died.

“We are deeply saddened by the death of a child in Lewis County associated with the ongoing measles outbreak. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the child’s family and loved ones and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time,” state health officials said in a statement.

The statement did not provide additional details about the child.

So far this year, 178 measles cases have been recorded in New York, according to the state Health Department. The vast majority — 170 cases — were outside New York City. Fifteen cases have been reported in Lewis County.

In October, Gov. Kathy Hochul declared the outbreak an emergency.

“Measles is highly contagious, and vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease,” she said in a statement after the death was announced Monday.

In neighboring Pennsylvania, health officials are fighting the country’s worst outbreak in 30 years. As of Monday, there have been 1,433 cases, according to the Pennsylvania Health Department, including 269 hospitalizations. Six people have died.

As of Friday, there have been 4,852 measles cases nationally, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

New York health officials said people should make sure they are current on their measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations.

The first dose is typically given at around 1 year of age and another at around age 5. Two doses offer 97% protection against measles, usually for life.

During outbreaks, babies as young as 6 months old are eligible for a dose ahead of those two recommended shots.
