In a letter sent today, Joseph warned that tensions surrounding the deployment of Salvadoran troops to Haiti could trigger further violence and reprisals, leaving civilians to bear the consequences.

A source confirmed that the United Nations had received the letter, AP reports.

The request follows the October 18 attack on four Salvadoran aviation technicians in Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, who remain missing. In response, El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele deployed more than 2,000 troops to Haiti.

Joseph expressed concern over Bukele’s statements, warning that the situation could escalate into a cycle of retaliation. He described 400 Mawozo as a “rebel group” and said he was prepared to participate in meetings aimed at reaching a peaceful agreement and establishing lasting stability.

“Given Mr. Nayib Bukele’s vengeful remarks, expectations, and threats, I fear this situation will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people would be the first victims,” he said.

In his two-page letter, Joseph claimed he had “officially raised the white flag” since August 20 and called for dialogue between international forces operating in Haiti and his gang. He also stressed that civilian protection, particularly for children and vulnerable families, should remain central to any international initiative.

However, the appeal comes as armed confrontations have intensified in areas near Port-au-Prince, where Haitian security forces and an international gang-suppression force, alongside private security firm Vectus Global, have been fighting armed groups.

Haiti continues to face a severe security crisis, with the United Nations reporting that more than 5,700 people were killed or injured across the country between January and mid-September.

World.title: Senior Justices of the Peace sworn in to strengthen response to domestic violence
World.content:
Senior Justices of the Peace sworn in to strengthen response to domestic violence

By Zoila Palma: Eighteen Select Senior Justices of the Peace were officially sworn in on Friday, October 30, 2026, at the Family Court in Belize City, strengthening Belize’s efforts to provide urgent legal protection for people experiencing domestic violence.

The newly appointed officers will help address situations where immediate protection is needed but a magistrate is unavailable, including outside regular court hours and during emergencies.

The appointments follow the introduction of the Justices of the Peace (Amendment) Act, 2025, which allows specially designated Senior Justices of the Peace to issue Emergency Interim Protection Orders. These orders may remain in effect for up to 72 hours, providing temporary protection while cases proceed through the appropriate court system. The measure is intended to close a gap in access to emergency legal assistance for people whose safety may be at risk.

Minister of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, Thea Garcia-Ramirez, emphasized the importance of ensuring that people seeking protection receive a timely response. “When someone reaches out for help, there must be a system capable of responding,” the Minister stated.

She urged the newly sworn-in officers to carry out their duties with sensitivity, fairness and respect, noting that domestic violence affects individuals, families and children. She also stressed that protecting survivors requires cooperation among the Judiciary, law enforcement, government ministries and agencies providing support services.

The 18 newly sworn-in Select Senior Justices of the Peace are Adrian Madrid, Amelio Miguel Cal Jr., Ayonie Briceno, Barrette Johnissa Belisle, Desol Neal, Francisca Guillerma Villamor, Giovanni Noel Tillett, Ion Anthony Cacho, Irene Sandra Cruz, Javier Antonio Williams, Jennifer Wright Braun, Maria Marina Tucker, Marie Lavern Tzul, Moses Martinez, Orlando Espat, Percival Willington Neal, Robert Mossiah and Thomas George Morrison.

The officers received specialized training in the legal procedures for emergency orders, confidentiality, record-keeping and working with vulnerable individuals as Belize strengthens its response to domestic violence.

World.title: Organization for International Regional Agricultural Health celebrates 73 years of regional cooperation
World.content:
Organization for International Regional Agricultural Health celebrates 73 years of regional cooperation

By Zoila Palma: Belize joined regional partners on Saturday, October 31, to celebrate 73 years of the Organization for International Regional Agricultural Health (OIRSA), recognizing its longstanding role in protecting agricultural health and strengthening cooperation across the region.

The observance of Regional Agricultural Health Day brought together authorities and representatives to reflect on the shared efforts to safeguard agriculture and support the sector’s development.

The ceremony was presided over by Minister of Agriculture, Food Security, and New and Growing Industries, Rodwell Ferguson, alongside OIRSA’s representative in Belize, Fermín Blanco.

The event highlighted the importance of regional collaboration in protecting animal and plant health while preserving the agricultural heritage of member countries.

A key feature of the celebration was a keynote address delivered by Rosario Gómez, OIRSA’s representative in Guatemala, titled “Current Situation and Perspectives of the El Niño Phenomenon in the Region.”

Her presentation examined the outlook for the climate phenomenon and its potential implications for agriculture, emphasizing the importance of understanding regional climate conditions and their effects on agricultural production.

The anniversary marked more than seven decades of shared work to strengthen agricultural health systems and cooperation among countries in the region.

World.title: Belize participates in Commonwealth Foreign Affairs Ministers’ Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda
World.content:
Belize participates in Commonwealth Foreign Affairs Ministers’ Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda

By Zoila Palma: CEO in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Oscar Arnold participated in the Commonwealth Foreign Affairs Ministers’ Meeting (CFAMM), contributing to important discussions on shared priorities and updating Commonwealth Foreign Ministers on matters of importance to Belize.

He was joined by Cherie Nisbet, High Commissioner of Belize to the United Kingdom and by Jordan Craig, Counsellor, Belize High Commission in London.

The Commonwealth Foreign Affairs Ministers Meeting took place today at the American University of Antigua in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda, alongside the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

World.title: International News: UN reports warn of irreversible damage to glaciers if global warming exceeds 1.5°C
World.content:
International News: UN reports warn of irreversible damage to glaciers if global warming exceeds 1.5°C

By Zoila Palma: Two United Nations reports released today warn that exceeding the 1.5°C global warming threshold could trigger large-scale and, in many cases, irreversible damage to glaciers, sea ice and other frozen regions of the Earth.

The reports call for urgent climate action, warning that rising temperatures could accelerate ice loss, sea-level rise and permafrost thaw, with serious consequences for communities worldwide, AFP reports.

The 2015 Paris Agreement commits countries to limiting global warming to well below 2°C while pursuing efforts to keep the increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. However, the reports state that current warming, estimated at 1.37°C, is already threatening the Arctic, Antarctic, mountain glaciers and polar oceans.

Researchers also point to visible damage, including the loss of approximately 20 percent of Switzerland’s glacial mass, and warn that crossing critical climate tipping points could lead to long-lasting changes even if temperatures later decline.

Despite the warnings, scientists say limiting warming and eventually returning to 1.5°C or lower remains possible with stronger political commitment and faster reductions in fossil fuel use.

Glaciers and sea ice may recover some of their losses if temperatures decline, but researchers caution that recovery could take decades or centuries.

World.title: ISSA clears KC of quota rule breach following Vauxhall complaint
World.content:
Samaure Taylor of Kingston College commits a foul against Astley Montaque of Vauxhall High during their ISSA Manning Cup match played at Stadium East in Kingston on Saturday October 31,2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) has cleared Kingston College (KC) of any breach of its quota rule after dismissing an allegation made by Vauxhall High concerning the eligibility of four players on the North Street-based school’s under-19 football team.

In a letter dated November 2, 2026, and addressed to Vauxhall’s principal, ISSA’s Competitions Department said its investigation confirmed that all four players identified in the complaint were legitimately registered to Kingston College.

The allegation, made by Vauxhall, identified the four active players on KC’s roster as quota players, raising questions about whether the school had breached ISSA’s quota regulations.

However, a review of ISSA’s registration database found that Kingston College was within its rights to field all four players.

The investigation did identify an issue involving the classification of one of the players, who began representing KC in 2025 after being admitted to its sixth-form programme from a private institution.

The player had previously been registered by an ISSA member school during the 2021-2022 academic year, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, but was subsequently designated as a non-quota player.

According to ISSA, that designation was removed before the player’s registration and participation for Kingston College in 2025.

The association explained that the decision was based on the absence of evidence that the student had represented any ISSA member school before his registration at Kingston College, despite having been listed on ISSA’s registration database for more than four years.

ISSA said its findings supported KC’s right to use all four players identified in Vauxhall’s complaint.

“The findings therefore suggest that Kingston College would be well within their rights to play all four players identified in the allegation,” the letter stated.

The association added that the checks and balances undertaken by its Competitions Department would have provided the necessary clearance for all four players to participate.

The ruling removes the eligibility cloud hanging over Kingston College following Vauxhall’s complaint and confirms that the school did not breach ISSA’s quota rule in relation to the four players.

Kingston College had defeated Vauxhall High 3-1 in their opening Zone 3 match at the Stadium East on Saturday.

World.title: ‘Weh Di Money Deh?’: Beenie Man takes hurricane relief criticism to studio
World.content:
Recording artiste Moses "Beenie Man" Davis (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Dancehall veteran Beenie Man is taking his criticism of the Government’s Hurricane Melissa relief efforts to the recording studio, teasing a new song titled We Di Money Deh, which questions the distribution of assistance to Jamaicans still struggling to rebuild their lives following the devastating storm.

The entertainer shared snippets of the unreleased track on Instagram, showing himself in the studio while listening to the song which echoes concerns about accountability, transparency and the pace of hurricane recovery efforts.

“Music has always been a voice for the people,” Beenie Man wrote in the caption accompanying the videos.

“Taking you inside the studio as we bring We Di Money Deh to life, a song inspired by the concerns of Jamaicans still waiting for help as they rebuild their lives from the hurricane,” he added, announcing that the track would be released soon.

In the snippets, the dancehall icon repeatedly questions the whereabouts of relief funds while highlighting the plight of Jamaicans still in need of basic necessities.

“Weh di money deh? Tell mi weh it reach,” he sings, before declaring, “Everybody want a roof when the rain come down.”

The song also appears to take aim at political divisions, referencing the colours associated with Jamaica’s two major political parties, in the lyrics: “Green and orange, everybody bleed, help must follow we.”

The forthcoming release comes amid a public exchange between the Grammy-winning entertainer and Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness over the Government’s handling of hurricane recovery funds.

During Wednesday’s reopening of the Black River Hospital in St Elizabeth, Holness appeared to respond to Beenie Man over his recent criticism, suggesting that the artiste should have been invited to witness the Government’s recovery efforts firsthand.

The prime minister disclosed that more than $300 million of the Government’s $3.8 billion post-hurricane allocation to the health sector had been spent rebuilding the hospital.

“[With] all the dignitaries… who are here, I thought to myself the Minister [of Health Dr Christopher Tufton] neglected to invite Beenie Man, because then he would see first-hand how the Government has been spending on the recovery,” Holness said.

READ: WATCH: Holness hits back at Beenie Man after Hurricane Melissa relief comments

His remarks followed an interview Beenie Man gave to British broadcaster ITV News, during which the entertainer questioned how millions of dollars in donations intended for hurricane victims were being distributed.

“This is nothing new that the Government get the money, the Government distribute the money the wrong way. The people who supposed to get the money haven’t been getting any,” Beenie Man claimed.

“These things, it’s a regular thing that happens. The money comes in and you nuh see where it go,” he added.

READ: ‘You don’t see where the money go’: Beenie Man criticises Gov’t hurricane relief spending

A release date for the track has not yet been announced.

World.title: Holness in Antigua for Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Prime Minister Andrew Holness is currently in Antigua and Barbuda, where he is leading Jamaica’s delegation to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

Holness is scheduled to participate in a leaders’ roundtable on Monday morning alongside Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Rwandan President Paul Kagame and two other world leaders.

The Jamaican delegation also includes Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith.

During the conference, Holness is expected to hold bilateral talks with Kagame before representing Jamaica at the Enterprise and Investment Summit on Monday afternoon.

Jamaica is among just five countries whose heads of government have been invited to address the summit.

The meeting, which runs from November 1 to 4 in St John’s, is being held under the theme “Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth”. King Charles III, head of the Commonwealth, is also in attendance.

Holness’ participation comes against the backdrop of a government directive imposing an immediate moratorium on official overseas travel across the public sector until March 31, 2027.

The measure, introduced to contain expenditure and redirect resources towards recovery and reconstruction following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa, applies to Cabinet ministers, ministers of state, permanent secretaries, senior public officers, heads of government agencies and other public sector personnel.

The restriction is to remain in place for the rest of the 2026/2027 financial year, subject to limited exceptions.

According to a government memorandum, the widespread destruction caused by the hurricane has placed significant pressure on Jamaica’s fiscal resources, prompting the administration to prioritise spending on national reconstruction.

READ: Gov’t halts overseas travel for public officials until March 2027

World.title: Glimmer of hope
World.content:
Merl Grove High School on Constant Spring Road, St Andrew (Naplhtai Junior)

A tenuous hope sparked at the weekend, following a decisive intervention by the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information, into the protracted five-year dispute that has shaken the

Merl Grove High School community.

The ministry’s Regional Educational Services, last Friday, mobilised an estimated 100 Merl Grove stakeholders and interested parties to the dispute which has pitted the school board, led by Chairman David Hall, against the principal of the institution, Dr Marjorie Fullerton.

Ahead of the meeting held under the theme ‘Restore, Rebuild, Renew’, the ministry advised the school to request parents to have their children study at home for the day, apparently to spare them any potential tension that could ensue.

But Jamaica Observer sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said in the hours before the gathering, the ministry turned down a request from the principal to have representatives accompany her to the meeting.

These would include her lawyer; the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA); the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS); a colleague school principal; and a human resource expert.

In particular, Fullerton wanted the school’s alumni association or alumni stakeholders to attend, “given the significant role that alumni continue to play in the development, support, and advancement of Merl Grove High School”, the sources said.

However, the ministry’s lead person explained that the discussions had not yet reached the stage where that level of representation was necessary but would be considered for the appropriate stage.

The meeting was being spearheaded by the ministry not as a formal hearing, but to allow internal stakeholders to express their concerns and work towards achieving a more harmonious and conducive environment, the sources told the

Observer.

In the end, the ministry agreed that the alumni representatives could attend as requested by Dr Fullerton. The newspaper also spotted two of her principal colleagues on the school compound Friday.

Adding a touch of drama to the day’s events, a group of teachers dressed in black carried out a silent protest on the campus.

The

Observer learned Sunday that the ministry would be reviewing the outcome of the discussions for a follow-up meeting to be decided. Some stakeholders said they were hopeful that the meeting would achieve a resolution but suggested that some of the issues were thorny and would require patience and a willingness to end the dispute.

“A lot of water has gone under the bridge. Egos were bruised and people felt that they were being slighted, hence the level of angst you are seeing,” a source, who attended the meeting, said.

The debacle at Merl Grove High School exploded into public view on September 10, 2021 after the controversial suspension of Principal Fullerton, whose appointment in 2015 set off a nasty struggle with Vice-Principal Loretta Ricketts.

What started off as a struggle between the two key leaders at the school, escalated into “all-out war” between the principal and Hall’s church-dominated school board which apparently sided with the vice-principal, resulting in the suspension and then dismissal of Dr Fullerton in 2022.

A March 2026 ruling by the Supreme Court of Jamaica, that Fullerton be reinstated, and intervention and prayers by the Assemblies of God church failed to douse the in-fighting, with Fullerton complaining that she been locked out of the school e-mail and the financial accounts, and not paid for the four years while she fought her dismissal in the courts.

Concerned about how the internal fight has been affecting students, the Merl Grove Parents Teachers’ Association (PTA) in September declared: “…whatever disagreements may exist between parents, the administration, or other stakeholders, students should never be made to carry the burden of those differences or be placed in circumstances where they feel caught between the adults responsible for their education and welfare”.

The JAPSS, worried about the circumstances under which Dr Fullerton had been working, last week entered the fray, requesting a meeting with the school board to seek a resolution.

“Our intention is to engage in a respectful and solution-oriented discussion with a view to exploring opportunities for mediation and facilitating an amicable and sustainable resolution that supports Dr Fullerton in the effective discharge of her duties, and advances the best interests of Merl Grove High and its wider community,” the JAPSS said.

For its part, the PTA urged the board of management and the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information “to move beyond informal interventions and undertake an objective and timely assessment of the present leadership situation”.

In summoning the stakeholders to Friday’s meeting, the ministry said: “Given the nature and frequency of the concerns raised by both parties in numerous e-mail communications, it is evident that substantive intervention is required to facilitate a resolution and strengthen the school’s governance and operational effectiveness.”

World.title: Breaking handout mentality one year after Hurricane Melissa
World.content:
Founder of Goals Have No Limits Foundation Anna-Kay McIntosh Richards has a discussion with her husband Rajay Richards on Saturday in Waterworks, Westmoreland.

WHILE many victims of the devastating October 28, 2025 Hurricane Melissa are still looking for handouts to get their lives back together — especially in western Jamaica — a native of Westmoreland, Anna-Kay McIntosh- Richards, returned to her hometown on Saturday to equip residents with knowledge that can turn their situations around, if applied properly.

Through her brainchild, Goals Have No Limit Foundation, she organised a team of volunteers to not only cook food and distribute it in Waterworks, Westmoreland — as well as distribute care packages — but, importantly, to impart knowledge about entrepreneurship and also how to make money from a social media-based business.

She brought in a team of young people from Kingston comprising her husband, brother, and church sisters to share “these very important messages to the people, who are still downtrodden and have found it difficult to rise above the devastation and trauma they faced last year”.

McIntosh-Richards also invited representatives from the State-run Forestry Department to spread messages about the importance of planting trees. There were other entities that were invited but which weren’t able to attend. However, that could not stop the mission, she insisted.

“The idea for us is to move people mentally from the state of, ‘If nobody brings it to us then we don’t have anything.’ We believe people have almost everything they need but lack training and empowerment to bring it out.

Even though we brought rice, sugar and flour for them, we can’t bring that every day because that is going to run out. We know that that need exists, but we wanted to go beyond that to see what we could help them with so that they can sustain themselves.

“We wanted to give to them ideas of how to restart their lives without saying that the Government didn’t bring anything and they are suffering. We are trying to break that mentality of them saying that they are poor and are paupers. If people don’t carry tangible things to you, what are the intangible things that you have — the skills, talents, gifts and ideas — that can materialise into helping yourself and other people, building businesses and achieving an income?” McIntosh-Richards told the Jamaica Observer.

She explained that the foundation was born in 2017 while she attended university. At that time, she would travel back to Westmoreland with a handful of friends to donate many things to the people, especially the children.

However, as time progressed and her volunteers started to focus on their own lives, the foundation’s work went on pause — until last year when Hurricane Melissa destroyed people’s homes and livelihoods, setting them back in a major way.

On Saturday, the compound of the Waterworks Church of God of Prophecy was the base McIntosh-Richards used to execute the event which attracted well over 50 people from the community, including children and the elderly.

There were appropriate activities for everyone from the different age groups. The children were engaged in a special session that allowed them to express themselves and were also taught lessons about resilience, based on the story of Job from the Bible.

In her interview with the Observer, McIntosh-Richards alluded to a conversation she had with pastor of the Waterworks Church of God of Prophecy, Reverend Damion Robinson, who expressed to her that the mindset of some of the people is the biggest obstacle they face in life.

She highlighted that many of the people received grants from the Government following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa one year ago, but failed to put the funds to good use and are still seeking handouts.

“As pastor rightfully said, some people are in the mindset of ‘We are Melissa victims and people should be coming to help us.’ A year later, it should be more than saying, ‘People need to see us, and all we have to do is stretch our hands.’ You can’t just sit there forever saying you don’t see anyone come to give you anything.

“Pastor said it that some of them got $200,000 grants and squandered it. How do you get those people to understand that they are living in a mindset that is going to be their defeat? No matter what people bring to you, your mindset and how you act and treat your reality is a part of a bigger issue. With that said, today was impactful for me,” she shared. “We planted a seed and we did well.

It may not have manifested in front of us like it did for one woman who came and said she was inspired, but there was somebody there who heard something that they are taking back with them — and if we continue to remind them, they will eventually act upon it. We don’t have a million dollars to give away; the real impact is giving people the opportunity to fish for themselves.

The idea is not just about feeding hungry people one day,” she said, emphasising that she had seen many foundations with large resources come and then disappear soon after, because whatever they sought to give to the people lacked the important element of sustainability.

Ann Salmon was one of the attendees who received instant inspiration from the event and the lessons that were imparted regarding entrepreneurship, especially. It relit a flame within her and brought back powerful memories of when her husband was alive and they operated a baking business together.

Just by being at the event at the church she started to explore ideas of how to jump back into business, but admitted she would need some help from the public to acquire a new stove with an oven, as well as some ingredients, to re-launch the bakery.

“The presentation was excellent, and it motivated me a lot to start back. It just reminded me of when we started baking and how I was taught to bake. My husband used to bake and ride and sell on the street in Savanna-La-Mar.

“He’d get orders from the people and he’d bake during Christmas time. He would get orders, like four cakes to one person, and we’d bring it to them. I was with him, walking and selling on the street. He’d ride his bicycle and go to Russia and all over Westmoreland.

People always liked our cake, and he always said to me that I was getting better than him,” she chuckled at the memory. She explained that whenever he became tired and could not manage too much of the workload, she would get up and do it on her own.

“Eleven years ago he died and I stopped, because every time I am to bake, I’d remember him and then I’d break down. But now, I’m ready to do it again because cake really sells, you know.

“I can make carrot cake and potato pudding — all of that, he taught me to make. Even oats cake. I just need a stove with an oven and some ingredients to start back. The devil made my phone drop in water, so people who would like to help can call my daughter to get through to me.

Her numbers are 876-892-2691 and 876-839-2440,” McIntosh-Richards said with a glint of hope in her eyes.

World.title: Waterworks church a tower of strength for Hurricane victims one year on
World.content:
Pastor Damian Robinson lifts his head and hands to the heavens inside what was once his main church hall. (Photo: Jamarie Thomas)

IN the immediate aftermath of the Category 5 Hurricane Melissa which destroyed numerous houses, crops, roads and other infrastructure in Westmoreland and other parts of the island — notably in the western end — on October 28 last year, Pastor Damian Robinson had to walk through hills and valleys just to locate members of his flock who were displaced by the disaster.

Prior to Melissa the official members of his flock numbered somewhere around 50 people, who all have numerous relatives indirectly connected to the church and who benefit from its services.

One year later, it has been a struggle for him to get things back to normal, but with God being his source of comfort and support, he shared, the man of God says he has decided that his church will not go down, despite losing its roof and almost everything of value during Hurricane Melissa.

“People are still hurting from the trauma they experienced during the hurricane, and even the very mention of Hurricane Melissa triggers an emotional breakdown among them,” said Robinson.

The Jamaica Observer visited the Church of God of Prophecy, Waterworks Tabernacle, in Westmoreland on Saturday, where Robinson has been the pastor for two years. He took the news team on a tour of what used to be the main church hall, as well as the tent outdoor where services are held these days. The tent is covered with tarpaulins.

Walking inside the main church hall on Saturday and looking up, one could only see the skies as there was absolutely no roof as he testified earlier.

“It has been a journey, and as I reflect on the passing of Hurricane Melissa and how I walked to find 98 per cent of my members — there were hilly terrains, there were roads, there were gullies, there were ponds, you know — [but] I was determined to walk and find them. Even when moments felt discouraging, I had to walk and find them because the other two per cent were elsewhere in St James or other parishes with their loved ones. I was glad to be able to give account for them as well.

“As I looked at the devastation, the question I asked the Lord was ‘God, do you think I’m able to still lead these people in this moment?’ It was terrible. Most of them lived on lands that are leased, and because of that, they were not able to have concrete structures. Most of them lived in wooden structures with zinc roofs. Majority of them ended up under tarpaulins that we sourced with the help of our national church and other donors and supporters. Some of them had to stay with loved ones who were living in concrete structures, and there were those who had to find other family members or relocate in Kingston and throughout the island,” Robinson said.

Tarpaulin became the most precious commodity of the day, Robinson added, pointing to a section of the church compound where services are now held in an outdoor setting. He explained that it has been a struggle trying to get things back to normal, but he is determined to ensure that normality is restored because the people are depending on him and the church in so many ways.

“What you see now is just an extended version of what we started with, because I remember when we just started in just a small area, the sun was there. By the time we started the service, the sun started coming in. So, we had to extend our worship; we had to watch where the sun would come from and we’d watch the time and adjust our church service during that time,” said the minister.

“There was one time we came into the lobby area, and it was just crammed. Where we worship now, we call it the Waterworks Tabernacle mini place of worship. It has been a journey,” he sighed.

But despite all the challenges and problems, he noted, people still put out the effort to come to church. He alluded to the fact that there were some who decided they had to get baptised in the immediate aftermath of the hurricane.

“It’s interesting to note that even after the passing of Hurricane Melissa, our numbers started climbing. I believe one of the contributing factors was the love we showed to the people, helping them to understand that there is more beyond the devastation. It was a moment for us to really show the love of God. Seeing what people were experiencing, it was that moment to show the love of God, so rich and pure, measureless and strong.

“To God be the glory, during that time we had over 12 persons getting saved. A month after the hurricane, the first baptism, we had three persons. The second month, we had four. It was a moment of reaping the seeds that we were sowing before Melissa — and this would include doing street meetings, going from door to door, and doing prayer walks. Melissa was another opportunity for the church to really show God.”

Though in need of a building, Robinson said the church remains a place of refuge where members of the community, whether they attend the church or not, can seek refuge and help.

“When a strange vehicle drives in on the church property, you know, everybody comes from every where to see what is coming. Is it appalling? Is it a care package? Is it food? The need is still great. Our church ground was used as the hub for most of these donors or sponsors, organisations or foundations, to use as a distribution point. A strange vehicle, a big vehicle, meant that something is coming. During that time it was like, ‘What’s coming next for me?’

“There are still many people under tarpaulins, trying to put the pieces back together. There are still steps that need to be taken. As you asked about our own building, now we’ll have to get a plan — a properly drawn plan, you know, by an architect, not just from our national office — to submit to them, but also the other regulatory bodies, you know, to ensure that we are building a resilient building.

“I want to be careful not to sound ungrateful but there is a part of you that says, ‘Oh boy,’ when [things get difficult], you get what a mean? Now and again it [that feeling] comes, and the feeling of discouragement, you know? But, there’s hope. We have a church who adopted us. We have persons who live overseas who, from time to time, send some money.

“We have foundations such as Goals Have No Limit Foundation that would come in and just be there for the people. In terms of the great financial help, we’re not seeing it yet. We are hopeful, and I believe that as we put things in place the Lord will open the doors for us to build back.”

World.title: Kevin Downswell to release Joy Is Here album
World.content:
Kevin Downwell (Photo: Cavaughn Edwards)

Gospel singer-songwriter Kevin Downswell is describing his fifth studio album, Joy Is Here, as his most vulnerable and personal project to date, reflecting the experiences, spiritual growth, and renewed convictions that have shaped his life.

The 10-track album was previewed during an intimate listening session at Tuff Gong Studios in Kingston on Thursday, October 22, where members of the music industry and media were given insight into the inspiration behind the music.

“If I never dropped the album this year I would have missed something. I don’t know if it was somebody who needed these kinds of songs — maybe it’s one; maybe it’s a thousand, or a million. You know when you just have that urgency? It feels like the most perfect thing I’ve ever done,” Downswell told the Jamaica Observer following the private listening.

The evening unfolded as a mixture of celebration, reflection, and worship, with several selections keeping guests rocking and dancing, while others moved some attendees to tears through their relatable and spiritually uplifting messages.

In an unconventional approach, guests were divided into groups to listen to selected tracks and share their interpretations before Downswell offered further insight into the inspiration behind each song. He also explored the recurring theme of rising higher despite life’s challenges.

The interactive concept was developed by music industry strategist and media communications executive Judith Bodley, who sought to encourage meaningful engagement between the artiste and his audience.

The album features collaborations with Papa San on Who Could It Be But God, Minister Marion Hall on You Remembered Me, Gramps Morgan on The Reason, and PantaSon on Bless Me. Other featured artistes include Kenya’s Moji Babaa and Samuel Medas.

For Downswell, working with entertainers from different musical backgrounds provides an opportunity to share his Christian faith with wider audiences.

“The kind of love and respect that I get from these artistes, I can’t find words. Gramps Morgan being on this album is one of the humblest things ever. Plus, Gramps is on the album talking about Jesus Christ; it’s the most amazing thing you could ever see,” he shared. “It’s humbling to be able to pull men who are used to a particular genre and have them declare Jesus Christ on your platform.”

The singer previously collaborated with dancehall veteran Bounty Killer on Call Him, a partnership that initially attracted criticism from some quarters.

“I got some lashing for it, and then a few months later the same people came back and said, ‘Now I see what you were doing.’ They recognised that Bounty didn’t pull me over, I was the one who pulled him over, because they saw changes,” Downswell recalled.

He maintained that, while artistes retain their individual musical identities, his Christian convictions remain non-negotiable.

“Anytime I am with an artiste, no matter where they are, it’s no compromise. It’s Jesus Christ every time,” he added.

Beyond the collaborations, Joy Is Here explores themes of gratitude, perseverance, divine reassurance, and spiritual growth through songs such as Higher (From the Fire), He’s Not Done With You Yet, and It’s Okay, I Got You.

Downswell also acknowledged the musicians who contributed to the production, including musical director and bassist Rhon Matthison, drummer Wendell Lawrence, keyboardists Chris Wright and Wade Johnson, and lead guitarist Brandon Benjamin.

The event was hosted by Love 101’s Sara-Ann Miller, with DJ Rebirth providing musical entertainment.

Among those in attendance was Downswell’s mentor, Dr Henley Morgan, who expressed pride in the singer’s artistic development. Guests from the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and other Caribbean territories were also present.

Downswell said his greatest desire is for the songs to resonate with people navigating everyday challenges and encourage them to find strength in their faith.

“My greatest desire is to see a girl with her earphones in heading to school singing, It’s Okay, I Got You; or a man driving and singing, ‘Your love lifts me higher’ — that is my greatest desire. Let everything else come after,” he said. “Let these songs get our eyes off ourselves and our battles and put them on the one who matters most.”

Joy Is Here has been available for pre-order before its October 30 release.

World.title: Yvonne Grinam-Nicholson on a roll; PhD followed by Canadian award
World.content:
Dr Yvonne Grinam-Nicholson, director of consumer and public affairs at the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR), and director-general of the OUR Ansord Hewitt

Determined that 2026 would be the year to finally grab hold of her Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), Yvonne Grinam-Nicholson did not expect a double accolade — that of the Women in Energy Award conceived by the Canadian Government and implemented by the High Commission of Canada in Jamaica.

Along with three other women — Jamaican Winsome Callum of the Jamaica Public Service, Melissa Newman of Jamaica Energy Partners, and Sheree Ebanks of the Caribbean Utilities Company Limited, Cayman Islands — Grinam-Nicholson, director of consumer and public affairs at the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR), is counting her lucky stars. But she knows that neither of her twin rewards came easily or by favours.

The Woman in Energy Awards “recognise and celebrate the extraordinary achievements of women who have made significant contributions to their country’s energy sector”.

The PhD is only for the dogged few willing to sacrifice sleep and numerous things in-between.

No wonder a proud hubby, A J Nicholson, the former attorney general and justice minister, was beside himself over his “incomparable life partner’s achievement”.

“Yvonne has made us so very proud. She is so talented! She has made me into a proud, cheerful, fulfilled human being; my family has been richly blessed and uplifted!” said A J, as he is affectionately called.

The energy award citation stated: “Canada proudly honours Yvonne Joyce Grinam Nicholson, PhD, for her contribution to consumer protection, regulatory governance, and public understanding within Jamaica’s utilities sector.

“At the Office of Utilities Regulation, Yvonne has spent more than a decade helping to place consumer experience at the centre of regulatory oversight. Her work has included national consumer satisfaction surveys; mystery-shopping research; and the development of communication strategies, programmes, and policies designed to strengthen the voice of Jamaicans in the governance of their utility services.

“Her expertise has also had international reach. As a technical volunteer and regional expert with NARUC and USAID, Yvonne has supported energy regulators in Nigeria, Zambia, and Bangladesh in strengthening complaints handling, stakeholder engagement, and protections for vulnerable customers.

“She led the planning committee for the 2016 and 2026 OOCUR Conference in Jamaica, a major regional gathering of utility regulators.

“In financial regulation, her earlier contributions to the Jamaica Stock Exchange included conceptualising stakeholder engagement and investor education programmes, the JSE Best Practices Awards, the JSE e-Campus, and its regional Conference on Investments and the Capital Markets.

“She has a PhD in communication studies from The University of the West Indies, Mona, and is an Accredited Business Communicator.

“Yvonne has built a career at the intersection of communication, consumer protection and accountable governance.

“Her leadership demonstrates the important role of informed and engaged consumers in building energy and utility sectors that are responsive, transparent, and trusted.”

Grinam-Nicholson, began her professional career as a journalist at The Gleaner and Jampress, the now-defunct government national news agency.

Across her career, she has combined strategic communication, research, education, and regulatory engagement to strengthen institutional credibility and public understanding in sectors that directly affect national development. Her body of work positions her as a respected professional at the intersection of consumer protection, utilities regulation, financial services education, and stakeholder-centred governance.

The award was presented by High Commissioner of Canada to Jamaica Mark Berman on October 15, 2026 at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel, New Kingston.

World.title: Les lobbies du tabac mettent le paquet à Bruxelles, alors que l’UE se penche sur le secteur
World.content:
Philip Morris International, le fabricant des cigarettes Marlboro, dont le nombre de réunions est le plus élevé parmi toutes les entreprises du secteur du tabac, a souligné sa contribution à l’économie européenne et a indiqué qu’être “engagée dans une profonde transformation vers un avenir sans tabac”.

“Nous sommes fiers de contribuer au dialogue démocratique et de dialoguer avec tout député européen, quel que soit son groupe politique, qui soit disposé à discuter en s’appuyant sur la science et les faits, ainsi que sur notre détermination à faire partie de la solution”, a déclaré le groupe, qui commercialise également des sachets de nicotine, des cigarettes électroniques et des produits du tabac chauffés.

Débat sur les traités internationaux

L’une des craintes soulevées par Tilly Metz et d’autres députés européens est de savoir si les règles antitabac de l’OMS sont correctement respectées.

Sa Convention-cadre stipule que les politiques de santé publique doivent être protégées contre les intérêts commerciaux de l’industrie du tabac. Elle n’interdit pas le lobbying, mais les lignes directrices relatives à la mise en œuvre du traité précisent que les décideurs politiques doivent limiter leurs interactions avec ce secteur au strict nécessaire aux fins de sa réglementation, et garantir la transparence de ces réunions.

L’industrie affirme qu’elle respecte les règles et expose son point de vue en toute transparence. Elle invoque également un arrêt rendu en 2022 par la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne, selon lequel le traité n’interdit pas sa participation à la mise en œuvre de la lutte antitabac ; il “vise uniquement à empêcher que les politiques de lutte antitabac des parties à la convention ne soient influencées par les intérêts de cette industrie”.

Par ailleurs, le secteur fait valoir que la Convention-cadre de l’OMS ne couvre pas les produits à base de nicotine sans tabac. Ces produits sont particulièrement visés par un durcissement de la réglementation, alors que l’Europe s’apprête à revoir les règles relatives aux produits du tabac et à la publicité, ainsi que les taxes minimales au niveau du continent.

World.title: Berlin unveils blueprint to catch up on AI
World.content:
Germany wants to secure access to the world’s leading models while strengthening European alternatives, particularly through expanded cooperation with France and Canada, according to the report.

“We are leveraging collaborations with like-minded partners in the EU and worldwide (especially France and Canada) to benefit the German AI ecosystem and ensure sovereign access,” the report noted. “We will also use intra-European collaborations,” such as with French AI company Mistral, “to achieve this leverage,” its authors added.

At the same time, “AI made in Germany” should stand out through its focus on industrial AI with “highly specialized models,” the report read.

“A key focus here is the development of innovative production systems to increase productivity through the use of AI,” the report noted. “The widespread use of AI and AI-based robotics can boost productivity and quality, optimize industrial processes, and improve control over complex systems.”

To help speed up the development of AI in Germany, the government plans to act as a “strategic anchor customer,” using public contracts and pilot projects to help European AI providers enter the market.

The plan comes as Germany struggles to catch up on AI while cultivating more strategic autonomy in the area. Much of the blueprint, however, lacks key details, including on financing. The measures “neither constitute funding decisions nor prejudge” future budget procedures, according to the report.

World.title: Europe’s supermarkets hit by new wave of cyberattacks targeting fridges
World.content:
It’s not confirmed that the attacks are connected or used the same software vulnerabilities that hit French chains, though one supermarket spokesperson said the incident is a cyberattack “similar to the one in France.”

Ken Munro, a cybersecurity researcher, said in an interview that supermarkets should have disconnected their refrigerators and the devices used to monitor and remotely manage them from the Internet. “I don't accept any other excuse … particularly in light of the earlier [attacks in France],” he said.

Inti De Ceukelaire, another cyber researcher, also said the incident suggests supermarkets did not take the necessary steps even after the France attacks. “It seems that some of them simply did not get patched, which is quite ridiculous,” he said.

Belgian media reported on Monday morning that temperatures in supermarket refrigerators had suddenly spiked, forcing them to throw food away. A spokesperson for the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium said the agency is “closely” following the incident, adding that the attackers are unknown and that it “may never be possible to identify them.”

John Billow, director of Sweden's National Cyber Security Centre, told POLITICO that there are "similarities" to the French incidents and that the agency is in touch with affected organizations. A European Commission spokesperson said it's aware of the incidents and is using the EU-Cyclone network to coordinate and share information.

Following France

French supermarkets were hit with a wave of similar incidents in mid-October, when attackers targeted refrigerators by Danfoss, a Danish manufacturer of store fridges. Danfoss did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The attacks in France triggered a response from the country’s prime minister and its cybersecurity agency.

World.title: King mulls De Wever’s resignation as Belgian budget talks fail
World.content:
After De Wever offered his resignation Monday morning, the palace said the king was “postponing his decision” and “will begin consultations tomorrow with the party leaders of the various coalition partners.” It added that the king “is appealing to everyone’s sense of responsibility and urges all stakeholders to prioritize the general interest and a spirit of compromise.”

The prime minister is expected to meet the king again on Friday.

De Wever had ruled out starting the new year with a temporary budget, which would let the government continue with the same budget as last year’s.

Budget talks have been ongoing for weeks, with tensions emerging mostly between the Flemish socialists of Forward and the Francophone center-right Reformist Movement.

The former asked for more contributions from the highest incomes, through taxes, while the latter ruled that out and pushed back against a wider reform of value-added tax.

There were still “far too many taxes on the table,” David Clarinval, deputy prime minister for the Reformist Movement, told reporters when talks broke up. He didn’t rule out discussions resuming today.

World.title: Has Shabana Mahmood won her immigration tussle?
World.content:
Are domestic political battles about to collide with diplomatic challenges for the prime minister?

As Andy Burnham jets off to the Caribbean, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood prepares to unveil one of the government’s most contentious policies: a major crackdown on legal migration.

A year after the plans were first proposed, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy look at whether Labour has quashed the internal rebellion and how much influence Angela Rayner has had on the PM’s position.

Plus, as the Commonwealth Summit gets underway in Antigua, the prime minister has issues to address on the international front — from potential reparations for slavery to U.S. and Chinese influence over the Caribbean.

World.title: Canada, coffins and confessionals
World.content:
The jet lag has barely worn off, but Brussels is already grappling with what its new relationship with Canada could actually look like.

After the 48-hour whirlwind EU-Canada summit in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney has given the EU six months to hash out what “associate membership” actually means. On the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur unpack the deals struck at the summit and what lies ahead for the relations between the two powers.

Next, after last month’s unwieldy European Council summit drew criticism of its president, Antonio Costa, he’s doubling down on his push to secure a budget by 2027. This week, his head of cabinet Pedro Lourtie will be holding so-called “confessionals” with national governments to get a sense of where they stand.

And finally, Europe’s coffin makers are afraid Chinese competitors could be the death of their business.

World.title: Allies fear Trump will target NATO in case of midterm loss
World.content:
“Usually what happens to lame duck presidents is a mix of venting frustrations and adventurism in foreign policy,” said one senior European defense official. And attacking NATO “seems to be a consistent part of [the] Trump worldview.”

White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told POLITICO that “President Trump has done more for NATO than anyone else,” citing his successes in securing agreements by allies to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, bolster U.S. military presence in Greenland, and efforts to end Russia's all-out war in Ukraine.

Yet he “remains firm that our NATO allies should have been there for the United States” over the war in Iran, she said, adding: “The President will never settle for the West’s managed decline and will continue to unapologetically advance our interests at home and abroad.”

Democrats are widely expected to win the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate, while Trump’s personal approval ratings have fallen to his lowest on record.

The worries underscore growing transatlantic tensions after a U.S. cutoff of Starlink satellite services for Ukraine and a fresh rapprochement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin weeks before the midterms. Further attacks would deal a fresh blow to NATO, just as Russia steps up its sabotage campaign and so-called hybrid war across Europe.

“He could be very pissed off,” said one of the NATO diplomats. If so, “he’ll be very harsh.”

World.title: British government sets out tougher rules for migrants looking to settle in the UK
World.content:
The British government on Monday set out its new "earned settlement model," which will double the amount of time many foreign workers must wait before they are eligible to settle permanently in the United Kingdom.

 

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood confirmed that the qualifying period for "indefinite leave to remain" (ILR) in the UK would jump from five years to 10 years for most workers. ILR gives a person the right to live, work and study in the country for as long as they wish.

High earners will be able to settle "within" three years, while those earning more than £50,271 (around €60,200), as well as some public service workers - including doctors, nurses and teachers – will be able to settle after five years, according to the Labour government.

Mahmood also announced exemptions for care workers following backlash from unions and some figures within the ruling Labour Party to initial proposals to tighten settlement rules.

"Those who earn £25,000 (roughly €29,900) a year working in the social sector care, which was the condition of their visa, will therefore be able to settle on their existing five-year pathway," Mahmood told parliament.

She said the revised policy recognised the service of those who had "worked hard and answered our call when we needed them."

The announcement followed a consultation period that saw the government receive more than 200,000 responses. It said the process had seen people raised concerns about "fairness, complexity and the effect on people already in the UK" but that there was also "support for a system that better recognises contribution, integration and compliance."

The government said its guiding principle moving forward was that "settlement should be earned rather than granted on the basis of time alone."

Under the new policy, people found to have breached immigration rules will have to wait 20 years to settle.

"Anyone who arrived by small boat, or another clandestine means of entry, will face an additional 10-year waiting period – meaning they could wait up to 30 years for settlement," the government said.

Refugees who arrive on approved routes will be able to apply for settlement after five years.

The new rules are reportedly due to come into effect next year. People who already have settled status will not be impacted.

In a statement, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the country had "lost control of immigration" following the divisive Brexit vote to leave the European Union.

"This Home Secretary is gripping this problem, and she has my full support in doing so," he added.

It comes amid increasing pressure from Britain's right, including from Nigel Farage's Reform UK party, over immigration.

Reform has pledged to scrap indefinite leave to remain should it get into power, instead bringing in a "five-year renewable work visa."

World.title: Britain’s 'oldest cars' hit the road for annual London to Brighton run
World.content:
Britain's motoring history took to the streets of London on Sunday, 1 November, as veteran cars took part in the annual London to Brighton Veteran Car Run.

 

The 97km journey from Hyde Park to the south coast saw some vehicles travelling at just 12 to 20 mph. The event marked 140 years since Karl Benz introduced his Patent-Motorwagen, widely regarded as the first production car.

One vehicle even broke down on The Mall, highlighting the mechanical challenges of driving these early models.

For participants, the run is as much about the experience as the destination. Driving a car from the early days of motoring requires patience and a good understanding of its mechanics.

Shaun Harborne, at the wheel of a 1901 Renault Type D, described the vehicles as fragile, with their suspension, brakes, clutch and gearbox all requiring careful handling.

Karl-Heinz Jungbeck, who travelled from Munich in a 1903 Lacoste & Battmann, said the event offers a taste of the adventure motorists would have experienced more than a century ago.

World.title: Ukraine says hopes of 'progress toward peace' knocked by attack on aid distribution centre
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said any hopes of "progress toward peace" following a localised truce last week had been dampened by deadly Russian strikes on an aid distribution centre in southeastern Ukraine.

 

The aerial bomb attack in the region of Zaporizhzhia killed at least 26 people, including two rescue workers and four police officers, on Monday, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS). Five others were also reportedly injured in the strikes.

Ivan Fedorov, the regional governor, said Russian forces had fired "at least nine KAB-3000 bombs" on the Komyshuvakha settlement throughout the day.

"All emergency services are working flat out at the scene, while municipal workers are clearing the rubble," he wrote in a post on Telegram.

Zelenskyy called it an "utterly horrific" attack, saying it had targeted "a school used for humanitarian purposes" where some people were receiving aid.

"After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover," he wrote on X.

Images shared by the DSNS from the scene show a building reduced to a pile of rubble and what appears to be a burned-out bus.

Russia 'counting on more killings'

In his post, Zelenskyy said the attacks had also knocked hopes of moving closer to a peace deal.

"After the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible," he wrote. Evacuees from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region arrived in Ukraine on Saturday after travelling through Belarus amid a rare humanitarian truce between Kyiv and Moscow.

But Zelenskyy said the Zaporizhzhia attack showed Russia was "sending an entirely opposite signal" and that it was "counting on more killings."

"There must be a response to this – a response from the world. A strong and tough response," he added.

Authorities in Kherson said Russia had resumed attacks on the region on Monday following a drone strike on the Korabelny district.

A 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man reportedly sustained blast injuries in the attack.

World.title: Recent virus outbreaks show urgent need to complete pandemic treaty, says WHO chief
World.content:
Deadly outbreaks such as the Ebola Bundibugyo virus currently spreading in Africa show the urgent need to complete an international pandemic treaty, World Health Organization (WHO) chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Monday during a negotiating meeting in Geneva.

 

Wealthy countries and developing nations remain at odds over how the Pandemic Treaty, adopted last year as a framework to handle future COVID-like pandemics, will work in practice.

When countries adopted the Pandemic Agreement in May 2025, they left out the tricky issue of how its key mechanism would operate, to get the deal over the line.

The agreement’s Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system governs how pathogens with pandemic potential can be obtained, and how products derived from them, such as vaccines, tests and treatments, are distributed.

Pointing to several recent deadly disease outbreaks caused by the new Ebola strain and hantavirus, Tedros stressed that completing a pandemic treaty was "about protecting people".

"A pathogen threat anywhere can become a threat everywhere, to people of every country," he said, according to a written version of his statement. "The outbreak of hantavirus earlier this year, and the ongoing Ebola epidemic in DRC remind us of this threat."

Tedros highlighted that, during the COVID-19 pandemic, “the world developed vaccines in record time, but too many countries were left waiting while others secured far more than they needed”.

“Timely access to vaccines and affordable medicines was a recurring concern raised by Member States during my meetings across all six WHO regions”, Hans Kluge, WHO Regional Director for Europe, currently on special leave as he is running for WHO Director-General.

“That is why we need a system where countries can quickly share pathogen samples and data, while ensuring that the vaccines, tests and treatments developed from them are shared fairly,” he said in a post on X, adding that the world cannot afford to repeat the inequalities we witnessed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: Climber rescued after being abandoned at 2,600 metres in Austrian Alps
World.content:
A German climber was rescued from the Austrian Alps over the weekend after being left behind by his two companions.

 

The 20-year-old man was eventually found at around 2,600 metres above sea level after a 14-hour rescue operation, according to the Austrian Mountain Rescue Service.

'Life-threatening for everyone'

The man set off as part of a trio along the Königsjodler trail on the Hochkönig mountain range on Saturday afternoon despite poor weather forecasts and a reported warning from another climber, the service said in a statement.

"At around 2,600 metres, one of the three Germans was unable to continue and made an emergency call at around 7 pm," it continued. "His companions nevertheless continued their ascent and reached the (already closed) Matrashaus (2,941 m) that same night."

A team from the Mühlbach Mountain Rescue Service was alerted and made their way to the "exhausted" climber.

“Even the ascent was challenging for our rescue team due to the prevailing weather conditions,” Wolfgang Haggenmüller, head of operations and local station manager for the Mühlbach team, said.

The rescue operation was complicated by the fact that a helicopter rescue crew was unable to fly due to the conditions.

Further heavy snowfall overnight made things even more difficult, but rescuers were able to reach the man shortly before midnight.

“He was roped up for the descent through deep snow. Around 20 cm of snow had fallen and the path was no longer visible; there was a risk of falling, and finding the way was very difficult," per the Mühlbach Mountain Rescue Service. "It was life-threatening for everyone. Amidst heavy snowfall and poor visibility, our team did not reach the Erichhütte until 8.18 am.”

The mountain rescuers also made only slow progress in the snowstorm Bergrettung Salzburg auf Instagram

Gerhard Kremser, the district manager of the Pongau Mountain Rescue Service, said the man likely would not have survived another night on the mountain due to the conditions.

"This operation shows once again how quickly overconfidence, a disregard for warnings and poor route planning can lead to a life-threatening situation. Mountaineering also means turning back in good time," he added.

Police have reportedly launched an investigation into the incident.

World.title: Inside Milipol Qatar, where drones and robots take on security and emergency response roles
World.content:
Milipol Qatar brought together around 280 companies from 33 countries in Doha, showcasing technology for security and emergency response. Exhibitors demonstrated how drones, robots and AI systems could support work ranging from traffic management to search and rescue.

 

Among the exhibits were a drone carrying traffic lights, a van fitted out as a mobile command centre and a remotely operated robot. Companies also explained how aerial photographs could help locate missing people and how boats could carry out missions without anyone on board.

Alongside the demonstrations, exhibitors discussed the role of human operators and the checks needed when using AI. Across the different applications, a common aim was to gather information and carry out tasks in places that could be dangerous for people.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”
