World.title: Trump touts Washington makeover as midterm campaign nears end
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump devoted his final public remarks before Tuesday’s midterm elections to touting renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, while Democrats sought to contain a rift in Michigan’s closely fought U.S. Senate race.

Over the weekend, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitter contest, switched to backing Republican Mike Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church. The race is critical to Democrats’ hopes of ending the 53-47 Senate majority of Trump’s Republicans in Tuesday’s vote.

In his only public remarks scheduled for Monday, Trump, a former real-estate developer, spent more than 20 minutes discussing pipes, joints, caulking, granite resurfacing, algae and leaks at the belated reopening of the Washington reflecting pool.

World.title: Long COVID recovery varies sharply by symptoms, study finds
World.content:
People whose long COVID affects multiple body systems are far less likely to improve than overall recovery estimates suggest, with fewer than one in five experiencing sustained improvement within three years of infection, according to a U.S. study.

Researchers followed 1,019 adults who still had probable long COVID a year after their initial infection. About half experienced sustained symptom improvement over the following three years, while roughly a quarter had complete symptom remission, the study, published Monday in Annals of Internal Medicine, found.

But outcomes differed dramatically depending on the pattern of illness. About 60% of people whose long COVID was dominated by changes in smell or taste had improved by three years, compared with less than 19% of those with symptoms affecting multiple body systems.

Long COVID can cause fatigue, cognitive impairment and post-exertional malaise — a worsening of symptoms after even modest physical or mental activity — along with problems involving numerous organ systems. There is no approved treatment for the condition.

The study, part of the U.S. National Institutes of Health-funded Recover initiative, tracked symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath and changes in smell or taste. Participants were considered to have improved when their symptom score remained below the threshold for likely long COVID at two successive study visits.

But the scoring system gives substantial weight to loss of smell or taste and chronic cough, said Ziyad Al-Aly, director of the Clinical Epidemiology Center at the VA St. Louis Health Care System, who wasn’t involved in the research. Although characteristic of COVID-19 infection, those symptoms aren’t central features of the chronic multisystem illness he associates with long COVID.

The multisystem group “is a different disease altogether,” Al-Aly said. “This is the real long COVID that will endure, and these patients do not appear to show a robust trajectory of recovery.”

The findings also illustrate a broader problem in determining how many people recover from long COVID: What counts as recovery.

The symptom index used in the study was developed using data from the Recover initiative and hasn’t been independently validated in other populations, said Nisreen Alwan, a professor of public health at the University of Southampton.

Long COVID symptoms can also fluctuate, with periods of improvement followed by relapse. Alwan and a colleague argued in the BMJ in June that inconsistent definitions make it difficult to distinguish lasting recovery from temporary remission.

World.title: Russian army suffers record losses in Ukraine as land gains slip
World.content:
The Russian military suffered record casualties in Ukraine last month while also ceding some territory to Kyiv’s forces, according to Western intelligence data and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

More than 54,000 Russian troops were killed and heavily wounded in October, the most since the full-scale invasion began almost five years ago, the Ukrainian leader said Sunday.

Ukraine uses drone footage to document casualty numbers, which have now exceeded Russia’s monthly recruitment rate.

World.title: Trump approval near career low ahead of elections, poll finds
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s approval rating held near a career low as a broad swath of the U.S. electorate saw their vote in Tuesday’s congressional midterm elections as a way to oppose the Republican president, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

The poll results underscore Republican vulnerabilities brought on by a surge in fuel prices since Trump launched a war on Iran in February. Voters in the nationwide poll said they preferred Democrats over Republicans — 46% to 38% — in what is known as a “generic ballot” question.

Still, that 8-percentage-point Democratic advantage was narrower than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted a week earlier, when Democrats led by 11 points.

The generic ballot question gives an overall view of which party voters nationwide would like to see in charge in Congress, though it does not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the U.S. Senate and U.S. House of Representatives.

Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in Congress.

Political strategists from both parties think Democrats have the best shot at winning control of the House, where all 435 seats are up for grabs. Democrats face a more difficult path to victory in the U.S. Senate, with the party on the defensive in Alaska and Michigan in recent days.

While Trump won’t be on the ballot, he looms large in the election.

Some 32% of poll respondents said they approved of the job Trump was doing in the White House, unchanged from a week earlier and just above his record-low reading of 31% two weeks ago.

Among registered voters, some 50% of independents said they saw their vote in congressional elections as a vote against Trump, compared with 13% who said it was a vote for Trump and 33% who said the president wasn’t a factor in their vote.

Some 78% of voters said the rising cost of living would be very important or the most important issue in deciding how to vote. Asked which party was better on the issue, voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43% to 32%.

Democrats appear to have more enthusiasm about voting, which the party hopes will lead to an advantage in voter turnout. Some 49% of Democratic voters said they are “very enthusiastic” about voting this year, compared with 33% of Republicans.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,765 U.S. adults online and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

World.title: Khamenei empowers talks as Trump says Iran deal could happen
World.content:
Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government has been granted more authority by the country’s supreme leader to pursue peace talks, as U.S. President Donald Trump hinted at progress in negotiations.

The comments on Monday signaled a potential diplomatic opening as fears grow of renewed conflict with the U.S. and Israel.

“We are striving to resolve the issue through dialogue and, in this regard, the Supreme Leader has also granted certain powers to the government,” the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency cited Pezeshkian as saying on Monday.

World.title: Supermarkets across Europe report new suspected freezer hack
World.content:
Supermarkets across Europe were hit by suspected cyberattacks that resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers on Monday, echoing a more widespread problem in France last month.

Incidents were reported in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland and Estonia, but the overall impact of the incidents appeared to be far more limited than the French cyberattacks, potentially affecting just dozens of locations.

Ahold Delhaize, Carrefour and Spar reported issues with their refrigerators and freezers in shops in Belgium. Supermarket chains in Sweden, Ireland and Finland were also affected, causing grocers to throw away food, according to spokespeople and local media reports. Ikea said that one of the company’s stores in Mons, Belgium, was affected.

World.title: Israel opposition meets to back Eisenkot, but Netanyahu says voters chose him
World.content:
Party heads in the Israeli opposition camp, led by Gadi Eisenkot, will meet on Tuesday after they all endorsed him for prime minister, while incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu has called for a broad coalition government under his leadership.

It will be the diverse opposition grouping’s first meeting since last week’s close-fought election delivered no majority for either camp.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party said the leaders of the “change” grouping would meet “to discuss coordinating the bloc’s next steps” in Herzliya on Tuesday morning.

World.title: Hong Kong’s malls must evolve into green sanctuaries to stay relevant
World.content:
Retail is making a comeback in Hong Kong. Deloitte China reported an encouraging HK$203 billion (US$25.9 billion) in sales volume in the first half of 2026, beating expectations. Accordingly, they forecast the retail market to reach HK$412 billion by the end of this year.

retail revival should directly translate into reduced vacancies for the city’s bricks-and-mortar stores. However, while high street vacancies dropped to 9.1 per cent, the lowest since 2020, vacancies in prime shopping centres rose to a record high of 13.7 per cent, according to Jones Lang LaSalle.

World.title: First Northern Metropolis Marathon trips up as  runners hit out at poor arrangements
World.content:
Water shortages, gruelling course conditions and a lengthy post-race walk marred Hong Kong’s inaugural Northern Metropolis Marathon on Sunday, participants have said, prompting calls for organisers to overhaul arrangements if the event is to return.

As the city seeks to establish itself as a premier hub for mega-events , experts warned the problems went beyond teething issues. They urged organisers to ensure they had the professional expertise required to host similar events in future.

Organised by the New Territories’ Heung Yee Kuk to mark the rural body’s centenary, the inaugural event drew about 15,000 registered runners across four race categories. The organisers had pitched the marathon as a showcase for the region’s development.

World.title: Long delays for Hong Kong court cases demand urgent action
World.content:
Justice delayed, it is often said, is justice denied. If that is true, many court users in Hong Kong are being failed by the system

Those involved in criminal cases at the Court of First Instance must wait 358 days on average for the hearing, the judiciary revealed last week. The figure for the District Court is 354 days, way above the court’s 100-day target. This is a cause of concern.

World.title: Northern Metropolis land clearance linked to surge in stray animals, study finds
World.content:
Over 40 per cent of stray animals taken in by shelters in Hong Kong in the first half of the year came from the Northern Metropolis development area, a study has found, with volunteers warning that more than 1,000 face abandonment as land resumption accelerates.

The Animal Welfare Advocacy Alliance, which released the findings on Monday, called for a review of euthanasia policies, the relaunch of a “trap-neuter-resettlement” programme, and the introduction of a positive duty of care for companion animals.

The pro bono study, conducted by Dr Kelvin Lam Ka-wang of Baptist University and Associate Professor Paul Wong Wai-ching of the University of Hong Kong, analysed intake records from six non-governmental animal rescue organisations between January and June.

World.title: Legal body’s new Hong Kong office targets developing Southeast Asian economies
World.content:
An international legal body’s new regional office in Hong Kong aims to help developing Southeast Asian economies and promote the wider use of uniform commercial law across the Asia-Pacific, its secretary general has said.

Ignacio Tirado, secretary general of the International Institute for the Unification of Private Law (Unidroit), said its new Asia-Pacific Liaison Office was receiving financial support from the Hong Kong government and seeking additional sponsors.

He was speaking after the opening ceremony for the office, the body’s first outside its Rome headquarters.

World.title: 3 former Hong Kong leaders head funeral committee for educator Ng Hon-mun
World.content:
Funeral proceedings for Ng Hon-mun, an influential pro-Beijing educator and long-serving Hong Kong deputy to the National People’s Congress (NPC), will begin on Wednesday, with three former city leaders heading the funeral committee.

Ng died peacefully on October 18, aged 100. His wake will be held at Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point from 5pm on Wednesday, followed by a memorial gathering at 7pm.

A public memorial service will take place at 10am on Thursday, according to an obituary seen by the South China Morning Post on Monday.

World.title: Ex-boyfriend planned to kill yoga instructor, Hong Kong murder trial hears
World.content:
A 23-year-old yoga instructor was found dead floating in a blood-filled bathtub in a luxury Hong Kong hotel room after sustaining more than 40 wounds, a court heard on the opening day of her former boyfriend’s murder trial.

Prosecutors told a High Court jury on Monday that the accused, Alex Lo Chun-ming, planned to kill his ex-girlfriend Chow Wai-yin with a sharp knife at the Ritz-Carlton hotel in West Kowloon on June 29 and 30, 2022.

Chow, known as “Aqua”, was popular on social media and had arranged a yoga trip to the United States, planning to fly out on June 30, the court heard.

World.title: Hong Kong’s first national security law convict among 4 released early, sources say
World.content:
The first person convicted in Hong Kong under the Beijing-imposed national security law and three others jailed in related high-profile cases have been released early, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Sources said on Monday that Leon Tong Ying-kit, 30, who was sentenced in July 2021 to nine years in prison for inciting secession and engaging in terrorist activities, had been granted early release.

He drove a motorcycle displaying a flag bearing the slogan “Liberate Hong Kong; revolution of our times” into police officers during a protest on July 1, 2020, hours after the Beijing-imposed national security law took effect.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.content:
China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.

Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.

As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.

Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

Fu, a 21-year-old viewer from the southern Guangdong province, told Sixth Tone that she found the show’s focus on friendship “refreshing” given how rarely such relationships take center stage on screen.

“We’re so used to understanding intimate relationships through the lens of romance, but rarely give serious thought to the love, possessiveness, jealousy, dependence, disappointment, and reconciliation that exist in friendships,” she said.

Another 21-year-old viewer based in Shanghai, surnamed You, added that the show’s appeal lies in friendship’s lack of definition.

“Friendship can be as intense and possessive as romance, full of love and resentment, or it can be something much more casual,” You said. “People can have very different ideas of what friendship means, and that alone can create tension.”

Contributions: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “I Miss You.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.title: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.content:
Many assume the writing is on the wall for human typographers. For decades, the industry has been slowly decimated by the advance of digital publishing software. Now, artificial intelligence is here to finish off the job.

That view has only strengthened since the launch of OpenAI’s Image 2.0 earlier this year. Until then, type designers and typographers had clung to the hope that AI would never be able to replace them: AI-generated fonts and layouts had always looked clunky, inconsistent, error-ridden, or somehow just a bit off.

But Image 2.0’s capabilities took many by surprise: it was able to produce beautifully designed documents featuring long passages of text in multiple languages, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. The work was not as good as that produced by professional type designers, but for a layperson looking to make a poster or a brochure, it was just fine.

Suddenly, typography — perhaps the last stronghold of graphic design still firmly controlled by professional designers — looked at risk of falling as well. If everyone can generate typefaces and layouts with a simple prompt, or even ask a frontier AI model to operate design software on its own — just as non-programmers can now “write code” through vibe coding — how many designers will lose their jobs?

In the English-speaking world, the AI revolution may indeed prove to be a hammer blow for the typography community. But things are likely to play out a little differently in China: the relationship between text and technology has always been more complex due to the nature of its writing system.

Most contemporary typographic practice derives from movable-type printing technology. Developed in medieval Germany, typography is closely tied to the inherent characteristics of the Latin alphabet: there are only a few dozen letters, and the same letters recur constantly throughout a printed text.

With these characteristics in mind, Johannes Gutenberg developed an entire technological process of carving, reproducing, retrieving, and repeatedly reusing individual letter forms. Once a complete set of letters had been produced, it could be used to print texts containing vast numbers of repetitions of exactly the same glyphs.

Gutenberg would later be credited as a pioneer of movable type printing, a technology whose logic has been carried intact from books to the screen you are now looking at. But applying this technique to Chinese characters is a huge challenge, as there is such a vast number of them. While function words such as de may appear repeatedly on a single page, most characters may occur only once or twice in a given text — or not at all.

Statistically, 3,500 characters is enough to cover most everyday text — studies have shown they account for 99.5% of character usage. But to avoid the awkward situation where a character outside the “common 3,500” can’t be rendered properly, the industry often sets 7,000 characters as the target size for a typeface. Some larger projects cover 27,000, or even 87,000 characters.

This means that Chinese typeface design has always been extremely labor-intensive. Designers have to invest huge resources in reproducing thousands of rare characters that are only used about 1% of the time. It’s one reason why Chinese printers — who actually invented movable type even earlier than Gutenberg — largely stuck with carving entire texts onto woodblocks to mass-print books for centuries. It saved producing and organizing thousands of characters that might never be used. Only gigantic projects, such as state-backed archives, would use movable-type printing.

But in the modern era, movable type-inspired workflows have come to dominate Chinese typeface design. As a result, advertisers who need to print a 20-character slogan may have to purchase the license for a typeface containing 7,000 characters. Understandably, many users are reluctant to pay type foundries, who also feel it’s an enormous burden to cover as many characters as possible.

This cost-efficiency problem is where AI can help. In fact, Chinese type foundries have been using internal AI tools to assist in typeface production for years.

Traditionally, when developing a new typeface, the lead designer will often create several hundred characters to establish the design direction, with the remaining thousands produced by a team along those lines. An AI model can also do this work with a little training: extracting patterns from those hundreds of directional characters, learning the typeface’s stylistic characteristics, and then applying them according to the structural features of different characters. The model doesn’t have to be advanced, and with human adjustment, it can deliver products with considerably increased productivity.

Since the early 2020s, open-source AI tools have also enabled independent designers to produce usable typefaces on their own. For example, designer Wang Tingrui has been using AI tools to develop typefaces reminiscent of classic lead-type printing. With the emergence of stronger models capable of generating high-quality glyph outlines, such work has become even easier.

These developments mark a new chapter for Chinese typeface design. Once a typeface’s design concept is established, whether by a lead designer or an independent practitioner, AI could be used to expand it across thousands of additional characters, making that long tail of less common characters far less of a burden.

AI may also unlock new possibilities for Chinese characters once incompatible with movable type or typefaces. The overwhelming majority of Chinese characters are created by flexibly combining different components. In theory, anyone can combine components to create a new Chinese character.

This happened in the 19th century, when Chinese chemists — tasked with translating the names of newly discovered elements into Chinese — created compound characters by combining a semantic component indicating the element type and a phonetic component based on the initial sound of its Western name. This system continues to this day, when scientists occasionally need to name new synthetic elements.

While inventing a new character is relatively simple, it used to be difficult to introduce them into everyday language because of the inherent barriers created by digital typefaces. Traditional typeface design is built around recording whole characters, not their components, so any new character would not appear in previously existing typefaces.

With AI, however, that could all change. The technology should allow users to render new characters in the style of an existing typeface, making it easier for them to gain traction.

Beyond this, AI is ushering in a fundamental shift in the nature of typography. While the modern typeface system uses the single character or letter as its basic unit, this is just one way to recreate text. In woodblock printing, for example, Chinese printers produced entire pages all at once.

Today’s leading AI models — including Qwen, Seedream, ChatGPT, and DALL-E — are moving towards a system that bypasses typefaces entirely. Text is generated directly onto posters, videos, and the cover images for posts on China’s version of TikTok, Douyin, in a particular visual style, according to a user’s preferences. Users specify the style they want using a prompt — or a handwritten demonstration — and the AI model simply creates a font, rather than using a commercial one.

This approach still has problems. One issue often raised is the inconsistency of AI-crafted characters, but this should be solvable as models become more advanced. There is also a debate over copyright, especially when generated text resembles existing typefaces. Yet these issues are unlikely to stop ordinary users from using AI to speed up their design work.

It is easy to imagine a not-so-distant future in which everyone can generate high-quality typefaces and typography through instructions, whether they are designing for an illustration, an , a poster, or even an entire book. For type foundries, AI is likely to be incorporated into their workflows, just like what has been happening in the “hybrid” mode of production in the film industry.

Then, what is left for professional type designers to do?

One thing is clear: they will no longer monopolize the creation of stylistic Chinese characters. Similar upheavals have happened in the past, when typewriters, computers, and smartphones granted more people the power to produce texts.

But professionals have a more important job: pushing the boundaries of design. In a world where the production of text becomes effortless and inexhaustible, designers’ role as the gatekeepers of taste and judgment only becomes more prominent.

We should keep experimenting to deliver high-quality work with novel and sophisticated aesthetics. The decades of training we have received won’t be wasted. Rather, it will continue to shape a philosophy that pioneers future designs, regardless of what technology is involved.

(Header image: Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.title: Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.content:
Breast milk from mothers with postpartum depression may negatively impact infants’ brain development, a Chinese study has found.

The study, published Oct. 27 in the top academic journal Cell Metabolism, was led by a team at Nanjing University, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Through a mouse model, it shows, for the first time, how depression-related changes in levels of microRNA, a type of gene-regulating molecule, contained in structures called extracellular vesicles in breast milk can affect offspring brains.

Between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide experience postpartum depression. Children of affected mothers are more likely to face challenges in cognition, language, behavior, and school performance, and are at a higher risk of developing depression themselves.

Past research has implicated genetics and the way mothers with postpartum depression bond with, and care for, their infants as contributing to this phenomenon, but the broad and long-lasting effects of postpartum depression on child development remain unclear, according to the researchers.

Because breast milk is increasingly viewed as a “signaling system orchestrating infant development,” the researchers wrote, they looked at the relationship between milk-based microRNAs and extracellular vesicles, key parts of this signaling. Because babies’ blood-brain barrier is more permeable than adults’, these vesicles can enter the brain during nursing, making its development more sensitive to diet.

The researchers compared the breast milk of 40 human mothers clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression, and 51 without, finding that those with depression had elevated levels of three types of microRNA implicated in psychiatric illness. The same was true of the breast milk of depressed mice.

To test nursing’s role in brain development, swapping mouse pups between healthy and depressed mouse mothers. Pups born to healthy mice but nursed by their depressed counterparts showed worse cognitive and emotional behavior than pups born to depressed mothers but nursed by healthy ones.

They also found that neurons in pups nursed by depressed mothers had shorter dendrites and fewer branches in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, a part of the brain believed to play a role in memory development and depression. The problems arose mainly as the neurons matured, were detectable by day 21 after birth, and persisted into adulthood, suggesting that early nursing-environment effects can last into later development.

Giving milk from depressed mothers to healthy pups was also enough to cause cognitive impairment after weaning, while milk where the vesicles had been removed had no such effect, the researchers found.

When the team inhibited Rab27a, a protein and key factor in vesicle secretion, in the mammary glands of depressed mothers, vesicle secretion fell by 58%, and the cognitive and neurodevelopmental deficits in their pups improved significantly.

The researchers also found that microRNA in milk vesicles from depressed mothers blocks a “brake” receptor called mGluR8 in pups’ brains. Without this brake, brain regions can become overstimulated, impairing the development of neural connections. As a result, new brain cells are more active overall but respond more weakly to memory tasks, helping explain the cognitive problems seen in pups nursed by depressed mothers.

The study offers the key findings of both a new communication pathway and a microRNA-based mechanism of inheritance between mothers and babies, according to the researchers.

Breastfeeding is widely seen as good for babies’ brain development, but this study also suggests that breastfeeding by mothers with postpartum depression may have a “double-edged effect on offspring health,” the researchers wrote.

“Elucidating the molecular mechanisms linking maternal postnatal depression to offspring neurological outcomes therefore holds considerable public health value and underscores the urgent need for targeted maternal mental health interventions during lactation,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.title: 90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.content:
Chinese prosecutors have exposed an invoice-trading network that illegally traded special value-added tax (VAT) invoices totaling more than 7.4 billion yuan ($1.1 billion) over three years.

Under the guise of a Shanghai-based advertising business, the group profited by issuing and charging service fees for fake invoices from shell companies it registered to customers seeking to illegally claim tax deductions — which can be claimed for special tax invoices, but not ordinary tax invoices in China — domestic media reported Tuesday.

The case has exposed major weaknesses in business-registration oversight, tax monitoring, and financial regulators’ ability to detect suspicious fund flows between affiliated company accounts, according to experts.

From June 2025 to June 2026, more than 90 criminal suspects on the case were processed by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Procuratorate, some of whom were ordered to return their illegal gains. Processing of the case is ongoing.

The group’s ringleaders, surnamed Cui and Shen, first had employees register over 70 shell companies in their own names. Invoices were then handled via three steps: a sales team first connected with customers, who transferred money to the group in order to receive invoices; then a team obtained invoices from both the operation’s registered shell companies or legitimate businesses with unused invoicing quotas; before another team returned funds to customers following invoice-fee deductions. Customers were charged a service fee of between 7% and 13% of the invoice value.

Chinese tax law requires contracts, fund transfers, invoices, and movement of goods to align. Falsely issuing invoices can result in fines of up to 500,000 yuan, while tax dodgers may be fined up to five times the underpaid tax. Both carry risks of criminal prosecution.

To circumvent the law, customers transferred the full invoice amount to the group, which then transferred the remaining funds back to the customer through a separate, third account.

The group illegally traded over 7.4 billion yuan in VAT invoices, involving more than 420 million yuan in VAT. It also conducted illegal foreign-exchange transactions totaling 420 million yuan.

“The scale of the crimes, the degree of organization, and the length of time over which they were committed were all relatively unusual,” Li Huaisheng, a professor at the School of Criminal Justice at China University of Political Science and Law, told state media outlet CCTV.

Similar cases involving companies that obtained invoices through intermediaries have made national headlines in recent years. Last year, a group allegedly used 15 shell companies to falsely issue almost 3,500 special VAT invoices totaling 300 million yuan, domestic media reported. The defendant, surnamed Li, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison and fined 500,000 yuan.

According to the State Taxation Administration, such companies often disguise themselves as consulting, advertising, or other business services in industries with low fixed-asset requirements, long industrial chains, and large transaction values, such as recycling, road freight transport, and information technology consulting.

Li Huaisheng recommended that market regulatory authorities establish early-warning models to flag suspicious company registrations, and tax authorities improve big-data checks on invoices, capital, contracts, and goods.

In an interview with CCTV, Zhou Xianbao, a lawyer at BZW Law Firm in Beijing, also recommended establishing a system requiring real-name authorization for invoice issuance and formal tax-compliance commitments.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.title: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019176/Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
World.content:
When most Chinese people think of World War I, they think of it as a “European war.” This is not simply an oversight. It is the result of a century of forgetting.

Few people are aware that between 1916 and 1918, Britain and France recruited around 140,000 Chinese laborers from Shandong, Hebei, Guangdong, Hong Kong, and other regions to work on the Western Front. They dug trenches, built defenses, and transported ammunition. After the fighting ended, they stayed on to help with reconstruction, clearing battlefields and filling in shell craters. Some did not return home until 1922.

Sending laborers overseas was not simply a matter of supplying manpower. It was also part of a carefully considered political strategy. Politicians such as Liang Shiyi — an influential adviser to then-President Yuan Shikai — believed that Germany and Austria-Hungary were unlikely to defeat Britain and France, and advocated a “laborers-as-soldiers” strategy that would allow China to participate indirectly in the war and break its diplomatic isolation. Meanwhile, figures associated with the New Culture Movement, an early 20th-century intellectual and cultural reform movement, saw sending laborers overseas as an opportunity to develop China’s working class. They included Li Shizeng, a French-educated anarchist and organizer of the Diligent Work-Frugal Study Movement, and Cai Yuanpei, a leading educator and president of Peking University.

Yet China’s participation in the Allied war effort did not bring the diplomatic gains its leaders had hoped for. At the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, the victorious powers agreed to transfer Germany’s former rights in Shandong province to Japan rather than return them to China, a decision that helped spark the May Fourth Movement, a wave of student-led protests that became a turning point in modern Chinese history.

The contributions of the Chinese laborers themselves also received little recognition. When they returned home in the 1920s, they found a country gripped by political upheaval and were often met with indifference or even suspicion.

The result was a double erasure. The West forgot their contributions, while China forgot their sacrifices.

In July 2019, a delegation from Belgium’s In Flanders Fields Museum visited Shanghai University. The two institutions agreed to jointly investigate, excavate, study, and exhibit the remains of Chinese labor camps on the Western Front during World War I. By then, scholars from the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Germany, Canada, and other countries, led by Professor Nicholas J. Saunders of the University of Bristol, had spent nearly a decade systematically surveying the physical remains and landscapes of the Western Front. Yet the Chinese labor camps remained a missing piece of the puzzle. Although frequently mentioned in historical records, they had never been systematically investigated or excavated by archaeologists.

In May 2023, Shanghai University officially launched the Chinese Labour Corps (CLC) Camp Project, in collaboration with the In Flanders Fields Museum, Ghent University, and Howest University of Applied Sciences. A non-invasive geophysical survey was completed in April 2024, and excavation began in February 2025. The project concluded in March 2026.

Before we began digging, information about the Chinese labor camps could be found in historical documents, but it was fragmented. Official military archives paid little attention to these noncombatants from China, while local records offered a more vivid picture. One example is the diary of Belgian priest Achiel Van Walleghem. In August 1917, he recorded the presence of two Chinese labor camps in the village of Reningelst, near the Belgian town of Ypres, a major battleground during World War I. In January 1918, he noted that some shop owners had begun learning Chinese to attract the laborers. And on the night of April 13, 1918, when one of the camps came under German artillery fire, he recorded 10 deaths and more than 30 injuries. In fact, the threat of shelling had already prompted strikes and protests among Chinese laborers in late 1917. British military records provided another crucial detail: the 75th Company of the Chinese Labour Corps was stationed there from August 1917 to April 1918. Gu Xingqing, an interpreter for the Chinese laborers, also described the night of the bombardment in his memoirs.

Historical records also reveal differences in how the British and French treated Chinese laborers. Those recruited by the French worked alongside locals under relatively loose supervision, making the remains of their camps difficult to identify. By contrast, British-recruited laborers — organized into the Chinese Labour Corps — were subject to military-style discipline and housed in enclosed camps surrounded by barbed wire. The camps followed a military organizational structure. Initially, each battalion consisted of 1,031 men, with 10 to 12 sharing a tent. Each camp had just one iron gate, which was locked at night. To leave, the men had to obtain permission and travel in groups, and they were forbidden from venturing more than 3 miles away.

Documents even record how the laborers died and were commemorated. The leading causes of death were tuberculosis and the 1918 influenza pandemic, rather than artillery fire. However, the death tolls vary considerably: British records put the figure at around 2,000, French records at approximately 1,500, while Chinese figures suggest that at least 20,000 did not come back to China. Chinese laborers recruited by the British were buried in military cemeteries. Their headstones followed the same style as those of British soldiers, but bore inscriptions in both languages, including the laborers’ names and places of origin in Chinese, alongside English epitaphs such as “Though Dead, He Still Liveth” and “A Noble Duty Bravely Done.”

After the war, returning French and Belgian residents sometimes blamed the surviving Chinese laborers for social unrest. Yet the laborers were still bound by their contracts and remained to clear the battlefields. Some stayed in France to work in mines until 1929, while others married and settled there permanently.

In June 1921, the British military issued a total of 93,357 commemorative medals at its Chinese labor base in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao. Some were presented in person, while others were mailed to the laborers’ homes. Even today, these medals can occasionally be found in remote villages across Shandong and Hebei.

If historical records tell us so much, why was archaeological excavation necessary? Because documents can tell us where the camps were and what happened there, but they cannot fully reveal what the camps looked like. Their layouts were never systematically recorded, and the sites had long since been cleared and leveled after the war. This is where archaeology comes in.

The non-invasive geophysical surveys of the site we commenced in spring 2024 used high-resolution electromagnetic induction and magnetic survey techniques. The data revealed numerous anomalies at depths of 1 to 1.5 meters, including fragments of artillery shells of various calibers. This was consistent with local farmers’ accounts of still unearthing shrapnel when plowing their fields.

The two intersecting trenches excavated in February 2025 covered 512 square meters. We uncovered two ash pits with traces of burning at their bases, eight shell craters ranging from 1 to 5 meters in diameter, foundation stones from barracks, tent pole bases, and clusters of communication cables. For the first time, we were able to reconstruct the layout of a camp whose physical arrangement had never been documented, identifying its barracks, tent area, and main road.

We also unearthed more than 520 artifacts that offered glimpses of everyday life: belt buckles, Royal Engineers and Royal Artillery cap badges, surgical forceps from a field hospital, piles of bullet and shell casings, and nearly intact British army-issued rum jars and lemonade bottles. If historical documents help us understand the Chinese labor camps, archaeology brings us closer to the people who lived in them.

The significance of the project extends beyond the discoveries themselves. For a long time, World War I archaeology was mainly the preserve of metal detectorists, while professional archaeologists generally avoided the subject. This began to change with archaeological investigations conducted ahead of construction of Belgium’s A19 highway in 2002, which helped establish the field as a serious area of academic research.

Our excavation of the Chinese labor camp was the first of its kind to be led by a Chinese academic institution.

The project also opened up new avenues for Chinese archaeological research in two fields. The first is conflict archaeology, which looks beyond weapons and battlefields to examine entire societies caught up in war. The second is industrial archaeology, which can shift attention away from industrial achievements alone and toward the people and human efforts behind them. At its heart, this approach is about focusing on people rather than objects.

The Chinese laborers were not merely supporting characters in World War I. They found themselves caught up in a conflict involving Eastern and Western societies, working and dying amid misunderstanding and hostility. Yet even in the face of constant danger, they found ways to express themselves, creating trench art engraved with dragon motifs and landscape scenes.

Even the idyllic scenery of Flanders today was partly shaped by Chinese laborers, who filled in many of the trenches and craters left by the war. The experiences of these 140,000 ordinary Chinese men lie at the intersection of 20th-century Chinese and world history, reflecting the interactions and tensions between different societies.

“In Flanders fields the poppies blow / Between the crosses, row on row,” wrote John McCrae in his poem “In Flanders Fields.” Today, the poppies still bloom every year. But among those fields and crosses, Chinese laborers once lived and worked. Archaeology cannot bring them back to life, but it can give the soil a voice and remind the world that they were here.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A British soldier and a Chinese laborer examine written identification ribbons during a roll call at a Chinese Labour Corps camp in Samer, France, May 26, 1918. From the collection of the Imperial War Museums)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.title: China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019180/China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
World.content:
China’s popular chili sauce brand Lao Gan Ma has drawn public scrutiny for adopting AI-driven production, allegedly at the expense of hundreds of jobs.

The controversy began after multiple domestic media outlets reported that Li Xin, Lao Gan Ma’s executive vice general manager and chief quality officer, touted the company’s use of AI at a provincial business conference last month in China’s southwestern Guizhou province, where the sauce originates.

Li reportedly said the number of workers on one production line fell from over 600 to just 48 after the company introduced an AI-powered pepper inspection system last year. He added that the company’s 2025 revenue reached a record 5.4 billion yuan ($810 million), crediting AI with reducing production errors to almost 0%. Li’s full remarks are not publicly available online.

The company’s history of touting its dedication to working people has drawn particular criticism over the potential layoffs, according to a commentary by Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper. Lao Gan Ma’s founder, Tao Huabi, whose portrait adorns the brand’s jars and is known across China, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997.

As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal has garnered more than 120 million views on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users said automation is a standard part of industrial upgrading that can help improve efficiency and ensure consistent product quality. Others argued that the company should consider its responsibilities to workers.

“If everything is done by AI and robots, and people have no jobs or income, they won’t be able to afford to consume. What’s the point of producing so much, then?” one highly upvoted Weibo comment read.

Many also called for a boycott of the brand, reposting one user’s comment: “If you lay off workers, we’ll get your products pulled from the shelves.”

Responding to the controversy, Lao Gan Ma human resources representatives stated in an interview with domestic media on Oct. 26 that Li had not referenced staffing figures in his remarks.

In response to the company’s denial, users scrutinized its social insurance enrollment figures, which often reflect a company’s workforce size. Corporate filings disclosed by business data platforms Tianyancha and Qichacha show that the number of employees insured by the company fell from nearly 3,000 in 2022 to 740 in 2025 — a roughly 75% decline.

However, changes in social insurance enrollment do not prove AI use drove the layoffs, as other factors such as retirement and employee turnover also affect employment figures.

The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative impacts on employment. On Oct. 23, the State Council issued guidelines calling for “maximizing AI’s potential to create jobs, empower workers in traditional occupations, improve job quality, and stimulate innovation” while “slowing down the impact of AI-related job replacement.”

The guidelines also urge companies to deploy AI with caution in labor-intensive industries. They encourage employers to provide transition periods for displaced workers, give advance notice before large-scale AI rollouts, and offer retraining and support for locating new jobs.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019174/Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.title: Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019174/Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
World.content:
When glimpsing the Terracotta Army for the first time, almost everyone is awestruck by its sheer scale: thousands of armored clay figures standing in perfect formation, their gray earthen bodies stretching rank upon rank. At first glance, the ghostly 2,000-year-old soldiers look as if they were cast from a single mold.

But look closer, and the impression of uniformity begins to dissolve. No two faces are exactly alike: brows thick or faint, eyes wide open or slightly narrowed, cheekbones high or low, jawlines rounded or square. When viewed individually, each warrior is far more than a figure: it is a work of art as intricate as many Renaissance statues.

Zhao Hui (Steve Zhao) has spent much of the past 25 years trying to capture this hidden artistry. A veteran photographer who trained under cinematographer Peter Levy in the 1980s, Zhao became well known for his portraiture. His 1996 project “China Story” has toured more than 30 countries.

Since 2001, he has applied his talent for portrait photography to the Terracotta Army, amassing images of more than 2,000 figures. The works offer a striking new perspective on the warriors, often zooming in close enough to highlight the carved stroke of an eyebrow, the turn of a cheekbone, or even faint fingerprints left in the clay by a Qin dynasty artisan.

For Zhao, the project is also about more than changing perceptions of the Terracotta Army; it’s part of a wider effort to document, classify, and analyze it. The vast photo archive helps researchers understand the production processes, craftsmanship, and organization behind the relics — and, most importantly for Zhao, the anonymous master sculptors who carved them.

In this interview, Sixth Tone sat down with Zhao to discuss how his project began and how it has shaped our understanding of the Terracotta Warriors. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: The Terracotta Army has long been a research focus for archaeologists and historians, but what led you to study them through high-definition photography?

Zhao: At first, it was just a routine assignment. In 2001, the China National Tourism Administration approached me to photograph the Terracotta Warriors. It was a rare opportunity, of course.

My task was to capture the warriors in the finest possible detail. That is far harder than most people imagine: heritage photography is not simply pointing a lens at an object. Every click of the shutter is a repeated negotiation with light, angle, material, and patience. The warriors are massive and their preservation conditions special, so every shoot requires meticulous preparation and on-site coordination.

After taking enough high-definition images, I began to notice striking details — the rise and fall of a brow ridge, the hooked line at the corner of an eye, the marks left by the sculptors’ hands. Perhaps it’s because I’m a portrait photographer, trained to observe people.

Looking at all those warrior faces, I noticed not only the differences between them but couldn’t stop wondering how those differences came about. Behind them lie the techniques and aesthetics of their makers. That is how I began studying the craftsmanship of the Terracotta Warriors — 25 years ago now.

Sixth Tone: You have said the creation of the Terracotta Army was not just a feat of manufacturing, but an artistic process. Why do you believe that?

Zhao: You have to distinguish between three separate steps in the production process. First, the rough cores of the heads, hands, and torsos were made separately; then a layer of fine clay was applied over the cores, and the details refined; finally, the parts were assembled and joined, air-dried, fired in kilns, and painted.

The key point is that the heads and torsos were made separately and joined only at the end. The torsos were mainly the work of craftsmen. They coiled strips of clay round and round to build up the body, tapering gradually from the legs to the waist, then carved the robes, armor, armor studs, and knotted cords. I’ve taken close-ups of torsos; magnified, you can see the traces of clay coils stacking and tightening upward.

As for the heads: a rough core was made first, then ears, topknots, braids, and caps or headcloths attached, followed by the fine carving of the facial features. This was the heart of the entire production — and the people responsible were probably not ordinary craftsmen, but a group of highly skilled sculptors and their assistants.

Sixth Tone: What evidence led you to that conclusion?

Zhao: Look carefully at the faces, and you’d reach the same conclusion. Those vivid, highly individualized faces are works of art: brows range from thick to sword-shaped; eyes are wide open, slightly narrowed, or upturned; the fullness of the cheeks, the height of the cheekbones, the roundness or squareness of the chins — all of them are different. These details embody each figure’s appearance, character, and psychology.

By carefully comparing different images, I can even recognize the signature techniques and styles of individual sculptors. Now, whenever I see a certain technique, I feel I’ve run into an old friend, and I want to say to that nameless sculptor: “Hi, it’s you again.”

In my view, these face-makers who left no names behind can rightly be called China’s Michelangelos.

Sixth Tone: But there’s a problem here. Even a sculptor as industrious as Michelangelo only produced a few dozen sculptures in his lifetime, while the Terracotta Army contains an estimated 8,000 figures. It’s hard to imagine so many high-level sculptors were available at that time.

Zhao: Good point. These sculptors made only faces — far less work than carving an entire figure — but 8,000 is still a staggering number. So I expect there was a “master-and-apprentice” model being used during production.

I’ve found some supporting clues: comparing groups of figures similar in style and technique, I often find that within a group there is one figure of finer modeling and more accurate proportions, while the others are relatively rough and unpolished. The former likely came from a master’s hand, the latter from apprentices.

Even so, the scale of the project still astounds me. In just over three years, they produced some 8,000 life-size figures with varied faces — a feat that pushed the limits of stamina and craft, and a testament to the Qin Empire’s extraordinary organizational capacity.

Sixth Tone: Back to your methodology. Your findings are largely based on observing the warriors up close through high-definition photographs. Now that 3D digitization technology is maturing, do you think it could provide further research breakthroughs?

Zhao: Digitization shouldn’t be oversimplified. If you can’t even take a good flat photograph, then creating a 3D model will be even harder. The workload and cost of 3D data acquisition are far higher than in 2D, and the processing difficulty grows exponentially.

Of course, photographing the warriors does “distort.” Turning three dimensions into two — how could it not? A single photograph is never a complete replica of “reality”; it is constrained by angle, lighting, and timing, and it carries the photographer’s choices and judgments. It is essentially a limited rendering of the objective world under specific conditions.

But don’t forget: my photography is a long process. When one photograph becomes 1,000, then 10,000; when images of different times, angles, and individuals converge into a system that can be cross-verified — photography becomes a cognitive tool for observing, comparing, and deducing. It prompts people to see cultural relics anew and provides material for further historical interpretation. That’s why I now call my work the “Visual Art of Archaeology.”

(Header image: Terracotta Warriors. Photo by Zhao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019171/Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.title: Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019171/Women, Teens Helped Build Terracotta Army, Chinese Study Says
World.content:
A new study has found that women and adolescents, not only men, helped build China’s 2,000-year-old Terracotta Army.

The study used fingerprints found on a portion of the 8,000 statues of soldiers and horses in the tomb of China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, to assess their makers’ ages and sexes for the first time, domestic media reported this week. The research was conducted by the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum in Xi’an, capital of the northwestern Shaanxi province, and Shandong University’s School of Archaeology, in the eastern city of Jinan, and will be published in Volume 82 of the Journal of Cultural Heritage at the end of the year.

Past studies of labor forces during the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) relied primarily on legal texts and largely treated men as the default workers, with 15 reportedly the minimum age for service. Prior research has also neglected to examine the genders and ages of the workers behind the Terracotta Army.

Previous analysis of the identities behind ancient fingerprints has also failed to account for factors such as similarities in fingerprint size and ridge distribution between women and teenage boys, differences between ancient and modern fingerprint size, and clay shrinkage after firing, the researchers said.

In contrast, the new study used a Bayesian mixture model to account for these factors and estimate fingerprint-related parameters at both the individual and population levels through probabilities. The model assigned the fingerprints possible ages and sexes, analyzed their mean ridge breadth (MRB) or thickness, and compared these to growth curve-projected values.

The team analyzed 79 well-preserved fingerprints from 36 figures in Pit 1 of the Qinshihuang mausoleum. The results showed that 45% belonged to males, 32.7% to females, and 22.3% to juveniles under 15.

The research provided quantitative biological evidence challenging previous assumptions that large-scale craft production in the Qin dynasty relied only on adult male labor. It also offers a better understanding of the Qin dynasty’s labor systems and institutionalization of apprenticeships.

While textual records and artifact-based inscriptions had previously challenged the theory that the project relied exclusively on male labor, the team’s findings offer a new framework for quantitatively studying ancient craft production and the ages and sexes of the laborers involved.

“This biological evidence highly corroborates numerous historical records, vividly reconstructing the production scene in the Qin dynasty’s state-run workshops where men and women served together, and adult artisans worked alongside juveniles, who may have been helpers or apprentices,” the study’s authors wrote.

However, they also identified several limitations of the study. For one, the percentages attributed to adult and juvenile, and male and female fingerprints may not equal the percentages of actual workers with those traits, they said, as multiple fingerprints may have come from the same person.

They also wrote that more experienced workers may have left fewer fingerprints, which may have increased the proportion of juvenile prints, while the reference database was both based on modern Czech-Caucasian fingerprints, not East-Asian prints, and contained more female samples, potentially skewing the results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Types of fingerprints on the terracotta figures. From Journal of Cultural Heritage and Xinhua)

World.title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump, lets California count all ballots
World.content:
INJUNCTION ORDER. A US judge blocks an order to detain British national Imran Ahmed, CEO of the Center for Countering Digital Hate

The decision represents another defeat for Trump as his fellow Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in the November 3 midterms. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold.

Acting on the eve of the US midterm elections, the Supreme Court quickly rejected on Monday, November 2, a bid by President Donald Trump‘s administration to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who federal officials allege are likely non-US citizens.

The justices denied the Justice Department’s emergency request just hours after it filed it, shutting down the administration’s claims over disputed ballots that could have affected thousands of voters and injected uncertainty into election outcomes.

The decision represented another defeat for Trump as his fellow Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterms. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold.

The administration intensified its focus on alleged noncitizen voting in the run-up to the midterms. Multiple studies and state audits show that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.

The Supreme Court’s brief, one-sentence order on Monday did not offer any explanation of its action, as is common when it handles emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision. The court also did not ask California for a response to the administration’s request, a step that, when taken, usually signals serious consideration of an emergency case.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, called the decision “a welcome sight for all Americans given the disgusting and dangerous attacks on our democracy by the federal government.”

“Tomorrow (Tuesday), Californians can feel secure in knowing the state will carry out a free and fair election — just as we’ve always done,” Newsom added.

A federal appeals court refused the administration’s request on Friday.

The administration had demanded that California separate any allegedly unlawful ballots from other ballots and not count them until those voters are determined to be US citizens.

“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” the Justice Department said in its request to the Supreme Court.

Trump has made false claims about widespread US voting fraud including in the 2020 election lost to Democrat Joe Biden.

“We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced,” acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent ​McCotter said in a social media post after the administration’s filing earlier in the day.

Constitutional questions

The US Constitution assigns the responsibility of administering elections to states, though the federal government has some oversight. The lawsuit marked a rare federal intervention in the voting process and signaled a willingness by the administration to contest the election results in court.

The administration already sought to restrict voting by mail — a mode of casting ballots used more often by Democratic-leaning voters — but the Supreme Court in September rebuffed that effort. And a federal judge on Sunday dismissed the administration’s lawsuit concerning the US Senate race in Alaska.

The list of 20,000 registered voters was amassed by the US Department of Homeland Security and sent to California officials and to Los Angeles County officials.

The Justice Department sued in federal court on October 15, claiming California is unlawfully preventing its enforcement of a 1996 US law that makes it a criminal offense for noncitizens to vote in federal elections. The department said California’s action violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which holds that federal law generally preempts state law.

California has said that the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and that the lawsuit threatens to deprive 20,000 people of their right to vote based on vague accusations. The administration’s process for scrutinizing voter lists to identify noncitizens is flawed and likely rife with errors, it said in court papers.

California has 52 seats in the House of Representatives, more than any other state. Democrats need a net gain of four House seats to win a majority in the chamber.

‘Bend to the will’

US District Judge David Carter in Los Angeles denied the administration’s request on October 28.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch,” Carter wrote.

Carter raised concerns over the reliability of the administration’s data, noting that people recently flagged by the federal government as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalized US citizens.

“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Carter wrote.

The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals also refused on Friday to block the ballots, emphasizing the state’s power over election procedures and California’s “comprehensive statutory scheme to ensure the integrity of its elections,” including a system for canceling registrations if a voter is shown to be ineligible. – Rappler.com

World.title: ICC wraps up pre-trial hearings as Duterte’s November 30 case nears
World.content:
DUTERTE. In this file photo, former president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the Trial Chamber III of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands on October 13, 2026.

Duterte skips his last status conference after waiving his right to appear. He will, howver, have to personally appear every day once his trial starts on November 30.

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III wrapped up its status conference hearings on Monday, November 2, weeks before the start of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s trial for his crimes against humanity case.

A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial. This is to ensure that the schedule and other legal matters proceed smoothly during the actual trial days.

Play Video

Duterte skipped his last status conference after waiving his right to appear. The chamber granted his request.

“Mr. [Peter] Haynes, we’ve agreed exceptionally because this is not likely to be a particularly lengthy status conference that Mr. Duterte need not attend this morning. But once the actual trial starts, we will expect, as we said, [his] attendance on a daily basis,” said Presiding Judge Joanna Korner.

The former president, who has been detained at The Hague, Netherlands since March 2025, appeared during his status conferences on September 16 and October 13, respectively. The September 16 schedule marked Duterte’s first-ever ICC appearance since his arrest in 2025.

During the Monday hearing, the parties said they will have opening statements when the trial starts on November 30. The prosecution will deliver a statement, followed by the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims or the lawyers of the victims.

Traditionally, the defense cannot deliver an opening statement, but Korner said the defense might want to give at least an outline of what Duterte’s defense will be.

“And I want to know if you’ve considered applying, not to open in full, but to give, if you like, the public and the court an outline of what your defense is going to be, along the lines of what happens in other jurisdictions?” Korner asked.

“We will certainly finalize that position within the next few days, and we’ll let you know for scheduling purposes. But I think it’s more likely than not that I will say something at the start of the case, given its stature, really, and the character of the accused and his status,” said Haynes, Duterte’s defense lawyer.

The prosecution said they will open their case and take about four to six hours, and around three hours for the victims.

Principal Counsel Office of Public Counsel for Victims Paolina Massidda said they asked the chamber if they can use Tagalog (Filipino) for parts of their opening statement.

“Our request is more, during the opening statement, we will make some remark in quoting parts of a narrative that victims provided to us, and we’d like to do that in Tagalog,” said Massidda.

“And the purpose is a lot of victims will be connecting to the hearing. For them, it’s also important to listen how we convey to the chamber what they narrated to us and their experiences, and they relate and connect much more if that is done in Tagalog,” she added.

But Korner reiterated that the Rome Statute or the treaty that created the ICC, provides for only English and French as the court’s working languages. Apart from saying that there are interpreters, Korner said Tagalog is not the language of all the victims.

“So while we understand that you want to relate to the victims, you want the victims to relate to what’s being said, all of it, everything you say, as I understand it…. will be translated in any event, interpreted,” the presiding judge explained.

Play Video

Schedule, witnesses

For the first batch of evidence, Korner said the chamber will adopt a new schedule. Like what had been announced in the past, there will be 30-minute breaks per hour to heed the experts’ advice that no sitting for Duterte beyond one hour. The schedule of sessions is as follows:

10:00 – 11:00 am

11:00 – 11:30 am (break)

11:30 am to 12:30 pm

12:30 to 1:30 pm (lunch break)

1:30 – 2:30 pm

2:30 – 3:00 pm (break)

3:00 – 4:00 pm

For the hearings in 2027, the parties — prosecution, victims, and defense — proposed the following schedule:

January 11 to 29 (three weeks)

One-week break (Feb 1-5)

February 8 to 19 (two weeks)

Two-week break (Feb 22-March 5)

March 8 to 26 (final three weeks)

“I think, from all of us, if it’s possible to have the week of the 22nd of February off, and that is because that is when it’s a school break for all the different schools, the Dutch, British, French, and so that affects many people, I think, on the different teams,” said the Prosecution’s senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls.

Meanwhile, the chamber said the prosecution will present five witnesses for the first batch of evidence. The first witness will take six hours, a “little much shorter” time for the other two, then four hours each for the last two witnesses.

Korner also asked the prosecution if it was possible to prioritize the in-person witnesses, before presenting witnesses who will testify via video link. Nicholls said they have at least 29 witnesses who will testify online.

Once again, the large data set of evidence against Duterte, a subject of debate in the last status conferences, was brought up.

Nicholls said they will discuss the matter to straighten things out.

“And so we’re planning on having meetings this week to see about ways we may be able to reach agreements, which, as we started talking about this, if we can come to some agreements, that may sort of extract the relevance of a lot of, or not relevance, but extract the need to rely on much of that if we can come to some agreements,” said the prosecution lawyer.

The court also went into private or closed sessions multiple times during the Monday hearing. The chamber does this when there are matters that are private or confidential in nature that need to be discussed. – Rappler.com

World.title: Filipino embalmers – last caretakers of the dead, seldom cared for
World.content:
Part 2: Trainers say a decade of reforms professionalized the embalming industry, but regulation, data, and pay have not kept pace

PART 1 | Inside the world of Filipino embalmers

Last of 2 parts

When Jonnel Cribello received his license to embalm in 2009, one question followed him everywhere.

“The most frequent question people asked me [was] whether I washed my hands before shaking theirs,” he said.

A registered nurse who once dreamed of becoming a surgeon, Cribello turned to embalming after coming across a media feature on an embalming school. “If I wanted to work with the human body, the easiest route for me then was to work in the mortuary industry,” he said.

Today, he helps teach the next generation of embalmers as an accredited trainer and program director at the Philippine College of Advanced Studies (PCAS) in Cebu, one of only four active accredited embalming schools in the country and the only one outside Luzon.

Embalmers disinfect, preserve, and restore a body so families can hold a wake — often for days — before burial or cremation.

But while the industry has made strides in shedding its perception as dirty work, the systems around it — licensing, data, and pay — have been slower to catch up with other medical-adjacent fields.

Changing image

For years, embalmers were seen as untidy and uneducated, said James Patrick Ovejera, president of the Professional Embalmers Association of the Philippines Inc. (PEAP).

“There was an idea that it’s dirty work, the person is untidy, the person is illiterate, and the person is technically a low-class person,” he said. “There were even depictions in the movies wherein it’s a person that works in a dark place… a hunchback.”

That image began to shift around 2010, when the Department of Health (DOH) set out to professionalize the field, Ovejera said.

The rules governing embalming date back to 1975, when then-president Ferdinand E. Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 856, or the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines. Its chapter XXI, on the disposal of dead persons, covers everything from burial grounds to funeral and embalming establishments.

Detailed rules for embalmers came only in 1996, more than two decades later. They called for the DOH to create a Committee of Examiners for Undertakers and Embalmers (DOH-CEUE), which licenses embalmers and accredits training schools.

In 2010, the DOH reinstated the committee with new members, who worked with the University of the Philippines to streamline the curriculum and licensure exam, under Administrative Order No. 2010-0033. The order also, for the first time, mandated minimum wage for all embalmers.

The committee and the five training schools at the time then went region by region to explain the rules to local officials. Feedback led to new measures, including a refresher program for embalmers with long-expired licenses and a Filipino version of the exam, which was previously in English.

“There are a lot of people [who] are very skilled coming from the provinces…but they couldn’t really understand English well,” said Ovejera. At the time, he had been teaching at the Philippine Embalmers and Undertakers Review and Training Center (PEURTC), and enlisted in the roadshow efforts.

In 2018, embalmers like Ovejera formed PEAP as their own professional counterpart to the Philippine Mortuary Association, which represents funeral homeowners.

“At the time, there was no collective body representing us, and we wanted to do something about that,” he said.

In the classroom

LEARNING. Embalming students at PCAS watch an instructor lead a demonstration on a cadaver. Photo courtesy of PCAS

Under current DOH rules, aspiring embalmers need a high school diploma, at least 140 hours of instruction from an accredited institution, and proof that they have embalmed at least 10 cadavers within a year. They then take a licensure exam held twice a year, every March and September.

Under rules revised in 2021, licenses are issued by the DOH’s Health Facilities and Services Regulatory Bureau (HFSRB) after applicants pass the committee’s exam. These are valid for three years and can be revoked if not renewed within five.

Students spend about two months in class and a month embalming real cadavers at partner funeral homes. Tuition ranges from about P27,000 to about P30,000 depending on the training institution.

Over half of Cribello’s students at PCAS have worked in funeral homes or come from families that own one. His oldest student was 75; the average age is around 45.
