That is why studying business experience has become one of the areas of our cooperation with TikTok,” said Aslan Kaligazin, a member of the board and deputy chairman of the board of the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs.

“This year, with the active participation of regional chambers of entrepreneurs, we updated the study and collected practical examples of how Kazakh companies use the platform,” he said.

The partnership builds on several initiatives. TikTok for Business was introduced in Kazakhstan in 2021, offering tools for businesses of different sizes. In 2022, TikTok and Astana Hub launched the TikTok Startup Academy, which had graduated three cohorts by 2025.

In 2024, TikTok and Atameken organized the Made in Kazakhstan competition, bringing together more than 800 micro and small enterprises working on social and environmental projects.

The latest survey suggests that TikTok has become a regular part of marketing for many of the businesses questioned, with some reporting substantial revenue linked to their activity on the platform. Whether that translates into a comparable impact across Kazakhstan’s wider SME sector remains an open question.

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens Small Modular Reactor Simulator for Nuclear Training
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has opened a training classroom featuring a simulator of the SMR-300 small modular reactor at the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Almaty on Oct. 30 to provide practical training for specialists in the nuclear energy sector.

The training complex was established under the FIRST program, in which Kazakhstan has participated since 2022, becoming the program’s first partner in Central Asia. Launched in 2019 under the U.S. Department of State, the Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) program harnesses the power of the nuclear industry and innovation to expedite deployment of SMRs worldwide.

According to Sayabek Sakhiev, director general of the Institute of Nuclear Physics, the facility builds on the institute’s longstanding work in training professionals for the nuclear industry, reported the Kazinform news agency.

“According to the recommendations of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), specialists with higher professional education for nuclear power plants should be trained on research reactors such as the one at the Institute of Nuclear Physics,” Sakhiev said.

The institute’s training centers have prepared more than 5,000 specialists for Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. The new facility is also expected to serve as a regional training center.

Based on the SMR-300 simulator, the complex is designed to support educational and practical training in small modular reactor technologies. The equipment has been installed and tested, with the facility intended to help students, young professionals, engineers and researchers develop practical skills.

Asset Makhambetov, deputy chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy, said nuclear energy was becoming a strategic area of the country’s development.

“The significance of the new training complex goes far beyond equipping it with modern technology. It will help improve the knowledge of Kazakh specialists and develop their practical skills,” he said.

The next stage will involve developing training programs, scenarios and practical exercises in cooperation with the simulator’s developers.

More than 1,300 students studying for nuclear sector

Gulzat Kobenova, vice minister of science and higher education, said 12 universities in Kazakhstan train specialists in nuclear energy, including through partnerships with research institutes and foreign universities.

The new classroom will support not only lessons but also research projects, master’s programs, doctoral research and scientific internships.

More than 1,300 students are currently enrolled in relevant programs at Kazakh universities, 96% of whom study under state-funded educational programs, according to Kobenova. The country’s annual demand for new specialists is estimated at approximately 200 to 300 people.

The Institute of Nuclear Physics is also preparing a separate classroom for senior-year students specialising in nuclear energy. The opening of the facility forms part of cooperation between Kazakhstan and the United States on the peaceful use of nuclear energy and the development of modern nuclear technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Samodelkina Finishes Fifth at Skate Canada Grand Prix
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina finished fifth at the Skate Canada Grand Prix, scoring a total of 206.89 points across the short and free programs.

Samodelkina earned 71.84 points for her short program and 135.05 for her free skate, securing a place in the top five among 12 competitors.

Japan’s Mao Shimada won the event with 235.44 points, followed by Estonia’s Nina Petrykina with 221.07. American Isabeau Levito took third place with 212.22, while Japan’s Saki Miyake finished fourth with 210.09.

Samodelkina, 19, has been training in the United States since 2025 under renowned coach Rafael Arutyunyan. She won bronze at the Denis Ten Memorial in Almaty earlier this season.

In a recent online meeting with Kazakh journalists, Samodelkina said her daily routine largely revolves around training, which typically takes six to seven hours a day, including three to three and a half hours on the ice, with the remaining time devoted to physical conditioning, running and walking, reported the Kazinform news agency.

She said Arutyunyan’s experience and attention to detail have changed her understanding of figure skating, including how seemingly small technical issues can affect a jump. According to Samodelkina, one of the defining features of his coaching is his ability to identify details other coaches might overlook.

“You can skate a program perfectly cleanly, and he will point out three things that need to be improved completely. So when a coach like that says ‘well done,’ it means you really have done well,” she said.

Samodelkina also cited American figure skater Nathan Chen, the 2022 Olympic champion and another of Arutyunyan’s students, as an example of the coach’s influence.

“He worked with Rafael Vladimirovich for 12 years, and I don’t have that much time anymore. Rafael Vladimirovich always says: he learned this in 12 years, and your task is to learn it in two years, otherwise you won’t make it in time,” she said.

Samodelkina said she hopes to continue competing through the 2030 Winter Olympics.

“I will definitely keep skating for another four years, and then we’ll see,” she said.

Learning Kazakh and staying connected to home

Despite her demanding schedule in California, Samodelkina said returning to Kazakhstan gives her an opportunity to relax, spend time with loved ones and feel at home. She described California primarily as a place for training, with much of her routine limited to travelling to the rink, practising and returning home.

The skater said she has seen little of California during her two years there because of her training commitments. She usually spends time at home only between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. and rarely gets the chance to go out with friends.

Samodelkina is also studying Kazakh through online lessons. She said representing Kazakhstan at international competitions and carrying the country’s flag have encouraged her to learn more about its language and culture.

Learning the language has not always been easy, she acknowledged, particularly because of differences in pronunciation and sounds that do not exist in Russian. Nevertheless, she continues to study and enjoys using Kazakh to greet supporters and thank them for their encouragement.

Following the Grand Prix events, Samodelkina is expected to return to Kazakhstan to perform in the ice show “Alice in Wonderland on Ice” in Almaty on Dec. 26. She may also compete at the Four Continents Figure Skating Championships, scheduled to take place in Almaty in February 2027.

World.title: OPEC+ Countries Agree to Keep Oil Production Levels Unchanged in December
World.content:
ASTANA – Seven OPEC+ countries, including Kazakhstan, have agreed to maintain oil production levels in December 2026 at the levels set for September, according to a statement published by the organization.

Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman held an online meeting on Nov. 1 to review developments in the global oil market and its outlook. The seven countries had previously announced additional voluntary production adjustments in April and November 2023.

Following the meeting, participants agreed to maintain their September 2026 production levels for December, according to the table published in the organization’s statement. The countries also reaffirmed their commitment to fully comply with the terms of the Declaration of Cooperation, which underpins coordination among OPEC+ members.

The seven countries will continue to hold monthly meetings to review global oil market conditions. Their next meeting is scheduled for Nov. 29.

World.title: ‘Certain circles in Russia and Eurasian Economic Union back secret plan by Armenian opposition’ – Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on secret plan by Russia and Armenian opposition

Armenia has reached a very important historic turning point, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the 2027 state budget. He described it as a moment that would have a decisive impact on the country’s political, economic and social development.

However, he said that forces both inside Armenia and abroad were seeking to prevent this historic moment from arriving. According to Pashinyan, similar forces had opposed Armenian statehood in the past, dating back to 2018. That was the year of Armenia’s “Velvet Revolution”, which brought him and his team to power. “But this year, their cards have been laid bare,” Pashinyan stressed.

He singled out the so-called “secret plan”, which opposition circles have been discussing recently.

“The aim of this plan is to prevent Armenia from continuing on its path of economic development. There are not enough resources inside Armenia to implement this secret plan, so its authors must do everything possible to secure resources from abroad,” he said.

The prime minister spoke about this “secret plan” a couple of weeks ago, but did not specify which countries he meant. This time, however, he openly named them:

“I do not want to hide the fact that certain circles within the Eurasian Economic Union, led by Russia, and in the Russian Federation itself support this plan. And there are reasons for this, because people have been sent to Armenia with specific promises and guarantees.”

Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition Strong Armenia party, has repeatedly spoken about a “secret plan” to change the government in Armenia. He made these remarks in response to a question about the steps the opposition intended to take to oust the current authorities. At his weekly briefing on 22 October, Nikol Pashinyan said that forces both inside Armenia and abroad were taking steps to effectively eliminate the country: “The aim is to provoke political instability inside Armenia. As a result, they intend to take control of the Armenian state. In other words, they want to strip Armenia of its independence – first de facto, and then de jure.” The prime minister also said that several similar attempts had taken place over the past three years. He cited, in particular, the events in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023 and hybrid attacks on Armenia during the parliamentary elections, which took place in June this year. He believes a third attempt is now under way. In particular, he was referring to an expert forecast by the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, which warned of an allegedly catastrophic economic downturn in Armenia if the country left the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU. “This is part of the ‘secret plan’ that people are actively discussing now,” Pashinyan said.

“Armenia’s political forces must understand that the people are their only guarantee”

The prime minister said that certain opposition figures had “received specific guarantees and been sent to Armenia”. He then asked: “So why are these guarantees not being honoured?” He went on to answer his own question, urging the opposition to look back at the history of the Armenian people. He said that whenever such “guarantors” had emerged, the outcome had invariably been another catastrophe.

“I am essentially doing our opposition colleagues a favour by pointing out that they still have time to avoid a similar catastrophe. I am talking about the political catastrophe facing opposition parties, which you all know about. I hope they will seize this opportunity to avoid it.”

He recalled that he had previously urged the opposition to stop relying on these “guarantors” and instead focus its efforts on strengthening Armenia’s independence and sovereignty. However, his proposal went unanswered.

“In effect, it was rejected through silence. I believe the window of opportunity has not yet closed. Ultimately, our political forces must understand that there is only one guarantee – the people of Armenia,” he stressed.

World.title: GYLA challenges conviction of defendant in case over storming of Georgia’s presidential palace
World.content:
According to the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), the case against Paata Manjgaladze, one of the leaders of the opposition Strategy Aghmashenebeli party, who was convicted in the so-called “4 October case”, lacks sufficient evidence that he planned, organised or led group violence.

In a detailed assessment, the association says the prosecution has failed to distinguish Manjgaladze’s political activities from any alleged involvement in violent acts.

In particular, it has presented no evidence linking him to the violence outside the presidential palace in Tbilisi.

On 4 October 2025, Georgia held local government elections. Much of the opposition boycotted the vote and staged a large-scale protest in Tbilisi that day. The demonstration ended with an attempt to storm the presidential palace.

GYLA argues that these claims are not substantiated by Manjgaladze’s previous political statements either, as some of them are undated and the circumstances in which they were made remain unclear.

“A political or organisational connection to a protest cannot in itself constitute grounds for liability for organising violence unless the defendant’s specific contribution is established,” GYLA writes.

Paata Manjgaladze

Paata Manjgaladze is the secretary-general of the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party and a former member of the Georgian parliament. On 4 October 2025, he took part in a protest in Tbilisi. Prosecutors accused him of organising group violence and leading it. On 7 May 2026, a court found him guilty and sentenced him to seven years in prison. His case is now before the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.

What Manjgaladze is accused of

Prosecutors charged Paata Manjgaladze on 6 October 2025. According to their account, he and other opposition figures arrested in connection with the case had urged citizens to overthrow the government by force. On 4 October, they then decided to organise group violence.

Opera singer Paata Burchuladze, who organised the rally and was later arrested in the same case, announced the plan at the protest. Murtaz Zodelava, a member of the United National Movement party, then called on the crowd to march towards the presidential palace and seize it.

To support the charges, prosecutors cite witness testimony, media reports, written documents, expert assessments, audio and video recordings from the scene, as well as objects found there and damaged equipment. The investigation also relied on search and seizure records and other materials gathered during the inquiry.

The prosecution maintains that this evidence is sufficient to establish the defendants’ involvement in the crime.

However, it remains unclear which specific pieces of evidence relate directly to Manjgaladze. In GYLA’s assessment, the indictment does not adequately explain what specific actions Manjgaladze himself took or what evidence demonstrates his involvement in the crime.

GYLA argues that political activity, attendance at a protest, a photograph with other organisers or a particular sequence of events cannot, in themselves, justify charging someone with organising group violence. This is especially important when the defendant is a politician. The charges must leave no doubt that the prosecution is not politically motivated.

Чего требует GYLA от Апелляционного суда

GYLA призывает Апелляционный суд проверить, какое конкретно действие приписывается Манджгаладзе, какие доказательства это подтверждают и как были оценены аргументы стороны защиты.

GYLA также отмечает, что по делу представил свое заключение народный защитник (омбудсмен), по мнению которого также не вырисовывается конкретная роль Манджгаладзе в организации группового насилия, а лишь упоминание его в качестве организатора акции недостаточно для привлечения к уголовной ответственности.

Организация считает, что если Апелляционный суд разделяет позиции GYLA и Народного защитника и для этого будут существовать правовые основания, он должен вынести в отношении Манджгаладзе оправдательный приговор.

Criminal proceedings have been launched against 64 people in connection with the events of 4 October. Prosecutors charged those detained with organising group violence, leading it or taking part in it, attempting to seize a strategic facility, and calling for the violent overthrow of the constitutional order. The case was divided into several separate proceedings.

The first-instance trials have now concluded. Of the 64 defendants:

One person was fined;

was fined; 29 people were sentenced to prison terms, three of them in absentia;

were sentenced to prison terms, three of them in absentia; 12 defendants had their sentences reduced under plea agreements;

had their sentences reduced under plea agreements; 22 people received suspended sentences under plea agreements and avoided prison.

World.title: Horrific discovery at cemetery renews debate over fate of stray dogs in Georgia
World.content:
Journalists and animal rights activists have discovered burial pits in Georgia’s capital Tbilisi, containing dozens of dead dogs dumped and covered with soil. Activists suspect the animals were healthy strays taken from the city streets. Judging by the condition of the bodies, veterinarians believe the dogs suffered greatly before they died.

The disturbing footage sparked widespread outrage on social media. Animal rights activists have called for an immediate investigation. A large protest took place in Tbilisi on the evening of 1 November. The city authorities deny accusations that they killed healthy dogs, dismiss them as a deliberate disinformation campaign and threaten criminal charges against activists who opened the burial pits without permission.

Nevertheless, Georgia’s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which concerns animal cruelty.

What do we know so far about the dog burial pits discovered in Tbilisi? Why do animal rights activists distrust the city authorities and municipal services? And why has Georgia been unable to solve its stray animal problem for years?

Night-time trips to Veli Cemetery

Blurred photograph of one of the burial sites at Veli Cemetery in Tbilisi. As the footage filmed by activists is extremely distressing, JAMnews has deliberately chosen not to use it in this article.

Under cover of darkness, a white minibus leaves Tbilisi’s municipal animal shelter. Someone has removed the shelter’s logo from the vehicle. The minibus soon stops at Veli Cemetery on the outskirts of the Georgian capital. The engine keeps running, but the driver switches off the headlights.

Two people get out. They wear the shelter’s uniform and latex gloves. In complete darkness, lit only by the moon, they take the bodies of dogs out of the vehicle and dump them into pits that someone has dug in advance.

This continues over several nights. On one occasion, the workers dump seven dogs into a pit, while an eighth falls beside the vehicle. Despite the darkness, the footage clearly shows a man wearing gloves dragging the animal towards the burial site.

On the third night, the makeshift grave is already full of dogs’ bodies, and the workers begin covering it with soil. They do this in darkness too, switching on the vehicle’s headlights only occasionally to check their progress.

These images come from a report that TV Pirveli broadcast on 31 October. It documents alleged cruelty towards stray animals in Tbilisi. Someone filmed the footage with a hidden camera over several nights.

According to the programme’s journalists, people regularly remove dozens of dead dogs from Tbilisi’s municipal animal shelter without permission and bury them in specially dug deep pits at the cemetery. Citing their sources, the journalists also report that the shelter has a quarantine area where staff euthanise healthy animals picked up from the streets.

Even before the report aired, shortly after the channel announced it, animal rights activists discovered additional burial sites near Veli Cemetery. They filmed and circulated even more disturbing footage. It shows graves filled with dogs whose eyes bulge and bodies appear twisted (JAMnews warning: the footage at this link is extremely distressing.)

The activists called the police to the site. Police representatives told TV Pirveli that they would investigate the matter step by step and report their findings.

Animal rights activists’ demands

After the story came to light, animal rights activists drew up a petition, calling on the prosecutor’s office to launch an immediate investigation. The petition’s authors point to an increasing number of suspicious cases in which dogs have disappeared across Georgia. They want investigators to examine the burial site at Veli Cemetery, exhume the remains and commission an independent veterinary and forensic examination to establish when and how the animals died.

The activists also urge prosecutors to check the microchips and other identification marks on stray animals, compare reports from members of the public about missing dogs with the remains found at the cemetery, and examine the shelter’s veterinary records on euthanasia and its accounts of drugs used for the procedure.

In their view, investigators must establish who ordered the animals’ burial, the legal grounds for removing their bodies and whether the burial process complied with the law. The petition’s authors stress that the public has the right to know how many animals died, under what circumstances and whether official statistics reflect the true scale of the situation.

Some people recognised among the dead dogs found at the burial site in Veli Cemetery strays they had been caring for. The image illustrates one such case: a Tbilisi resident writes on social media that a dog he looked after is lying in the pit (right-hand photo).

Tbilisi City Hall denies killing animals

The Animal Monitoring Agency, which operates under Tbilisi City Hall, denies the allegations. In an official statement, the agency says that “the footage broadcast by TV Pirveli shows a procedure permitted by law”.

The agency claims that the burial site at Veli Cemetery holds the remains of dogs that died in Tbilisi for various reasons, including illness, road accidents and other incidents, as well as natural causes.

“Across the capital, hundreds of animals die through euthanasia every year, while thousands die of natural causes,” the agency says in its statement.

It categorically denies allegations of mass, deliberate killings, insisting that the information circulated by journalists and activists amounts to disinformation intended to discredit the Animal Monitoring Agency and damage its reputation.

Tbilisi City Hall also says that unauthorised exhumations and the removal of remains violate the law, risk biological contamination and pose a threat to public health. On these grounds, the city authorities have threatened activists with criminal liability.

“We have already asked law enforcement agencies to investigate acts of vandalism committed by a particular group and take appropriate legal action,” City Hall said.

Signs of torture on the animals’ bodies

Animal rights activists question the agency’s claims that the dogs found at Veli Cemetery died of natural causes or were humanely euthanised. Activist Keso Baramidze, who has had dozens of animals euthanised when it was genuinely necessary, says dogs usually retain a peaceful expression after euthanasia.

“Sadly, dozens of animals have fallen asleep in my arms. Not one of them had an expression like the dogs found in the burial pits. They all simply looked as though they were sleeping. That is why the procedure is called ‘putting to sleep’,” she says in a social media post.

Baramidze outlines several possible causes of muscle tension and facial distortion in animals after death. These include:

Mechanical asphyxiation (strangulation) with a rope or wire, as well as burying an animal alive or while it still shows signs of life. This can deprive it of oxygen and cause severe agony;

with a rope or wire, as well as burying an animal alive or while it still shows signs of life. This can deprive it of oxygen and cause severe agony; Improperly administered chemical euthanasia – using drugs that cause muscle paralysis or other toxic substances without adequate anaesthesia. In such cases, the animal may die while still conscious;

– using drugs that cause muscle paralysis or other toxic substances without adequate anaesthesia. In such cases, the animal may die while still conscious; Severe physical trauma or electric shock – a powerful blow to the head or neck, or exposure to an electric current, which can cause severe muscle spasms and body tension.

“With any of these methods, when a dog dies amid extreme stress, fear, struggle and muscle exhaustion, its reserves of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) are depleted almost immediately. This causes rigor mortis to set in very early, almost instantly, within the first 10–20 minutes.

“Since rigor mortis always begins in the facial and jaw muscles, any grimace caused during the animal’s death throes becomes ‘frozen’. Even while the body remains warm, the face stays contorted,” Baramidze writes, citing scientific sources from abroad.

Protests and investigation

On Sunday, 1 November, the day after the report aired, animal rights activists staged a protest outside the government chancellery in Tbilisi. “We demand answers. Punish the officials responsible,” they called.

“Dogs tortured to death”, “Where have you taken the dogs?”, “I speak for those without a voice” read the banners held by protesters, including both activists and ordinary animal lovers. Many brought their pets to the demonstration.

“What we have been saying for several months has now been confirmed. They are continuing to exterminate stray dogs instead of sterilising and vaccinating them in an effort to reduce their numbers. I hope society will now become more active. Because if there aren’t enough of us, they will obviously not stop,” said Lasha Chkhartishvili, one of the protest organisers.

Protest outside the Government Chancellery on 1 November 2026. Photo: Rusudan Jakeli.

“A dog tortured to death” – reads the banner at the 1 November protest.

That same evening, Georgia’s Interior Ministry announced that it had opened an investigation under Article 259 of the Criminal Code, which covers torture, cruel treatment and other forms of violence against animals.

Not an isolated incident, but a pattern

This is not the first case, nor the first footage to emerge showing alleged cruelty towards stray animals in Georgia.

In mid-October, a video filmed on a mobile phone at the municipal animal shelter in the town of Gori spread across social media. It showed a filthy enclosure measuring just five to seven square metres, with a damp floor and crammed with dozens of puppies. Many of the animals looked extremely thin and malnourished.

The following day, volunteers rescued the puppies from the enclosures, set up temporary shelters for them and began treating them. Social media users also launched a fundraising campaign to help the puppies and the people who had taken them in.

Earlier, in April 2026, disturbing footage from Gori also emerged, apparently showing animals being burned at a crematorium. However, the Gori shelter insisted that it had cremated dead dogs or amputated body parts.

Stray animals on the streets have long been a serious problem in Georgia. The streets are full of stray dogs, some of which are aggressive and pose a danger to passers-by. Yet no one knows exactly how many homeless animals live in the country. Georgia has never maintained comprehensive statistics on their numbers. Animal rights activists estimate that the population could reach hundreds of thousands.

Georgia has been running a new stray animal population management programme for the past two years. In theory, it should reduce the number of stray dogs through humane methods. However, animal rights activists suspect that the authorities are trying to solve the problem through straightforward extermination. They say dogs have been disappearing from the streets in large numbers since the programme began.

JAMnews reported on the situation in May 2026, when activists across Georgia raised the alarm over dogs taken from the streets and then reported missing. Some of the animals had been cared for by specific individuals, vaccinated, sterilised and identified.

The World Organisation for Animal Health recommends the CNVR method – Collect, Neuter, Vaccinate and Return – in its guidelines for managing stray dog populations. When properly implemented, this approach can gradually reduce the number of animals without resorting to mass killing.

Activists in Georgia also regard this as the best approach. None of them wants packs of stray dogs roaming the streets. But they insist that the authorities must tackle the problem humanely. The footage that has emerged in recent weeks has raised growing questions about the conduct of government agencies and strengthened suspicions that the authorities intend to reduce the stray animal population by killing the dogs.

World.title: Azerbaijan gets just $65 of every $120 barrel of oil – where does rest go?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s oil revenues

The price of Azerbaijani oil on the global market fluctuated between $120 and $130 a barrel in October, reaching $133 on 9 October. However, the state budget was drawn up on the basis of a forecast price of $65 a barrel.

The government is now using the same benchmark price for the 2027 budget.

Yet rising oil prices have not translated into the expected increase in either the State Oil Fund’s assets or state budget revenues.

According to a report published by the State Oil Fund on 20 October, its assets have increased by just $462 million since the beginning of the year. Meanwhile, transfers from the fund to the state budget have fallen by 11.4% compared with the same period last year.

JAMnews previously reported that the government plans to reduce transfers from the Oil Fund and increase income tax deductions from salaries in the 2027 budget. Now another question arises:

If oil is selling for significantly more than the price assumed in the budget, where is the additional revenue going?

Why is the budget based on a price of $65 a barrel?

Every year, when preparing the state budget, the government forecasts the average oil price for the coming year. It uses this estimate to calculate tax receipts and other revenues.

In November 2025, Finance Minister Sahil Babayev told parliament that the government had set its 2026 oil price forecast at $65 a barrel based on average estimates from 22 organisations. At the time, Brent crude traded at $64–65 a barrel.

However, the situation changed in early 2026.

In its July report, the State Oil Fund noted that the conflict between the US and Iran had triggered “high volatility” in energy markets. According to figures that Samir Nasirov, head of the Central Bank’s Statistics Department, presented in September, Azerbaijani oil averaged $94.5 a barrel in the first half of the year.

That was 33% higher than in the same period last year and approximately 45% above the price assumed in the budget.

According to the Finance Ministry’s preliminary figures, the 2027 budget also assumes an oil price of $65 a barrel. However, in its medium-term expenditure framework for 2027–2030, the ministry describes the likelihood of oil prices falling below $65 next year as “low”.

In other words, the budget relies on a price close to what the ministry itself considers one of the less favourable scenarios.

Using a lower forecast price means that additional oil revenues go to the State Oil Fund rather than directly into the state budget.

Economist Natig Jafarli made this point back in March, when oil prices began to rise.

He said higher prices would affect “not the state budget directly”, but the consolidated budget, which also includes the State Oil Fund’s resources.

According to Jafarli’s calculations, every $1 increase in the oil price brings the fund approximately $450,000 in additional revenue each day.

Supporters of the government’s policy see this additional revenue as a reserve that could help finance security spending.

In March, Vugar Bayramov, a member of the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, told OC Media that the additional revenue would allow the government to fund “priority areas such as national security”.

Why are higher oil prices not bringing additional revenue into the state budget?

The government determines how much money the State Oil Fund must transfer to the state budget each year before the financial year begins. It sets the amount out in the fund’s budget.

According to the Finance Ministry, the fund transferred 9.628 billion manats (approximately $5.663 billion) to the state budget between January and September, exactly as planned.

However, this was 1.23 billion manats (approximately $723 million) less than in the same period last year.

Total state budget revenue from the oil and gas sector reached 12.93 billion manats (approximately $7.6 billion). This was 625.5 million manats (approximately $368 million), or 5.1%, above the forecast.

Since the State Oil Fund made transfers as planned, tax payments from oil companies accounted for the additional revenue.

According to the ministry, the Shah Deniz project paid 1.54 billion manats in taxes (approximately $906 million), SOCAR paid 1.3 billion manats (approximately $765 million), and the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli project contributed 461 million manats (approximately $271.2 million).

Overall, state budget revenues in the first nine months exceeded the forecast by 2.8%.

In other words:

In the first half of the year, oil prices were approximately 45% above the level assumed in the budget.

Yet total state budget revenues exceeded the forecast by just 2.8% in the first nine months.

Если деньги остаются в фонде, почему его активы не растут?

Согласно отчету Нефтяного фонда, значительная часть дополнительных доходов либо не поступила в фонд, либо была поглощена другими расходами и убытками.

Нефтяной фонд, январь–сентябрь 2026 года (млн манатов):

Indicator Amount Revenues from the sale of profitable oil and gas 7 343,9 Proceeds from the sale of the state’s stake in the Southern Gas Corridor 1 390,9 Other oil and gas revenues 5,8 Income from asset management 3 600,7 Total revenues 12 341,3 Transfers to the state budget -9 628,0 Expenditure on project implementation and management -53,2 Losses due to changes in gold prices and foreign exchange rates -1 874,0 Increase in the Fund’s assets 786.1 (approximately $462 million)

Source: State Oil Fund. JAMnews calculated the figure in the final row using the fund’s published data on asset growth.

The figures point to three conclusions.

First, the fund’s revenue from oil and gas sales (7.34 billion manats) fell 2.3 billion manats short of the amount it transferred to the state budget (9.63 billion manats). Revenue from the fund’s overseas investments and proceeds from the sale of the state’s stake in the Southern Gas Corridor helped cover the gap.

Second, changes in gold prices and exchange rates caused losses of 1.87 billion manats (approximately $1.01 billion). At the end of the first half of the year, losses stood at 3.69 billion manats (approximately $2.17 billion), but they narrowed in the third quarter. Gold has become one of the fund’s key assets in recent years. In its assessment of the fund’s 2026 budget, the Chamber of Accounts noted that rising gold prices had generated a significant share of the fund’s non-budget revenues in the first nine months of 2025. The same assessment warned that, as oil revenues and production volumes decline, the fund’s assets could “be rapidly depleted”.

Third, despite higher oil prices, the fund’s oil revenues did not grow at a comparable rate. According to the fund’s report, receipts from the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli field averaged 729 million manats (approximately $428.8 million) a month in the first half of the year, compared with 732 million manats (approximately $430.6 million) in the third quarter. JAMnews calculated these figures using data from the State Oil Fund.

Oil production is declining

According to preliminary figures from the Energy Ministry, Azerbaijan produced 19.9 million tonnes of oil, including gas condensate, between January and September. This was 3.9% less than in the same period last year.

Exports show a similar trend. According to State Customs Committee data for January–August, the physical volume of crude oil exports fell by 7.8% compared with the same period last year, while their value increased by just 10.5%.

In other words, although Azerbaijan sells each barrel of oil at a higher price, it exports less oil. Falling production partly offsets the additional revenue from higher prices.

In September, economist Elchin Mammadov highlighted this contradiction in an interview with Sfera.az:

“Although the average oil price has risen by around 30% this year compared with 2025, the latest published statistics point to a continued decline in the oil and gas sector.”

He said the sector’s gross domestic product had fallen by 0.8%.

In the assessment mentioned above, the Chamber of Accounts also forecast that oil production at the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli fields would fall to 120.1 million barrels in 2026, down 3 million barrels from the previous year.

What will change for citizens?

According to the preliminary 2027 budget figures presented by the government, transfers from the State Oil Fund will fall by 935 million manats to 11.9 billion manats (approximately $550 million).

The income tax rate on the portion of salaries up to 2,500 manats (approximately $1,470) in the private non-oil and gas sector will rise from 3% to 5%. It will increase further to 7% in 2028. Meanwhile, the government plans to cover 2.75 billion manats (approximately $1.617 billion) of the projected budget deficit of 3.17 billion manats (approximately $1.867 billion) through borrowing.

News that the country’s foreign exchange reserves had exceeded $90 billion had already sparked public debate. Critics called on the government to use some of these funds to improve living standards.

The government, meanwhile, sees reducing the budget’s dependence on oil revenues as a positive trend. Commenting on the preliminary 2027 budget figures, Vugar Bayramov welcomed the increase in the share of non-oil revenues to more than 60%, saying this would make the budget more resilient.

Under this approach, the less the budget depends on oil revenues, the less vulnerable it becomes to falling oil prices.

What happens next?

Oil prices through the end of this year and into next year will depend largely on developments in the Middle East.

However, the Finance Ministry’s forecast suggests that even if oil prices remain high, the State Oil Fund’s assets will not grow. According to the ministry’s medium-term expenditure framework, the fund’s assets are expected to stand at $73.9 billion by 2030. That is below their current level of $74 billion.

An analysis by Meydan TV, based on the document, forecasts a 25.5% decline in oil and gas revenues to the budget between 2026 and 2030. Meanwhile, debt servicing costs are expected to rise to around 3 billion manats (approximately $1.765 billion).

The government’s draft budget for 2027 once again assumes an oil price of $65 a barrel. It also provides for lower transfers from the State Oil Fund and higher income tax deductions from salaries.

Azerbaijan’s oil revenues

World.title: Podcast “Protests in Georgia” – pro-European Saturday march in Tbilisi, video and photos
World.content:
Georgia protests, video and photos

703 days of continuous pro-European protests in Georgia, marked by another traditional Saturday march in Tbilisi on 31 October. As in recent weeks, the main message was the slogan: “Georgia against [oligarch] Ivanishvili!”

The march was joined by family members of activists detained during pro-European demonstrations.

Context

The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for more than 700 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia calls for investigation into alleged abuses by Russian company running railway
World.content:
Aram Sargsyan, leader of the Republic Party, has called on Armenia’s prosecutor general to investigate the activities of South Caucasus Railway. If the investigation uncovers any abuses, the politician insists that prosecutors open a criminal case.

Armenia’s railways operate under a concession agreement with South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. Armenia signed a 30-year concession agreement in 2008, handing the management of Armenian Railways CJSC to Russian Railways. However, freight traffic has since halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the company has yet to fulfil its mandatory investment commitments.

Sargsyan says the authorities need to examine:

the efficiency of the company’s operations;

its compliance with its contractual management obligations;

the protection of the state’s property interests.

“I ask you to accept this statement and consider it a report of a suspected criminal offence under the procedure established by the Criminal Procedure Code of the Republic of Armenia,” he said.

The politician’s appeal to the prosecutor general comes amid talks between Armenia and Russia over the railway concession.

Yerevan has long called for changes to the concession arrangement. It argues that a new format would make Armenia’s railway more competitive. In particular, the Armenian authorities have proposed transferring the concession to a third party. Moscow, however, has yet to accept the proposal.

Two weeks ago, Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozyorov visited Yerevan. Following their meeting, Armenia’s prime minister announced that the two sides had agreed to set up a joint working group. According to Nikol Pashinyan, the group has three months to examine specific questions from the Armenian government and provide answers. The key issue is whether Russia is prepared to invest in the railway. Yerevan will decide on its next steps after receiving the group’s findings.

The Prosecutor General’s Office issued a brief statement, offering no further comment. It said that it had accepted Aram Sargsyan’s application for consideration.

From dismantling infrastructure to declining freight volumes

In his appeal, the leader of the Republic Party recalled an interview that Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan gave to the Russian newspaper Kommersant on 10 September 2018. Discussing South Caucasus Railway, Pashinyan said the company’s alleged abuses amounted to approximately $60 million. He also said law enforcement agencies were investigating the matter and that the public would soon learn the findings.

“I believe it is necessary to clarify how the investigation conducted at the time concluded, what results it produced and whether the state received compensation for any damage it may have suffered,” Sargsyan wrote.

Following Pashinyan’s statement in 2018, the authorities launched criminal proceedings. However, they discontinued the case in March 2021. No further developments have emerged since then. Nor has anyone reported whether the company compensated the state for the alleged damage.

The politician identified five issues in his appeal to the prosecutor general:

1. Dismantling railway infrastructure

“It is necessary to establish the circumstances surrounding the dismantling of railway infrastructure along the Meghri–Kapan section, which stretches for approximately 40km. The investigation should also establish the legal grounds for the work, determine what happened to the dismantled assets, assess whether the company lawfully disposed of the property and examine how it used the proceeds from any sale.”

2. The Ijevan–Aghstafa railway line

“It is necessary to examine the circumstances surrounding the dismantling or deterioration of railway infrastructure along a section of approximately 17km within Armenia. The investigation should assess whether the decisions taken in this regard were lawful and determine whether they caused damage to the state.”

3. Declining freight volumes

“According to published data, railway freight volumes fell significantly during South Caucasus Railway’s management of the network. It is necessary to compare the figures for 2008 with those from subsequent years, identify the reasons for the decline and establish whether poor management, failure to meet contractual obligations or other violations caused it.”

4. Reduction in the workforce

“It is necessary to examine the reasons behind the significant reduction in the number of employees, assess whether the company fulfilled its commitments and identify any possible violations during this process.”

5. Implementation of the concession agreement

“It is necessary to analyse the concession agreement signed in 2008, including its investment and other obligations, assess how the company has fulfilled them in practice, examine the effectiveness of state oversight and determine whether the company has lawfully maintained and used railway assets owned by Armenia.”

Aram Sargsyan stressed that the competent authorities must conduct a comprehensive and impartial investigation.

“The potential damage was inflicted on Armenia and, consequently, its citizens”

The politician believes the issue he has raised with law enforcement agencies is of critical importance. He says the authorities must first and foremost protect state property. He also stresses that the matter concerns Armenia’s economic security, the restoration of railway links and the country’s ability to realise its transit potential.

“The potential damage was inflicted on Armenia and, consequently, its citizens,” Sargsyan argues.

He has therefore asked the authorities to verify the facts that the prime minister presented in 2018 and report the findings of the investigation conducted at the time. He also expects law enforcement agencies to assess the five issues he has raised. If they uncover evidence of a criminal offence, he demands that they open a new criminal case.

Sargsyan says the authorities must establish the scale of the financial damage the state may have suffered and identify those responsible.

“If the authorities establish that a crime took place and caused damage to the state, they must take the measures required by law to secure compensation, recover property that was unlawfully disposed of or reclaim its value,” Sargsyan stressed.

He expects the prosecutor’s office to provide a written response outlining the investigation’s findings and the decisions it has taken.

Investigation into South Caucasus Railway: Aram Sargsyan’s appeal

World.title: Will Turkey open its border with Armenia amid tensions with Baku? Views from Yerevan
World.content:
Turkey-Armenia border: Will it open?

Discussions about the possible opening of the Armenian-Turkish border have intensified in Armenia in recent weeks. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan has not ruled out the possibility that the border could open before the two sides agree on candidates for new special envoys to oversee the normalisation process.

“The border remains closed, but I believe the process has reached a fairly advanced stage. It is entirely possible that we will wake up tomorrow morning and see a headline in the news: ‘The border between Armenia and Turkey is open’,” he said.

Armenian analysts say opening the border would clearly benefit Armenia, but would also serve Turkey’s interests. Some suggest that Turkey wants to open the border because this could:

expand its trade and transport opportunities;

provide an alternative to existing routes through Georgia;

strengthen its role in regional connectivity.

However, not everyone shares this view. Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan is sceptical about the prospects for an early border opening.

In an interview with JAMnews, he also discussed the recent cooling of relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan. Some in Armenia see this as a factor that could accelerate the normalisation process. Some experts suggest that, under these circumstances, Turkey could open the border without taking Baku’s position into account. Azerbaijan insists that Turkey should not move ahead before the two countries settle their relations with Armenia.

However, Alexander Iskandaryan believes that disagreements between Ankara and Baku do not mean Turkey will change its policy towards Armenia. He argues that relations with Azerbaijan remain strategically important to Turkey, and that “economic factors alone are unlikely to outweigh political calculations”.

Political analyst and director of the Caucasus Institute Alexander Iskandaryan

What matters is not brotherhood but rational political calculation

“Azerbaijan is extremely wary of the prospect of the Armenian-Turkish border opening. It sees the border closure as a means of putting pressure on Armenia. This has been the case since the conflict began, including during ‘football diplomacy’, when the two sides discussed opening the border without preconditions. However, Turkey eventually tied the process to a resolution of the Karabakh conflict, largely under pressure from the Azerbaijani lobby.

The process of normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey, known as ‘football diplomacy’, began in 2008. Serzh Sargsyan, who was Armenia’s president at the time, initiated it. At his invitation, Turkish President Abdullah Gül first visited Armenia. The two presidents watched a football match between their national teams. In 2009, Sargsyan travelled to Turkey, where the two national teams again played a match. ‘Football diplomacy’ resulted in the so-called Zurich Protocols, which the two countries’ foreign ministers signed in 2009. The documents set out plans to establish diplomatic relations and the principles governing bilateral ties. However, neither side ratified the protocols.

Despite the changes in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict, the border remains closed. Turkey and Azerbaijan continue to set conditions, including the signing of a peace treaty. This shows that no clear ‘red line’ exists beyond which the pressure would stop. The demands keep changing, and there is no guarantee that meeting them would change the situation. From Azerbaijan’s perspective, keeping these levers of pressure makes perfect sense.

The current debate in Armenia and Azerbaijan stems primarily from the disagreements between Baku and Ankara that have recently come into the open. The Armenian government apparently hopes these differences could weaken Azerbaijan’s influence over Turkey’s position and prompt Ankara to open the Armenian-Turkish border despite Baku’s objections.

However, I do not think the border is likely to open in the near future. On the contrary, the chances are quite low.

Disagreements between Azerbaijan and Turkey have always existed. They simply attracted less public attention in the past and remained largely unnoticed by wider audiences.

For example, the two countries take different approaches to relations with Israel. Azerbaijan maintains fairly close ties with Israel, while Turkey’s relations with the country have deteriorated over time, at times leading to serious disputes. Another example is the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. Ankara has openly urged Baku to recognise it, but Azerbaijan has not done so.

The recent surge in attention to disagreements between the two countries, including the dispute over the hijab ban in Azerbaijani schools, is merely the visible part of long-standing tensions. However, I would not expect these differences to make Baku and Ankara stop listening to each other. Disagreements between Azerbaijan and Turkey certainly exist, but that does not mean they will lead either country to rethink the relationship.

When it comes to Armenia, Turkey consistently supports Azerbaijan. It would be methodologically wrong to explain this policy solely through cultural affinity, the idea of ‘one nation, two states’ or feelings of brotherhood. This is not about sentiment but about rational political calculation, which underpins relations between the two countries.”

Political obstacles outweigh potential economic benefits

“Claims that opening the border with Armenia would bring Turkey significant economic benefits seem misleading or, at the very least, poorly informed. Armenia is not a large enough market for Turkey for the economic gains from opening the border to outweigh the political obstacles, which are far more significant.

The experience of ‘football diplomacy’ shows that Ankara was then seeking political gains in its relations with the West rather than closer economic ties with Armenia. At the time, the Armenian issue formed part of Turkey’s agenda in its relations with Europe and the European Union, and Ankara hoped to secure certain political benefits from it. There is no comparable rapprochement with the EU today. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, is already a reliable partner, and Turkey has a strong interest in maintaining its relations with Baku.

Never say ‘never’. But, in my view, hopes for an early border opening stem either from bias or from a failure to understand the situation. Even agreements that the two sides have reached do not always translate into action. For example, they have been discussing the restoration of the historic Ani Bridge for three years, while the completion of the tender process is presented as a major achievement. That is why I consider a border opening in the near future unlikely.”

Why does Turkey need another route?

“The argument that opening the Armenian-Turkish border would give Turkey an additional gateway to Central Asian markets is unconvincing. A railway route through Georgia already exists: the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars line, which remains underused. If Turkey had a serious interest in increasing freight traffic in this direction, it could make better use of the existing route. It is also unclear what additional freight volumes would require a new route through Armenia.”

Opening the border does not guarantee normalisation

“Opening the border with Turkey could bring Armenia economic and political benefits. Above all, it would make transport links with Europe easier and reduce transport costs. Turkey has a large economy and could become an important market for Armenian businesses, although the Turkish regions bordering Armenia rank among the least developed in the country. Nevertheless, Armenian entrepreneurs could find opportunities there to export goods and services.

Opening the border could therefore create new economic opportunities for Armenia. However, it would not, in itself, mean a full normalisation of Armenian-Turkish relations.”

Turkey-Armenia border: Will it open?

World.title: Gas tariffs in Georgia set to change, with new rates due in December
World.content:
Gas prices in Georgia

In May, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze promised that gas tariffs would remain unchanged. However, in October, parliament fast-tracked legislation authorising the National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC) to introduce higher tariffs for households with higher consumption.

Georgia has yet to officially announce any increase in gas prices.

However, on 29 October, parliament passed a law allowing the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC) to set household gas tariffs according to consumption levels.

The new tariffs are due to be set in December.

The authorities say the change aims to promote social fairness and encourage energy conservation.

However, the figures point to a different picture. Georgia’s annual gas consumption is rising, while supplies of cheaper Azerbaijani gas remain unchanged. The country covers the resulting shortfall with more expensive gas, mainly from Russia.

Against this backdrop, introducing tiered tariffs could allow the authorities to pass some of the rising costs on to consumers while formally keeping the “base tariff” unchanged — the very tariff the government promised in May not to raise.

For now, this remains a hypothesis based on analysis. The December decision by GNERC, when it sets specific consumption thresholds and the corresponding tariffs, will confirm or disprove it.

What has been decided — and what remains unclear

Parliament passed the law at its third reading, with 75 MPs voting in favour and five against. GNERC now has the authority to introduce different gas tariffs for household consumers according to their consumption levels. The powers will remain in force until 1 January 2038.

Parliament fast-tracked the bill and passed it within three days. The current gas tariff expires in December, so lawmakers needed to approve the new system before GNERC makes its decision at the end of the year.

At present, households pay the same price for each cubic metre of gas, regardless of how much they consume. The Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC) sets separate tariffs for the service areas of individual gas distribution companies. Customers of Tbilisi Energy, which mainly serves the capital, pay 53.9 tetri (about $0.21) per cubic metre.

Customers of SOCAR Georgia Gas pay 56.9 tetri. The company is a subsidiary of Azerbaijan’s state-owned SOCAR and serves most of the country, apart from Tbilisi and several other settlements.

Customers of Sakorgaz also pay 56.9 tetri, while households served by the small regional company Telavgaz pay 58.9 tetri.

On 21 October, GNERC chairman Davit Narmania said that the commission would review gas and water tariffs by the end of the year, as the current tariff period expires in December. Narmania did not specify what changes the commission might introduce.

Shota Berekashvili, one of the bill’s sponsors and chairman of parliament’s Economic Policy Committee, explained the proposed model as follows: “Those who consume more will pay higher tariffs.” Asked about the specific consumption thresholds and prices, he referred the question to GNERC, saying: “GNERC sets the tariff and the final price.”

In its statement, GNERC said the changes aim to protect socially vulnerable households, ensure access to utility services and encourage the efficient use of resources.

Neither the commission nor the bill’s sponsors have said how many households could face higher tariffs.

The explanatory note accompanying the bill justifies the changes solely on social grounds. It makes no mention of gas prices, imports, Azerbaijan or Russia. Moreover, the six MPs from the parliamentary majority who drafted the bill explicitly state that it has no connection with any international agreements.

The explanatory note contains no assessment of the financial impact on households. The authors did not consult experts or examine the experience of other countries. One detail is particularly noteworthy: they say the new mechanism will introduce tariff changes gradually for different consumer groups. In other words, the document already provides for tariff changes — hardly an unexpected development.

The May promise and the October law

Last December, GNERC ruled out the possibility of an increase in gas prices.

On 17 December 2025, GNERC chairman Davit Narmania said: “At this stage, there are neither expectations nor grounds for an increase in natural gas tariffs.” According to Civil.ge, following consultations with the government, the commission decided to keep gas prices unchanged for one year.

On 18 May 2026, Georgia and Azerbaijan extended their 2003 gas purchase and sale agreement for another 20 years. The following day, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the new agreement would allow Georgia to maintain existing household tariffs.

He described the terms as “ideal” but declined to disclose specific details, citing commercial confidentiality. In June, Kobakhidze clarified that Georgia would continue to receive 500 million cubic metres of gas annually at a “social” (subsidised) price.

Even before the agreement, energy expert Murman Margvelashvili had warned that hopes of maintaining the previous terms were unrealistic. “It is naive to believe that anyone would willingly continue supplying gas on the same terms,” he told Batumelebi in an interview in April.

According to Margvelashvili, Georgia had been paying $70-75 per 1,000 cubic metres for this gas. If the price rose to $120, the country would have to pay an additional $60-70 million annually for the same volume.

The price set under the new agreement has not been made public.

Economist Roman Gotsiridze, a former president of the National Bank and an opposition politician, argues that the parties signed only an intergovernmental agreement in May, while they have yet to conclude a commercial contract for additional gas supplies. “We know how much gas we will receive from Azerbaijan, but nobody knows the price yet,” he said on PalitraNews.

Gotsiridze said Georgia had bought gas from the Shah Deniz field at $70 per 1,000 cubic metres, but that preferential pricing arrangement expires at the end of the year. This contradicts the prime minister’s claim that Georgia had secured the continuation of the subsidised tariff. Since the authorities have not disclosed the exact price, it is impossible to verify either account.

“The government misled us by claiming that the contract with Azerbaijan was so favourable that the subsidised gas tariff would not rise,” Gotsiridze said. He concluded that gas costs would increase for everyone, adding: “It is a fact — they have decided to raise the tariff.” However, he provided no evidence to support his claims.

Analyst Kakha Kakishvili takes a more cautious position. “I am not claiming that a decision to increase natural gas prices has already been made,” he said.

He questioned why the authorities had introduced a new mechanism so urgently in October, just before the start of the heating season, if the prime minister had promised in May to keep tariffs unchanged. “What has changed in these five months?” Kakishvili asked.

He also disagreed with the assumption that households consuming more gas can necessarily afford to pay higher tariffs. High gas consumption often occurs in large families, among pensioners and in homes with poor insulation.

“In these circumstances, higher gas consumption is not a luxury but a necessity,” he wrote.

Kakishvili believes the government should publish specific figures showing how many households will keep their current tariff and how many will face an increase.

The price of cheaper gas is fixed, but consumption is rising

According to a 2025 report by the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC), Georgia consumed 3.172 billion cubic metres of gas last year.

Imports accounted for 99.6% of this volume: 71.7% came from Azerbaijan and 27.9% from Russia.

Russian gas imports reached 886 million cubic metres, a 12% increase on 2024.

The regulator itself has explained the reason for this rise. According to GNERC member Givi Sanikidze, annual imports from Azerbaijan remained at around 2.3 billion cubic metres between 2020 and 2025, while consumption rose from 2.6 billion to almost 3.2 billion cubic metres.

Georgia covered the shortfall with Russian gas. Imports from Russia increased from 204 million to 886 million cubic metres over the same period.

Russian gas comes at a high price. Under Prime Ministerial Decree No. 2212 of 25 December 2025, Georgia pays $215 per 1,000 cubic metres for the first 250 million cubic metres of Russian gas, and $185 per 1,000 cubic metres for volumes above that threshold. By comparison, Margvelashvili said additional gas from Azerbaijan cost $70-75 per 1,000 cubic metres. This pricing structure has been in place since 2017.

According to BM.GE, the government website published a decree with an attached document specifying the exact prices. The authorities removed the document after experts and media outlets drew attention to it. The decree itself classified the attachment as a “commercial secret”.

In the first quarter of 2025, Georgia spent more on Russian gas than on Azerbaijani gas for the first time in 18 years.

According to the plan published by the Ministry of Economy, Georgia intended to import just 400 million cubic metres of gas from Russia in 2026, equivalent to 12% of total consumption. That is half the volume imported last year, when Russian gas accounted for almost 28% of total consumption.

The plan offers no explanation for the intended reduction in Russia’s share this year, particularly given that consumption is not falling but rising. Actual figures already contradict the plan. According to Netgazeti, the value of Russian gas purchases continued to increase between January and September 2026.

For many years, the state-owned Georgian Oil and Gas Corporation has kept household gas prices low. The corporation buys gas and sells it to distribution companies at a price below its own purchase cost. It covers the difference from its own revenue.

In 2013, the corporation cut the tariff in this way, using its own funds. According to calculations published by BM.GE in 2021, the subsidy cost the company 500 million lari over two years. Earlier this year, energy expert Gia Arabidze said that this arrangement places a heavy burden on the corporation.

This mechanism helps explain why the government may need a system of tiered tariffs, although the authorities have not said so explicitly. The volume of cheaper Azerbaijani gas remains unchanged from year to year.

As domestic gas consumption rises, more expensive supplies — mainly from Russia — cover the additional demand. Under a system of tiered tariffs, households with the highest consumption would take on some of the cost of this more expensive gas, shifting the burden away from the state-owned company.

Who will be affected?

According to figures published on the basis of a GNERC report, the average household in Tbilisi consumes 1,304 cubic metres of gas a year. In the towns of the Shida Kartli region, the figure stands at 1,416 cubic metres, while in the villages of Racha-Lechkhumi it is 503 cubic metres.

At the current tariff, an average household in Tbilisi pays around 704 lari a year. Most of this amount goes towards heating during the winter months.

Much will depend on the model GNERC chooses. Neighbouring countries use different approaches. Azerbaijan has operated an annual quota system since 2016. Households pay the lowest rate for consumption of up to 1,200 cubic metres a year, a medium rate for up to 2,500 cubic metres, and the highest rate for any consumption above that level.

Turkey introduced monthly consumption limits in spring 2026, setting higher thresholds for colder provinces. In both countries, the higher tariff applies only to the gas consumed above the established limit.

Armenia, by contrast, has a single tariff. The average annual consumption of a household in Tbilisi — 1,304 cubic metres — already exceeds the lowest threshold under Azerbaijan’s system. In other words, if Georgia adopted a similar model, the average household in Tbilisi would have to pay the higher rate.

Another important question is whether the authorities will set annual or monthly limits. Georgia already uses monthly consumption limits for electricity. If the authorities apply the same approach to gas, many households will move into a higher tariff category during the winter, when they heat their homes.

As a result, households that use gas for heating will pay more. These will not necessarily be the wealthiest households.

Critics say tariff increases are being “packaged” to make them more palatable

Gotsiridze sees the proposed model as a way to “package” a price increase so that consumers find it less painful.

“Tariffs will rise for everyone, although the impact will vary: some households will feel a smaller increase, while others will face a more significant one,” he said.

In a social media post, he argues that consumption levels do not reliably indicate household income. Large families and people living in poorly insulated homes, for example, naturally need more gas.

He believes the authorities should provide social support through targeted programmes rather than shift the financial burden from one group of consumers to another.

Electricity tariffs offer a warning. Georgia has operated a tiered electricity pricing system for years, but the increase in April 2026 affected every tariff band. Household rates charged by Telmiko now range from 20.041 to 28.537 tetri per kWh. According to Civil.ge, the increase ranged from 18% to 34%.

Gotsiridze says the steepest rise — almost 35% — affected households that consume up to 100 kWh of electricity a month. The tiered system therefore failed to protect the most economical consumers from higher prices.

The opposition sees the change as an attempt to increase household expenses ahead of the winter season. Lasha Parulava, a member of the political council of the Unity – National Movement party, called for the tariff revision to be cancelled, saying: “This is a path to social terror!”

He argues that higher utility bills will increase business costs, eventually pushing up the prices of bread and other bakery products.

Sopio Khorguani, an MP from the Gakharia for Georgia party, recalled the May agreement, which the government had presented as a success. She questioned why gas prices could rise if the agreement was genuinely so favourable.

Khorguani claims the government has already decided to raise tariffs. In her view, a simultaneous increase for all consumer groups could trigger public protests. The authorities are therefore presenting the changes as though only wealthier households will have to pay more. However, Khorguani provides no evidence to support this claim.

Nikoloz Alavidze, a former deputy economy minister and co-founder of the organisation Djeri Sakartvelo, noted that parliament passed the law in an extremely short time, without assessing its potential impact or properly informing the public.

How Georgia’s gas situation developed: a brief history

Until the mid-2000s, Georgia received almost all its gas from Russia. On 22 January 2006, during a particularly harsh winter, two explosions in North Ossetia damaged both gas pipelines leading to Georgia. A third explosion several hours later knocked out a power transmission line.

For several days, much of the population remained without gas or electricity. Emergency supplies from Azerbaijan and Iran helped the country through the crisis. President Mikheil Saakashvili accused Russia of carrying out deliberate sabotage, while Moscow blamed insurgents. Authorities never established who was responsible.

Later that year, Russia imposed an embargo on Georgian wine and mineral water. In October, it completely cut transport and communications links with Georgia. By the end of the year, Gazprom demanded that Georgia double gas prices and offered lower rates only if Tbilisi sold it the main gas pipeline. Georgia refused.

The South Caucasus Pipeline provided an alternative. Under an agreement reached in October 2003, before the Rose Revolution, Georgia secured the right to receive 5% of the gas transported through the pipeline as a transit fee. The agreement also allowed it to buy additional gas at a preferential price. The pipeline began operating in late 2006.

By 2009, gas imports from Azerbaijan had exceeded supplies from Russia. When the United National Movement left power in 2012, Tbilisi residents paid 50.62 tetri per cubic metre of gas. Russia mainly supplied gas to Georgia as payment in kind for transit deliveries to Armenia.

During the 2012 election campaign, Bidzina Ivanishvili said that gas prices could fall threefold. In March 2013, the tariff did fall, although not by three times: it dropped from 51 to 46 tetri. The state-owned corporation covered the difference.

In 2017, the government accepted Gazprom’s demand to replace gas payments for transit with cash payments. Energy Minister Kakha Kaladze said the agreement’s details were a commercial secret. In Tbilisi, the household tariff rose from 46.1 to 54 tetri in June 2021 and has remained at that level ever since.

Prices for businesses, which the government does not regulate, have risen much more sharply. According to a 2024 review by the Transport Corridor Research Center, business gas tariffs increased by 72% between September 2018 and January 2024, rising from 75 tetri to 1.29 lari. The report identified the depreciation of the Georgian lari as the main reason.
