Follow all the action in our live Melbourne Cup coverage It takes a special kind of horse to win a Melbourne Cup. It also takes a combination of good planning and good luck. In our comprehensive runner-by-runner guide, 2015 Melbourne Cup winning-jockey Michelle Payne and The Age racing writer Danny Russell cast an eye over the field, taking into variables such as lead-up form, weights and barriers. Point of Law rockets into Melbourne Cup favouritism after winning the Geelong Cup. Getty Images The horses are named in order of their saddle cloth numbers – from top weight down to bottom weight.



Ciaron Maher has seven runners, while Irish trainer Joseph O’Brien has five. 1. Sons And Lovers (GB)

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait Barrier: 3

6yoG (gelding) 57.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Dylan Browne McMonagle

Career: 23: 6-2-6 Last start: Second of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes Leopardstown Michelle Payne says: The stable is very confident. He sounds like he’s thrived since he’s been here, and I think the barrier certainly brings him right into contention.



Russell says: A dual group 2 winner from Ireland who sounds more like a midday soapie than a racehorse. That being said, in our view he has more chance of winning an Emmy than the Melbourne Cup, considering he has to lug 57.5 kilograms to victory first-up in Australia. Related Article Cox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington 2. Trustyourinstinct (IRE) Barrier: 18

7yoG 57kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: James McDonald

Career: 30: 9-7-4 Last start: 4th of 7 G1 Irish St Leger 2816m Payne says: For me, he is the pick of Joseph O’Brien’s runners. The barrier is not ideal, but he can overcome that wide gate if we have a firm track. He won’t be as well suited if the rain comes.



Russell says: If you believe in the saying, ‘follow the money’, this is the horse for you. He’s owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus, who used to be a bookmaker. That’s a good lead right there. He is also a group 2 winner with a serious chance. Watch to see if McManus bets up big on Cup eve. Top five hope. Robbie Dolan rides Knight’s Choice to a famous win in the 2024 Melbourne Cup. Getty 3. Knight’s Choice Barrier: 2

7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: John Symons and Sheila Laxon. Jockey: Robbie Dolan

Career: 31: 6-3-3 Last start: 14th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: Needs a firm track. But from a good barrier, who knows if the 2024 winner can cause another upset? He is going well enough if you look at his Caulfield run two starts back in the Herbert Power.



Russell says: The shock 2024 winner was robbed of the chance to defend his crown in 2025 because of the equine equivalent of a lockdown. Not COVID-19, but strangles – a contagious bacterial disease – that was detected at Macedon Lodge on the eve of last year’s spring. Great run in the Herbert Power two starts back, might have copped interference in Caulfield Cup. Can’t win. 4. Middle Earth (GB) Barrier: 1

7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Mark Zahra

Career: 26: 6-2-3 Last start: Eighth of 12 G1 Cox Plate 2040m Payne says: He sounds like he is the best chance of the Ciaron Maher runners. Ran third last year and is going just as well. A bit more weight, but drawn barrier one, proven at two miles and if he gets luck in running, he’ll figure in the finish. Russell says: If this galloper’s name has been plucked from J.R.R. Tolkien mythology, then surely his trainer, Ciaron Maher, qualifies as a modern-day wizard. Maher is on fire and has given this fellow the old-fashioned Cup preparation.



Bart Cummings’ rule was 10 kilometres – he has racked up 9.94km in five lead-up races. He looked good late in the Cox Plate. A winning chance. 5. Vauban (FRA) Barrier: 22

9yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott. Jockey: Jordan Childs

Career: 33: 10-5-6 Last start: Ninth of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Loading Payne says: I love this horse. Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott have taken a different approach this year. Coming in fresh off one run, so who knows? I can’t rule him out.



Russell says: The veteran is lining up for his fourth Melbourne Cup – the first two for Irish trainer Willie Mullins before he was sold to Australian connections to be trained by Waterhouse and Bott. He finished sixth last year, but might not be going as well. Although he was first-up in the Geelong Cup, so hard to tell. 6. Enfjaar (IRE) Barrier: 8

7yoG 56kg

Trainer: Roger Varian. Jockey: Ray Dawson

Career: 17: 5-2-3 Last start: Third of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: He looks good in a lot of ways. His run in the Caulfield Cup was excellent, and that has to put him in with a chance. Yet to run beyond 2400m, so the distance is a query. Trainer Ciaron Maher will have a number of horses running in the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images



Russell says: Best of internationals in the Caulfield Cup, and in my view, internationals need an impressive lead-up run in Australia if they are to win the Melbourne Cup. He ticks that box. And for those struggling to pronounce his name, Google says Enfjaar means “burst” in Arabic. Top 10. 7. Royal Supremacy (IRE) Barrier: 21

6yoG 56kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ben Allen

Career: 22: 7-3-4 Last start: 15th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: I think he has to improve. Didn’t have the best of runs in the Caulfield Cup, but I think I’d be leaning towards others, especially from the wide barrier. Russell says: One of Ciaron Maher’s seven runners, but a lesser chance. Cooked in the Caulfield Cup by a head-scratching ride from visiting hoop Jamie Spencer, he bolted to the front, whacked on the handbrakes and then looked confused when the pressure went back on from the 800m. He was flying before that. Outside the top 10.



8. Wine Dark Sea (GB) Barrier: 23

5yoG 56kg

Trainer: Harry Charlton. Jockey: Damian Lane

Career: 11: 4-2-0

Last start: 11th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: He also had excuses in the Caulfield Cup. There was an air of confidence about this horse leading into that race, so he may be able to turn his form around. Russell says: Purchased abroad by Australian Bloodstock, who have won the Cup with Protectionist and Gold Trip, and was a massive spruik horse leading into the Caulfield Cup. Sadly for punters, he didn’t live up to expectations. Needs a gigantic turnaround. 9. Asterix (NZ)



Barrier: 6

8yoG 55kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Jye McNeil

Career: 33: 8-1-2 Last start: 12th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: I think others are going better. He has run two miles in New Zealand and is by Tavistock, so a wet track would bring him into contention. Russell says: Caught up in the backwash of the tragic fall in the Caulfield Cup. A group 1-winning stayer from New Zealand owned by former Kiwi cricket great Mark Greatbatch and now in the Chris Waller barn. An outsider, but any rain will help. Goodie Two Shoes (left, with green and yellow silks) finishes second behind Half Yours in the 2025 Melbourne Cup. Joe Armao 10. Goodie Two Shoes (IRE)



Barrier: 19

8yoM (mare) 55kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Wayne Lordan

Career: 31: 14-2-7 Last start: Tenth of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m Payne says: She was excellent last year. She has to carry more weight this year, and did have a disappointing run last start, but this stable has to be respected so that can be overlooked. Russell says: A former hurdler who ran a surprise second in the Melbourne Cup last year. Trained by Joseph O’Brien, who has already won the race twice, and owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus. Slightly disappointing last start, but that might have been a pipe opener. Top 10 finish. 11. Juja Kibo (IRE) Barrier: 14

6yoG 55kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Sam Clipperton

Career: 20: 6-3-6 Last start: First of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m



Payne says: A beautiful confidence-boosting lead-in run to this year’s Melbourne Cup when he won the Moonee Valley Gold Cup. Having said that, might not be good enough to win, so I’m leaning towards others. Russell says: In hot form, having won its past two starts, including a big win in the group 2 Metropolitan at Randwick on October 3. Didn’t make the cut for the Caulfield Cup, but many believed he could have won the race. Copped a 1.5kg for the MV Gold Cup win. Still think he brings the B-grade form. Top 10. Hopewell Rock is Michelle Payne’s top pick for the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images 12. Hopewell Rock (IRE)



Barrier: 15

5yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: George Boughey. Jockey: Zac Lloyd

Career: 10: 3-3-2 Last start: Second of 22 Ebor Handicap 2787m Payne says: He’s my top selection. He helps himself. He puts himself into a reasonable position, puts himself to sleep, and has a nice turn of foot. Plus, he’s only carrying 54.5kg. I think he ticks a lot of boxes. Russell says: Another international with decent credentials, but will have to defy history to win this year’s Cup. No runner has come out of York’s Ebor Handicap and saluted on the first Tuesday in November. But a few have been close – Heartbreak City ran second in 2017, while Purple Moon was a runner-up in 2007. Onesmoothoperator wins the Geelong Cup in 2024. Getty Images 13. Onesmoothoperator (US)



Barrier: 13

9yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Tim Fitzsimmons. Jockey: Declan Bates

Career: 51: 6-11-6 Last start: 11th of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Payne says: I think he looked talented last year, but I’m just not sure he’s going as well this year. Russell says: Has gone off the boil. The veteran started second favourite and ran 12th in the 2024 Melbourne Cup after winning the Geelong Cup in the lead-up. Won the MV Gold Cup last year before finishing 16th in the Cup. Not going as well this year. Will be grateful they pay back to last. 14. Soul Of Spain (IRE) Barrier: 5

6yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Tommy Berry

Career: 26: 5-5-6 Last start: Eight of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m



Payne says: He’s very fit and has had a lot of racing. Master trainer in Chris Waller, but he may struggle to beat some of these horses. Russell says: Ran second in the Sydney Cup over 3200m but has been slightly disappointing at his past two starts, including a seventh in The Metropolitan. Might have been ridden upside down in the Caulfield Cup. Needs to improve. 15. Zahrann (IRE) Barrier: 11

5yoH 54.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ben Melham

Career: 12: 4-2-1 Last start: Sixth of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Loading



Payne says: The Maher team are saying he’s the forgotten horse, so you have to respect their opinion. A good, honest run in the Caulfield Cup, and blinkers on. He’s definitely in with some sort of chance. Russell says: This year’s smoky, considering he started second favourite in the Caulfield Cup and was clearly disadvantaged after being caught up in the tragic mid-race fall. Has not raced over 2400m, but being Irish-bred should relish the two miles. Top five chance. 16. So You Are Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing This horse is barred from running in Cup week after failing a drug test – that its trainer requested Barrier: 7

5yoG 54kg

Trainer: Bjorn Baker. Jockey: Rachel King

Career: 28: 8-6-6 Last start: First of 13 G3 Bendigo Cup 2400m



Payne says: He was good winning the Bendigo Cup. He’s a good, honest galloper who will put himself into a good position from barrier seven. Just a question of whether he’s got the class. Russell says: Jumped into the field after a being handed a 1kg penalty for an impressive win in Wednesday’s Bendigo Cup. He is a horse in form, having won four staying races on the trot and has a top trainer-jockey combination. Since March, he has started 13 times and travelled 21.8km. That’s one fit horse. A top-five chance. 17. Future History (GB) Barrier: 12

9yoG 53.5kg

Trainer: Gregory Hickman. Jockey: Jamie Melham

Career: 47: 10-6-6 Last start: Ninth of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m Loading



Payne says: I actually tipped this horse last year, and he had no luck at all. He’s had a change of trainer and is another year older, but he certainly has the talent. Nice to see Jamie Melham with the ride. She certainly knows how to win the Cup. Russell says: He jumps into the field after the scratching of Stinger Glass on Friday, giving last year’s winning jockey Jamie Melham a chance to defend her crown. Until then, she did not have a ride. He was caught three wide in the Gold Cup, so that’s a forgive run, but it’s a stretch to say he can finish top 10. 18. James J Braddock (GB) Barrier: 24

4yoH 53.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Craig Williams

Career: 8: 2-1-2 Last start: 6th of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m James J Braddock under the watchful eye of trainer Joseph O’Brien and racing manager Kevin Blake. Getty Images



Payne says: Sounds like a very exciting horse with a well-connected ownership group. I’m sure they’ll be disappointed with barrier 24, but the stable have not brought him out here for fun. Have to give him a good chance. Russell says: Another northern hemisphere three-year-old bought by a big group of Aussies. Three things to consider here: He is still trained by O’Brien. Tick. He was sourced by big Melbourne buyer Ozzie Kheir. Tick. Craig Williams sought the ride. Double tick. He is a group 3 winner, lightly raced, and will carry a light weight. First-up in Australia the only concern. A first-four pick. 19. Kizlyar (IRE) Barrier: 20

5yoG 53.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien Jockey: Beau Mertens

Career: 11: 3-2-2 Last start: 11th of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m Payne says: There was a bit of confidence before his last run in the Moonee Valley Gold Cup, but he didn’t get a strong enough tempo to suit. He’s a strong stayer and I think he’ll be ridden to use that strength on Tuesday. Look for improvement with a light weight.



Russell says: Looked like he was going to bowl to the front and set a free-rolling European-style tempo in the MV Gold Cup before jockey Ben Melham surprisingly took a sit. He was left flat-footed in the sprint home but will get a suitable hot pace in the Cup, and will relish 3200m. Top 10 chance. Ethan Brown salutes his Geelong Cup win on Point of Law. Getty Images 20. Point Of Law (GB) Barrier: 9

4yoH 53kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ethan Brown

Career: 5: 3-1-0 Last start: First of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington



Payne says: Sounds like he’s got some behavioral issues, which is not ideal. But if he can put it all together, he looks like he’ll run a strong 3200m. Huge win in the Geelong Cup when he set the tempo. We have to see if he can keep it together on the big day. It’s going to be an amazing effort if he wins a Melbourne Cup in his first preparation. Russell says: Point to the winner’s circle more like it. This striking specimen’s Geelong Cup victory was the greatest Melbourne Cup audition since Dunaden did the Geelong-Melbourne double in 2011. A northern hemisphere three-year-old who supposedly cost his Aussie owners $3.5 million, and might be worth every cent. Maher did caution about him being inexperienced. Top three. 21. Strictly Business Barrier: 4

4yoM 53kg

Trainer: Thomas Carberry. Jockey: Dean Yendall

Career: 11: 2-2-0 Last start: 16th of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m Payne says: Last year’s Oaks winner, but she really needs to improve on her recent runs. Still, if you’re in it, you’ve got a chance.



Russell says: One of the stories of last spring when she won the VRC Oaks for a big group of Irish expats and small-time Ballarat trainer Carberry. Ballarat’s Miners Rest Tavern has never been the same since. But she has struggled to make the transition from three-year-old to open company. Not going well enough. 22. Mr Monaco (GB) Barrier: 16

6yoG 52.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Jabez Johnstone

Career: 20: 6-2-2 Last start: Third of 16 G2 Moonee Valley Gold Cup 2500m Mr Monaco takes out the Group 3 Bart Cummings at Flemington earlier this month. Getty Images



Payne says: He looks a lovely staying-type of a horse. He was great in the lead-up race behind his stablemate Juja Kibo and does everything to help himself. I’m just not sure he’s got the class of the others. Russell says: Flopped in this year’s Sydney Cup despite starting second favourite, which is a bit of a concern. Qualified for the race by winning the group 3 Bart Cummings (2500m) on a heavy Flemington track on October 3. Maybe a rung below the top-liners, but any rain will help. 23. Zakouma Barrier: 10

Trainer: Grahame Begg. Jockey: William Pike

Career: 18: 5-2-1 Last start: 11th of 11 G2 Crystal Mile 1600m Payne says: They have targeted this race from a long way out. They’ve not been too worried about his lead-up runs, focusing instead on the Cup. Great trainer in Grahame Begg and an inform rider in Willie Pike. Can’t be ruled out.



Russell says: Booked a golden ticket in May by winning the Andrew Ramsden Stakes (2800m). That form looks like an egg-and-spoon race compared to other Cup form lines. World.title: ‘Savage political attack’: One Nation volunteer bashed over corflutes
World.content:
NationalVictoriaOne Nation ‘Savage political attack’: One Nation volunteer bashed over corflutes James Costa November 3, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content. A One Nation volunteer is in hospital after he was attacked by a man and a teenager with a baseball bat on his front lawn in a coastal town on the Great Ocean Road. Victoria Police said in a statement on Tuesday the 60-year-old was recovering from serious, non-life-threatening injuries after he confronted a 14-year-old boy who was allegedly damaging a corflute outside a home in Torquay on Sunday evening. The man was then allegedly attacked with a baseball bat by the teenager and a 37-year-old man.



Speaking outside Geelong Hospital on Tuesday, where the man is recovering, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the volunteer was kicked so badly he “lost consciousness”, and had bleeding of the brain and “from basically every orifice” in his face. In contradiction to the police’s assessment, Hanson said the attack “was life-threatening. Even now, with the bleed, it still could be life-threatening.” Hanson and One Nation Victoria deputy leader Colleen Harkin visited the man before speaking with media outside the hospital, where she claimed the alleged attackers were walking along the highway when they spotted the One Nation campaign signs outside the man’s house. “I’m very emotional about this because I respect people who support me, I really do. I don’t take it for granted. It means a lot to me, and that’s when, in times like this, you have to, you know, be there for them as well,” she said. “This kind of vicious and savage violence has to stop, and the consequences have to be made real.”



Harkin called the alleged assault a “savage attack on a person” because of their politics. Victoria Police said the teenager and 37-year-old Hampton East man were arrested after the alleged attack, which occurred around 7.45pm on Sunday. The man was charged with intentionally causing injury and other offences, while the teenager was issued a caution. Pauline Hanson at a One Nation press conference in Melbourne on Monday morning with Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Eamon Gallagher Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said the alleged attack was “shocking” and he had met with the electoral commissioner to discuss it.



“It should never be occurring,” Carol said. “Whether you’re wearing a red, a blue, an orange, or a green T-shirt, they are volunteers. They are out there doing what they believe is right, and no one should be coming under attack.“



Carroll called for a “civil, peaceful election” due in just over three weeks, and said he was considering whether extra security was needed for candidates of all parties. Opposition leader Jess Wilson said the alleged attack on the volunteer was “absolutely appalling” and her thoughts are with the man and his family. “Every Victorian has the right to express their political views and support the party of their choice without fear of violence or intimidation,” Wilson said. “We can disagree strongly about politics, but violence is never the answer. One Nation Victoria leader Warren Pickering condemned the attack in a statement, calling it “un-Australian”.



“Political violence or intimidation of any kind against anyone is unacceptable in this country. If you don’t like someone’s politics, you vote accordingly. You don’t assault them”, Pickering said. “Our thoughts are with our volunteer and his family. We’re informed he has serious injuries. This attack is un-Australian and unacceptable.” Emma McGinness, a nearby resident of the victim, was home at the time but did not witness the incident. She said the alleged attack had put a “dampener on the safety around the area”. “It’s a lovely place, a nice quiet dead-end street, so it’s definitely something that has never happened before,” McGinness said. “We’ve always felt very safe and let our kids ride around the streets, like the other neighbours do.”



Hanson said an online fundraiser had been started to support the victim and his family, including his wife and two teenage sons. The 37-year-old man was remanded to appear at Geelong Magistrates’ Court on November 10. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Lotto ticket on four legs’: How to get your own Melbourne Cup horse
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup ‘Lotto ticket on four legs’: How to get your own Melbourne Cup horse Andrew Wu Updated November 3, 2026 — 1:15pm ,first published November 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow all the action in our live Melbourne Cup coverage It’s taken 10 years and about 30 horses for Anya and Paul Podbury to find Shockletz, the Australasian-bred mare who will realise the Woodend couple’s lifelong ambition of owning a Melbourne Cup runner. The first step in former Richmond footballer Justin Pickering’s path to Juja Kibo started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when he and a few mates landed juicy quaddies in Melbourne and Sydney on the same day. Paul (left) and Anya Podbury are part-owners of Cup runner Shockletz. Then there’s vet Rob McInnes, who got extremely lucky – then felt the wrath of the racing gods. He liked the horse he was inspecting so much, he bought a share. That horse was Defiantly, one of the favourites in this year’s great race – until his withdrawal on Saturday morning.



Of all the cherished items in Australian sport – think the premiership trophies of the AFL and NRL or cricket’s baggy green – the Melbourne Cup is the one that is attainable to the average punter. Theoretically. Justin Pickering (holding the Cup) is one of the owners of Juja Kibo. Deep pockets help, of course, but through racehorse syndication everyday mums and dads with the unfashionably bred horse can knock off the bluebloods of the rich and famous. As has become the norm over the past 15 years or so, this year’s field has predominantly come from Europe, arriving on these shores after being bought by bloodstock agents for leading syndicators and owners. Jamie Lovett, a director for one of the country’s biggest syndication companies Australian Bloodstock, spends hours watching replays from races in Europe, studying form and cross-referencing times and measurements.



He also has a global team of about eight or nine, mainly on the ground in Europe, including jockeys and trackwork riders, who feed him intel. “There’s a lot of tentacles to the business to try and land on the right horses,” Lovett said. Based in Australia, he does not see many of the horses he buys in the flesh. That, he said, is the job of his vets. Once a horse is identified, Lovett approaches its owners or buys it at sales. He bought a few just last week from the Tattersalls sales in the UK. Australian Bloodstock, which generally has about 100 to 150 thoroughbreds at a time on its books, has had two Cup winners in its silks – Protectionist (2014) and Gold Trip (2022), both from Europe. The European imports do not come cheap, their price tags swelled by the demand from Australian interests desperate to find a cups horse, and the market in the Middle East searching for talent to run at Dubai’s lucrative World Cup meeting.



Gold Trip, who had come fourth in France’s famous L’Arc de Triomphe in 2020, cost about $2 million, which, at the time, was the most expensive horse Lovett had bought. Australian Bloodstock have three runners in this year’s race – Royal Supremacy, Vauban and Wine Dark Sea. A fourth, the aforementioned Defiantly, failed a vet test. Royal Supremacy, bought as a three-year-old after a third in the Italian Derby – one of Europe’s lesser derbies – “wouldn’t have been top of the top”, Lovett said. Royal Supremacy gets some beach time in ahead of the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images “You’re not buying for $200,000 to $300,000, put it that way,” Lovett said.



In a cruel irony for those involved with Defiantly, a half-brother to last year’s Cox Plate runner-up Buckaroo and Melbourne Cup placegetter Middle Earth, the gelding had impressed McInnes so much during an inspection for Australian Bloodstock the vet shelled out $18,500 for a 2.5 per cent share. Related Article Melbourne Cup briefing

Melbourne Cup Buck of the Irish: The internationals who lit up Melbourne Cup betting “He was sound, beautifully natured, and everything was clean with his X-rays,” McInnes said before Defiantly’s withdrawal. “His demeanour was good.” Presciently, he had also likened owning a horse to having a “Tattslotto ticket on four legs”. Pickering, then, has found the winning ticket three times. That’s how many of the dozen or so horses he has part-owned who have run in the Cup. The former Richmond wingman played his 59 V/AFL games in the 1980s and ’90s, long before the money could set you up for life.



McInnes’ in was through his vet work. Pickering’s came through a friend of a friend. He is part of several syndicates, many run by his mate Gerard Mulcahy, who lives next door to Mick Johnston and his wife Alise. Mulcahy often gets tipped into horses from the Johnstons, and relays the information to Pickering and his friends. Their foray into racehorse ownership started during the many COVID-19 lockdowns when he and his friends started punting together to stay connected. After one particularly successful day, they decided to plunge their winnings into a horse. It landed them in an imported stayer called Delphi, who won the Herbert Power in 2021 on his way to seventh in that year’s Melbourne Cup. They kept rolling their slice of the prizemoney into more horses. A happy Pickering among friends at Flemington.



“We occasionally take a dividend just to prove to our wives that it is profitable with racehorses,” Pickering joked. Their next star was another European stayer, Circle Of Fire, who won the 2024 Sydney Cup, worth $1.3 million to the winner. He ran sixth later that year in the big one. Their latest horse is Juja Kibo. There are 15 in the Happy Hippo syndicate who splashed out about $30,000 – or about $2000 each – for a 10 per cent share in the Ciaron Maher-trained gelding. They have even produced their own merchandise – stubby holders and ties adorned with Juja Kibo’s distinctive racing colours. The owners of Juja Kibo have produced their own merch. Many of them were at Flemington on Cox Plate Day when the six-year-old booked his ticket into Tuesday’s race with victory in the $750,000 Moonee Valley Cup.



“It was so good – you turn around and hug one of your best mates,” Pickering said. “It’s not going to be good for my health if he happens to win. I’m willing to take that risk.” They were back at headquarters on Saturday night for the barrier draw, cheering loudly when their stayer drew gate 14 of 24. It’s been a nervous few days for Pickering, his wife Sally, and the Happy Hippo syndicate. “For some reason, this one’s keeping me up at night just thinking about it,” Pickering said. “I’ve loved the way he’s gone about it and genuinely think he’s a fair chance.” The Podburys have gone down a different route to finding their Cup runner. Folk like them are racing’s lifeblood – passionate owners who love sharing the thrill of raceday with friends and family. Paul and Anya Podbury with sons Bailey (right) and Charlie.



They have part-owned about 30 horses – just a few per cent each time. Several have been with prominent owner Laurence Eales, who won the 2009 Melbourne Cup with Shocking and owned the cult hero Whobegotyou. The Podburys’ best is sprinting mare Benedetta, who won Adelaide’s group 1 Goodwood in 2024 and banked nearly $2.4 million in her career. They bought into Benedetta with the prizemoney won by another of Eales’ horses Horrifying, a son of Shocking who banked about $300,000 in a month in 2022. As the Podburys’ relationship with Eales grew, they were invited to lunch at South Melbourne’s O’Connell’s Hotel to discuss a 10 per cent share for $7500 in Horrifying’s unraced sister, which he had bred in New Zealand. That filly was Shockletz. There are seven in the Podburys’ Plodalong – Zelt syndicate, each paying just over $1000 for a share in a mare that is one of the leading chances in the race. The Podburys are in the ownership game for love, not money.



The beauty of buying an untried horse, such as Shockletz, is the lower cost, though the risk is higher as there is no exposed form to assess. Like the major syndicators purchasing stock from Europe, Paul, an accountant, studies form and watches trials as part of his due diligence before buying. On this occasion, he bought on trust from their positive experience racing with Eales. Related Article Melbourne Cup He’d just ridden his first group 1 race. Then came the death threats “You’re not guaranteeing a collect, but you’re buying a known commodity to a certain extent, you know there’s some ability there, rather than buying a two-year-old stayer,” Paul said. “We were pretty lucky.” As the saying goes, the best way to make a small fortune in racing is to start with a large one. Asked if they are ahead financially, Anya says: “yes – with gritted teeth”.



“If you did it for money, it would be unwise. You have to be prepared to invest knowing you may not get money back,” Anya said. For the Podburys, it’s the romance of the turf. Anya has loved the Cup since she was a kid watching the race at primary school in Port Fairy. “This is 10-year-old Anya talking now,” she said. “I dreamed of playing for Hawthorn, which in the ’80s and ’90s was not possible, and the other dream was having a runner in the Melbourne Cup. “The people who own Shockletz, we’re normal, average people who work every day, have families and kids. We live a conservative lifestyle, we don’t go overseas; our treat is racing. It absolutely can happen to the average person. That’s the magic of it.” Read more from our racing coverage

World.title: Laptops down: Year 5 NAPLAN tests return to pen and paper amid backlash against devices
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation Laptops down: Year 5 NAPLAN tests return to pen and paper amid backlash against devices Alex Crowe November 3, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Year 5 students will return to pen and paper for NAPLAN tests in Victoria from 2028 after education ministers agreed to scrap online testing in primary schools in response to declining academic results. Education ministers decided to return to handwritten testing for the cohort amid a growing backlash against classroom technology, with some advocates of limiting device use arguing the reversal does not go far enough. Year 5 students will now join year 3 students and take the tests by hand, but whether years 7 and 9 students will take the test offline hasn’t been decided. All primary school NAPLAN participants will use pen and paper from 2028. Justin McManus Australia recorded its worst result in the most recent Programme for International Student Assessment, with the global test revealing Australian students spent an average of 2.6 hours a day on digital devices, compared with the OECD average of 1.7 hours a day.



NAPLAN results also reveal about a third of Australian students are failing to meet literacy and numeracy benchmarks. The Heads Up Alliance, a growing community of parents lobbying against digital devices, said scrapping online testing for year 5 students was just a start. Related Article Education ‘Humans were built to learn from other humans’: The schools capping screen time Ahead of the education ministers’ meeting on Monday, the alliance wrote to every minister, reminding them that tens of thousands of parents and teachers had signed a petition calling for the restoration of handwriting as a core education policy. “Changes to year five NAPLAN are a start,” they said in a statement. “But stay with us; with your continued support, there’s a lot more to achieve.”



NSW Education Minister Prue Car is pushing for years 7 and 9 NAPLAN to also be pen and paper tests. “The evidence from our classrooms points clearly to the ongoing value of handwriting and its importance for student development and engaging a different way of learning,” she said. “We’re listening to teachers and families who want a sensible, balanced approach to technology use in schools.” Victoria has led the way in reducing digital device use and banning mobile phones in public school classrooms. From the start of the 2027 school year, students at all government, Catholic and independent schools will also be required to have personal devices, including smart glasses, phones and smartwatches, switched off and stored during school hours.



State school pupils in years 3 to 6 will also be restricted to 90 minutes of screen time a day from next year, while pupils in prep to year 2 will have minimal exposure to devices. Teachers at state secondary schools will be required to plan device-free learning, although time limits won’t be enforced. Victorian Education Minister Gabrielle Williams said she supported the shift to pen and paper testing for year 5 pupils and would consider her position on years 7 and 9 students making the shift, alongside her interstate colleagues. “Victorian students are the best in the nation in NAPLAN – and we support these changes that will help lift results even further,” she said. World.title: ‘Oh God, so it’s all my fault’: Albanese and King Charles joke over travel backlash
World.content:
WorldEuropePolitical leadership ‘Oh God, so it’s all my fault’: Albanese and King Charles joke over travel backlash David Crowe Updated November 3, 2026 — 1:40pm ,first published November 3, 2026 — 9:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

St John’s, Antigua and Barbuda: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has hit back at critics of his overseas travel as he joked with King Charles about the number of times he was asked why he was attending this week’s Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean. With the Coalition arguing he should not be overseas, Albanese acknowledged the economic pressures at home and insisted the government was working “each and every day” to lift living standards. Loading But Albanese also shared a light-hearted exchange with the King about the political attacks. The prime minister responded to media questions on Monday morning by arguing it was in Australia’s interest to be at the Antigua summit, before adding: “At the personal invitation of King Charles, of His Majesty, I agreed to come to this meeting.”



A few hours later, Albanese met the King and told him that he had been asked “why are you here?” and chosen to name the King as one of the reasons. The remark was caught on video and microphone as the two spoke at the launch of an environmental initiative. “I said because His Majesty invited me,” Albanese told the King about his remark to the media. The King replied: “Oh God, so it’s all my fault – oh, no.” He made the remark with a smile. Anthony Albanese mingles with King Charles and Andrew Forrest at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. Jenny Magee While he joked with the King about the political dispute, Albanese sharply rebuked Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and others in the Coalition for saying he should not go to the summit – known as the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) – because of economic news at home.



“They often quote John Howard as their oracle, and on this John Howard is right,” Albanese said. “Australia is a participant in the Commonwealth, and at the personal invitation of King Charles, of His Majesty, I agreed to come to this meeting. “And it’s important that we engage in the world. The world is complicated, is complex, is turbulent, and in these uncertain times, it’s important [to be here] for Australia’s national interest.” Albanese has met British counterpart Andy Burnham and will tomorrow talk with Canadian leader Mark Carney at the summit, discussing how national economies deal with the energy price shocks from the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham holding the Rabbitohs hat he was given by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ahead of a bilateral meeting. Getty Images



At a press conference in Antigua on Monday, Albanese spoke of “middle powers” working together – a major theme in an address by Carney to the World Economic Forum in Davos. Switzerland earlier this year. While Carney argued that middle powers needed to help each other when US President Donald Trump was imposing tariffs and other penalties on allies, Albanese used the term without any direct criticism of the US. “This is an opportunity to engage with the countries in our region to show leadership on behalf of the Pacific, but also to engage with middle powers and to strengthen Australia’s economic position,” he said. “And it’s never been more important to connect with the world because the world has never been more interconnected.” He named trade, the global economy and the development of artificial intelligence as some of the issues to be discussed with other world leaders.



Howard attended each meeting of the Commonwealth Heads of Government during his time as prime minister. Related Article Updated

Political leadership Albanese warns world leaders of growing threat to democracy after Haines attack Taylor argued on Sunday that Albanese should not go to CHOGM because of the economic conditions at home, despite Howard’s example. “The reality is in a normal set of circumstances, of course, the prime minister should go to CHOGM – and John Howard is right on that,” Taylor said on 2GB on Sunday. “The problem is this is not a normal set of circumstances. We are going to have the seventeenth interest rate rise under Labor if the Reserve Bank moves on Tuesday, as is widely expected, and this is on the government’s watch.”



Taylor argued the government did not have spending under control and was not putting downward pressure on inflation and interest rates. The federal government’s gross debt is forecast to surpass $1 trillion this financial year. The budget papers do not forecast a surplus or specify a timeframe to paying off the debt, while interest payments continue to rise. While Treasurer Jim Chalmers claimed the budget in May delivered $26.1 billion in savings over several years, the budget deficit is tipped to deteriorate. It is forecast to be $28.2 billion this year and $31.5 billion next year. Asked whether the government was making enough savings in the budget to ease pressure on inflation, Albanese insisted he and the cabinet were acting on the economy. “My message to Australians is that we’ll continue to work each and every day to keep our economy stronger, and that includes engaging in global trade and engaging in the world,” Albanese said.



British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised the prospect of more international travel for Albanese next year when the UK hosts the G20 summit in Manchester. Related Article King Charles III King Charles joins Albanese, Forrest aboard climate ship “We’ve got the chance, you and I, to cut the first steel on the first AUKUS sub sometime next year,” Burnham told Albanese when they meet on Monday night (about 11am on Tuesday, AEDT). The AUKUS submarine will be built to a design being used by the UK and Australia for a new fleet for the long-term, with the first of them to be made in Barrow-in-Furness, north of Liverpool. Albanese and Burnham also discussed Australia’s proposal for changes to the visa rules for young British working holiday makers so that more of them are required to work in regional areas to continue their visas. There was no announcement of any change.



Burnham prefaced his remarks to Albanese with words of sympathy for Victorian MP Helen Haines, who is recovering from an attack last month that forced surgeons to amputate both her legs. “We send our thoughts to Helen Haines,” Burnham said. He added that the attack on Haines raised broader questions about violence against politicians on all sides. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter here.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of former 2GB broadcaster Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial in the historic Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Today, The Sydney Morning Herald’s chief investigative reporter, Kate McClymont, has been called to give evidence by the Crown.

Kate McClymont arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court this morning flanked by Herald editor Jordan Baker, left, and deputy editor Nick Ralston, right. Audrey Richardson

World.title: ‘Ticks a lot of boxes’: Why Michelle Payne is tipping this horse to conquer all in the Melbourne Cup
World.content:
Updated SportRacingMelbourne Cup ‘Ticks a lot of boxes’: Why Michelle Payne is tipping this horse to conquer all in the Melbourne Cup Michelle Payne and Danny Russell Updated November 3, 2026 — 1:21pm ,first published October 27, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow all the action in our live Melbourne Cup coverage It takes a special kind of horse to win a Melbourne Cup. It also takes a combination of good planning and good luck. In our comprehensive runner-by-runner guide, 2015 Melbourne Cup winning-jockey Michelle Payne and The Age racing writer Danny Russell cast an eye over the field, taking into variables such as lead-up form, weights and barriers. Point of Law rockets into Melbourne Cup favouritism after winning the Geelong Cup. Getty Images The horses are named in order of their saddle cloth numbers – from top weight down to bottom weight.



Ciaron Maher has seven runners, while Irish trainer Joseph O’Brien has five. 1. Sons And Lovers (GB)

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait Barrier: 3

6yoG (gelding) 57.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Dylan Browne McMonagle

Career: 23: 6-2-6 Last start: Second of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes Leopardstown Michelle Payne says: The stable is very confident. He sounds like he’s thrived since he’s been here, and I think the barrier certainly brings him right into contention.



Russell says: A dual group 2 winner from Ireland who sounds more like a midday soapie than a racehorse. That being said, in our view he has more chance of winning an Emmy than the Melbourne Cup, considering he has to lug 57.5 kilograms to victory first-up in Australia. Related Article Cox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington 2. Trustyourinstinct (IRE) Barrier: 18

7yoG 57kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: James McDonald

Career: 30: 9-7-4 Last start: 4th of 7 G1 Irish St Leger 2816m Payne says: For me, he is the pick of Joseph O’Brien’s runners. The barrier is not ideal, but he can overcome that wide gate if we have a firm track. He won’t be as well suited if the rain comes.



Russell says: If you believe in the saying, ‘follow the money’, this is the horse for you. He’s owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus, who used to be a bookmaker. That’s a good lead right there. He is also a group 2 winner with a serious chance. Watch to see if McManus bets up big on Cup eve. Top five hope. Robbie Dolan rides Knight’s Choice to a famous win in the 2024 Melbourne Cup. Getty 3. Knight’s Choice Barrier: 2

7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: John Symons and Sheila Laxon. Jockey: Robbie Dolan

Career: 31: 6-3-3 Last start: 14th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: Needs a firm track. But from a good barrier, who knows if the 2024 winner can cause another upset? He is going well enough if you look at his Caulfield run two starts back in the Herbert Power.



Russell says: The shock 2024 winner was robbed of the chance to defend his crown in 2025 because of the equine equivalent of a lockdown. Not COVID-19, but strangles – a contagious bacterial disease – that was detected at Macedon Lodge on the eve of last year’s spring. Great run in the Herbert Power two starts back, might have copped interference in Caulfield Cup. Can’t win. 4. Middle Earth (GB) Barrier: 1

7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Mark Zahra

Career: 26: 6-2-3 Last start: Eighth of 12 G1 Cox Plate 2040m Payne says: He sounds like he is the best chance of the Ciaron Maher runners. Ran third last year and is going just as well. A bit more weight, but drawn barrier one, proven at two miles and if he gets luck in running, he’ll figure in the finish. Russell says: If this galloper’s name has been plucked from J.R.R. Tolkien mythology, then surely his trainer, Ciaron Maher, qualifies as a modern-day wizard. Maher is on fire and has given this fellow the old-fashioned Cup preparation.



Bart Cummings’ rule was 10 kilometres – he has racked up 9.94km in five lead-up races. He looked good late in the Cox Plate. A winning chance. 5. Vauban (FRA) Barrier: 22

9yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott. Jockey: Jordan Childs

Career: 33: 10-5-6 Last start: Ninth of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Loading Payne says: I love this horse. Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott have taken a different approach this year. Coming in fresh off one run, so who knows? I can’t rule him out.



Russell says: The veteran is lining up for his fourth Melbourne Cup – the first two for Irish trainer Willie Mullins before he was sold to Australian connections to be trained by Waterhouse and Bott. He finished sixth last year, but might not be going as well. Although he was first-up in the Geelong Cup, so hard to tell. 6. Enfjaar (IRE) Barrier: 8

7yoG 56kg

Trainer: Roger Varian. Jockey: Ray Dawson

Career: 17: 5-2-3 Last start: Third of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: He looks good in a lot of ways. His run in the Caulfield Cup was excellent, and that has to put him in with a chance. Yet to run beyond 2400m, so the distance is a query. Trainer Ciaron Maher will have a number of horses running in the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images



Russell says: Best of internationals in the Caulfield Cup, and in my view, internationals need an impressive lead-up run in Australia if they are to win the Melbourne Cup. He ticks that box. And for those struggling to pronounce his name, Google says Enfjaar means “burst” in Arabic. Top 10. 7. Royal Supremacy (IRE) Barrier: 21

6yoG 56kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ben Allen

Career: 22: 7-3-4 Last start: 15th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: I think he has to improve. Didn’t have the best of runs in the Caulfield Cup, but I think I’d be leaning towards others, especially from the wide barrier. Russell says: One of Ciaron Maher’s seven runners, but a lesser chance. Cooked in the Caulfield Cup by a head-scratching ride from visiting hoop Jamie Spencer, he bolted to the front, whacked on the handbrakes and then looked confused when the pressure went back on from the 800m. He was flying before that. Outside the top 10.



8. Wine Dark Sea (GB) Barrier: 23

5yoG 56kg

Trainer: Harry Charlton. Jockey: Damian Lane

Career: 11: 4-2-0

Last start: 11th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: He also had excuses in the Caulfield Cup. There was an air of confidence about this horse leading into that race, so he may be able to turn his form around. Russell says: Purchased abroad by Australian Bloodstock, who have won the Cup with Protectionist and Gold Trip, and was a massive spruik horse leading into the Caulfield Cup. Sadly for punters, he didn’t live up to expectations. Needs a gigantic turnaround. 9. Asterix (NZ)



Barrier: 6

8yoG 55kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Jye McNeil

Career: 33: 8-1-2 Last start: 12th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Payne says: I think others are going better. He has run two miles in New Zealand and is by Tavistock, so a wet track would bring him into contention. Russell says: Caught up in the backwash of the tragic fall in the Caulfield Cup. A group 1-winning stayer from New Zealand owned by former Kiwi cricket great Mark Greatbatch and now in the Chris Waller barn. An outsider, but any rain will help. Goodie Two Shoes (left, with green and yellow silks) finishes second behind Half Yours in the 2025 Melbourne Cup. Joe Armao 10. Goodie Two Shoes (IRE)



Barrier: 19

8yoM (mare) 55kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Wayne Lordan

Career: 31: 14-2-7 Last start: Tenth of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m Payne says: She was excellent last year. She has to carry more weight this year, and did have a disappointing run last start, but this stable has to be respected so that can be overlooked. Russell says: A former hurdler who ran a surprise second in the Melbourne Cup last year. Trained by Joseph O’Brien, who has already won the race twice, and owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus. Slightly disappointing last start, but that might have been a pipe opener. Top 10 finish. 11. Juja Kibo (IRE) Barrier: 14

6yoG 55kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Sam Clipperton

Career: 20: 6-3-6 Last start: First of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m



Payne says: A beautiful confidence-boosting lead-in run to this year’s Melbourne Cup when he won the Moonee Valley Gold Cup. Having said that, might not be good enough to win, so I’m leaning towards others. Russell says: In hot form, having won its past two starts, including a big win in the group 2 Metropolitan at Randwick on October 3. Didn’t make the cut for the Caulfield Cup, but many believed he could have won the race. Copped a 1.5kg for the MV Gold Cup win. Still think he brings the B-grade form. Top 10. Hopewell Rock is Michelle Payne’s top pick for the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images 12. Hopewell Rock (IRE)



Barrier: 15

5yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: George Boughey. Jockey: Zac Lloyd

Career: 10: 3-3-2 Last start: Second of 22 Ebor Handicap 2787m Payne says: He’s my top selection. He helps himself. He puts himself into a reasonable position, puts himself to sleep, and has a nice turn of foot. Plus, he’s only carrying 54.5kg. I think he ticks a lot of boxes. Russell says: Another international with decent credentials, but will have to defy history to win this year’s Cup. No runner has come out of York’s Ebor Handicap and saluted on the first Tuesday in November. But a few have been close – Heartbreak City ran second in 2017, while Purple Moon was a runner-up in 2007. Onesmoothoperator wins the Geelong Cup in 2024. Getty Images 13. Onesmoothoperator (US)



Barrier: 13

9yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Tim Fitzsimmons. Jockey: Declan Bates

Career: 51: 6-11-6 Last start: 11th of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Payne says: I think he looked talented last year, but I’m just not sure he’s going as well this year. Russell says: Has gone off the boil. The veteran started second favourite and ran 12th in the 2024 Melbourne Cup after winning the Geelong Cup in the lead-up. Won the MV Gold Cup last year before finishing 16th in the Cup. Not going as well this year. Will be grateful they pay back to last. 14. Soul Of Spain (IRE) Barrier: 5

6yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Tommy Berry

Career: 26: 5-5-6 Last start: Eight of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m



Payne says: He’s very fit and has had a lot of racing. Master trainer in Chris Waller, but he may struggle to beat some of these horses. Russell says: Ran second in the Sydney Cup over 3200m but has been slightly disappointing at his past two starts, including a seventh in The Metropolitan. Might have been ridden upside down in the Caulfield Cup. Needs to improve. 15. Zahrann (IRE) Barrier: 11

5yoH 54.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ben Melham

Career: 12: 4-2-1 Last start: Sixth of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Loading



Payne says: The Maher team are saying he’s the forgotten horse, so you have to respect their opinion. A good, honest run in the Caulfield Cup, and blinkers on. He’s definitely in with some sort of chance. Russell says: This year’s smoky, considering he started second favourite in the Caulfield Cup and was clearly disadvantaged after being caught up in the tragic mid-race fall. Has not raced over 2400m, but being Irish-bred should relish the two miles. Top five chance. 16. So You Are Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing This horse is barred from running in Cup week after failing a drug test – that its trainer requested Barrier: 7

5yoG 54kg

Trainer: Bjorn Baker. Jockey: Rachel King

Career: 28: 8-6-6 Last start: First of 13 G3 Bendigo Cup 2400m



Payne says: He was good winning the Bendigo Cup. He’s a good, honest galloper who will put himself into a good position from barrier seven. Just a question of whether he’s got the class. Russell says: Jumped into the field after a being handed a 1kg penalty for an impressive win in Wednesday’s Bendigo Cup. He is a horse in form, having won four staying races on the trot and has a top trainer-jockey combination. Since March, he has started 13 times and travelled 21.8km. That’s one fit horse. A top-five chance. 17. Future History (GB) Barrier: 12

9yoG 53.5kg

Trainer: Gregory Hickman. Jockey: Jamie Melham

Career: 47: 10-6-6 Last start: Ninth of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m Loading



Payne says: I actually tipped this horse last year, and he had no luck at all. He’s had a change of trainer and is another year older, but he certainly has the talent. Nice to see Jamie Melham with the ride. She certainly knows how to win the Cup. Russell says: He jumps into the field after the scratching of Stinger Glass on Friday, giving last year’s winning jockey Jamie Melham a chance to defend her crown. Until then, she did not have a ride. He was caught three wide in the Gold Cup, so that’s a forgive run, but it’s a stretch to say he can finish top 10. 18. James J Braddock (GB) Barrier: 24

4yoH 53.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Craig Williams

Career: 8: 2-1-2 Last start: 6th of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m James J Braddock under the watchful eye of trainer Joseph O’Brien and racing manager Kevin Blake. Getty Images



Payne says: Sounds like a very exciting horse with a well-connected ownership group. I’m sure they’ll be disappointed with barrier 24, but the stable have not brought him out here for fun. Have to give him a good chance. Russell says: Another northern hemisphere three-year-old bought by a big group of Aussies. Three things to consider here: He is still trained by O’Brien. Tick. He was sourced by big Melbourne buyer Ozzie Kheir. Tick. Craig Williams sought the ride. Double tick. He is a group 3 winner, lightly raced, and will carry a light weight. First-up in Australia the only concern. A first-four pick. 19. Kizlyar (IRE) Barrier: 20

5yoG 53.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien Jockey: Beau Mertens

Career: 11: 3-2-2 Last start: 11th of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m Payne says: There was a bit of confidence before his last run in the Moonee Valley Gold Cup, but he didn’t get a strong enough tempo to suit. He’s a strong stayer and I think he’ll be ridden to use that strength on Tuesday. Look for improvement with a light weight.



Russell says: Looked like he was going to bowl to the front and set a free-rolling European-style tempo in the MV Gold Cup before jockey Ben Melham surprisingly took a sit. He was left flat-footed in the sprint home but will get a suitable hot pace in the Cup, and will relish 3200m. Top 10 chance. Ethan Brown salutes his Geelong Cup win on Point of Law. Getty Images 20. Point Of Law (GB) Barrier: 9

4yoH 53kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ethan Brown

World.title: ‘Savage political attack’: One Nation volunteer bashed over corflutes
World.content:
NationalVictoriaOne Nation ‘Savage political attack’: One Nation volunteer bashed over corflutes James Costa November 3, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content. A One Nation volunteer is in hospital after he was attacked by a man and a teenager with a baseball bat on his front lawn in a coastal town on the Great Ocean Road. Victoria Police said in a statement on Tuesday the 60-year-old was recovering from serious, non-life-threatening injuries after he confronted a 14-year-old boy who was allegedly damaging a corflute outside a home in Torquay on Sunday evening. The man was then allegedly attacked with a baseball bat by the teenager and a 37-year-old man.



Speaking outside Geelong Hospital on Tuesday, where the man is recovering, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the volunteer was kicked so badly he “lost consciousness”, and had bleeding of the brain and “from basically every orifice” in his face. In contradiction to the police’s assessment, Hanson said the attack “was life-threatening. Even now, with the bleed, it still could be life-threatening.” Hanson and One Nation Victoria deputy leader Colleen Harkin visited the man before speaking with media outside the hospital, where she claimed the alleged attackers were walking along the highway when they spotted the One Nation campaign signs outside the man’s house. “I’m very emotional about this because I respect people who support me, I really do. I don’t take it for granted. It means a lot to me, and that’s when, in times like this, you have to, you know, be there for them as well,” she said. “This kind of vicious and savage violence has to stop, and the consequences have to be made real.”



Harkin called the alleged assault a “savage attack on a person” because of their politics. Victoria Police said the teenager and 37-year-old Hampton East man were arrested after the alleged attack, which occurred around 7.45pm on Sunday. The man was charged with intentionally causing injury and other offences, while the teenager was issued a caution. Pauline Hanson at a One Nation press conference in Melbourne on Monday morning with Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Eamon Gallagher Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said the alleged attack was “shocking” and he had met with the electoral commissioner to discuss it.



“It should never be occurring,” Carol said. “Whether you’re wearing a red, a blue, an orange, or a green T-shirt, they are volunteers. They are out there doing what they believe is right, and no one should be coming under attack.“



Carroll called for a “civil, peaceful election” due in just over three weeks, and said he was considering whether extra security was needed for candidates of all parties. Opposition leader Jess Wilson said the alleged attack on the volunteer was “absolutely appalling” and her thoughts are with the man and his family. “Every Victorian has the right to express their political views and support the party of their choice without fear of violence or intimidation,” Wilson said. “We can disagree strongly about politics, but violence is never the answer. One Nation Victoria leader Warren Pickering condemned the attack in a statement, calling it “un-Australian”.



“Political violence or intimidation of any kind against anyone is unacceptable in this country. If you don’t like someone’s politics, you vote accordingly. You don’t assault them”, Pickering said. “Our thoughts are with our volunteer and his family. We’re informed he has serious injuries. This attack is un-Australian and unacceptable.” Emma McGinness, a nearby resident of the victim, was home at the time but did not witness the incident. She said the alleged attack had put a “dampener on the safety around the area”. “It’s a lovely place, a nice quiet dead-end street, so it’s definitely something that has never happened before,” McGinness said. “We’ve always felt very safe and let our kids ride around the streets, like the other neighbours do.”



Hanson said an online fundraiser had been started to support the victim and his family, including his wife and two teenage sons. The 37-year-old man was remanded to appear at Geelong Magistrates’ Court on November 10. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Lotto ticket on four legs’: How to get your own Melbourne Cup horse
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup ‘Lotto ticket on four legs’: How to get your own Melbourne Cup horse Andrew Wu Updated November 3, 2026 — 1:15pm ,first published November 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow all the action in our live Melbourne Cup coverage It’s taken 10 years and about 30 horses for Anya and Paul Podbury to find Shockletz, the Australasian-bred mare who will realise the Woodend couple’s lifelong ambition of owning a Melbourne Cup runner. The first step in former Richmond footballer Justin Pickering’s path to Juja Kibo started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when he and a few mates landed juicy quaddies in Melbourne and Sydney on the same day. Paul (left) and Anya Podbury are part-owners of Cup runner Shockletz. Then there’s vet Rob McInnes, who got extremely lucky – then felt the wrath of the racing gods. He liked the horse he was inspecting so much, he bought a share. That horse was Defiantly, one of the favourites in this year’s great race – until his withdrawal on Saturday morning.



Of all the cherished items in Australian sport – think the premiership trophies of the AFL and NRL or cricket’s baggy green – the Melbourne Cup is the one that is attainable to the average punter. Theoretically. Justin Pickering (holding the Cup) is one of the owners of Juja Kibo. Deep pockets help, of course, but through racehorse syndication everyday mums and dads with the unfashionably bred horse can knock off the bluebloods of the rich and famous. As has become the norm over the past 15 years or so, this year’s field has predominantly come from Europe, arriving on these shores after being bought by bloodstock agents for leading syndicators and owners. Jamie Lovett, a director for one of the country’s biggest syndication companies Australian Bloodstock, spends hours watching replays from races in Europe, studying form and cross-referencing times and measurements.



He also has a global team of about eight or nine, mainly on the ground in Europe, including jockeys and trackwork riders, who feed him intel. “There’s a lot of tentacles to the business to try and land on the right horses,” Lovett said. Based in Australia, he does not see many of the horses he buys in the flesh. That, he said, is the job of his vets. Once a horse is identified, Lovett approaches its owners or buys it at sales. He bought a few just last week from the Tattersalls sales in the UK. Australian Bloodstock, which generally has about 100 to 150 thoroughbreds at a time on its books, has had two Cup winners in its silks – Protectionist (2014) and Gold Trip (2022), both from Europe. The European imports do not come cheap, their price tags swelled by the demand from Australian interests desperate to find a cups horse, and the market in the Middle East searching for talent to run at Dubai’s lucrative World Cup meeting.



Gold Trip, who had come fourth in France’s famous L’Arc de Triomphe in 2020, cost about $2 million, which, at the time, was the most expensive horse Lovett had bought. Australian Bloodstock have three runners in this year’s race – Royal Supremacy, Vauban and Wine Dark Sea. A fourth, the aforementioned Defiantly, failed a vet test. Royal Supremacy, bought as a three-year-old after a third in the Italian Derby – one of Europe’s lesser derbies – “wouldn’t have been top of the top”, Lovett said. Royal Supremacy gets some beach time in ahead of the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images “You’re not buying for $200,000 to $300,000, put it that way,” Lovett said.



In a cruel irony for those involved with Defiantly, a half-brother to last year’s Cox Plate runner-up Buckaroo and Melbourne Cup placegetter Middle Earth, the gelding had impressed McInnes so much during an inspection for Australian Bloodstock the vet shelled out $18,500 for a 2.5 per cent share. Related Article Melbourne Cup briefing

Melbourne Cup Buck of the Irish: The internationals who lit up Melbourne Cup betting “He was sound, beautifully natured, and everything was clean with his X-rays,” McInnes said before Defiantly’s withdrawal. “His demeanour was good.” Presciently, he had also likened owning a horse to having a “Tattslotto ticket on four legs”. Pickering, then, has found the winning ticket three times. That’s how many of the dozen or so horses he has part-owned who have run in the Cup. The former Richmond wingman played his 59 V/AFL games in the 1980s and ’90s, long before the money could set you up for life.



McInnes’ in was through his vet work. Pickering’s came through a friend of a friend. He is part of several syndicates, many run by his mate Gerard Mulcahy, who lives next door to Mick Johnston and his wife Alise. Mulcahy often gets tipped into horses from the Johnstons, and relays the information to Pickering and his friends. Their foray into racehorse ownership started during the many COVID-19 lockdowns when he and his friends started punting together to stay connected. After one particularly successful day, they decided to plunge their winnings into a horse. It landed them in an imported stayer called Delphi, who won the Herbert Power in 2021 on his way to seventh in that year’s Melbourne Cup. They kept rolling their slice of the prizemoney into more horses. A happy Pickering among friends at Flemington.



“We occasionally take a dividend just to prove to our wives that it is profitable with racehorses,” Pickering joked. Their next star was another European stayer, Circle Of Fire, who won the 2024 Sydney Cup, worth $1.3 million to the winner. He ran sixth later that year in the big one. Their latest horse is Juja Kibo. There are 15 in the Happy Hippo syndicate who splashed out about $30,000 – or about $2000 each – for a 10 per cent share in the Ciaron Maher-trained gelding. They have even produced their own merchandise – stubby holders and ties adorned with Juja Kibo’s distinctive racing colours. The owners of Juja Kibo have produced their own merch. Many of them were at Flemington on Cox Plate Day when the six-year-old booked his ticket into Tuesday’s race with victory in the $750,000 Moonee Valley Cup.



“It was so good – you turn around and hug one of your best mates,” Pickering said. “It’s not going to be good for my health if he happens to win. I’m willing to take that risk.” They were back at headquarters on Saturday night for the barrier draw, cheering loudly when their stayer drew gate 14 of 24. It’s been a nervous few days for Pickering, his wife Sally, and the Happy Hippo syndicate. “For some reason, this one’s keeping me up at night just thinking about it,” Pickering said. “I’ve loved the way he’s gone about it and genuinely think he’s a fair chance.” The Podburys have gone down a different route to finding their Cup runner. Folk like them are racing’s lifeblood – passionate owners who love sharing the thrill of raceday with friends and family. Paul and Anya Podbury with sons Bailey (right) and Charlie.



They have part-owned about 30 horses – just a few per cent each time. Several have been with prominent owner Laurence Eales, who won the 2009 Melbourne Cup with Shocking and owned the cult hero Whobegotyou. The Podburys’ best is sprinting mare Benedetta, who won Adelaide’s group 1 Goodwood in 2024 and banked nearly $2.4 million in her career. They bought into Benedetta with the prizemoney won by another of Eales’ horses Horrifying, a son of Shocking who banked about $300,000 in a month in 2022. As the Podburys’ relationship with Eales grew, they were invited to lunch at South Melbourne’s O’Connell’s Hotel to discuss a 10 per cent share for $7500 in Horrifying’s unraced sister, which he had bred in New Zealand. That filly was Shockletz. There are seven in the Podburys’ Plodalong – Zelt syndicate, each paying just over $1000 for a share in a mare that is one of the leading chances in the race. The Podburys are in the ownership game for love, not money.



The beauty of buying an untried horse, such as Shockletz, is the lower cost, though the risk is higher as there is no exposed form to assess. Like the major syndicators purchasing stock from Europe, Paul, an accountant, studies form and watches trials as part of his due diligence before buying. On this occasion, he bought on trust from their positive experience racing with Eales. Related Article Melbourne Cup He’d just ridden his first group 1 race. Then came the death threats “You’re not guaranteeing a collect, but you’re buying a known commodity to a certain extent, you know there’s some ability there, rather than buying a two-year-old stayer,” Paul said. “We were pretty lucky.” As the saying goes, the best way to make a small fortune in racing is to start with a large one. Asked if they are ahead financially, Anya says: “yes – with gritted teeth”.



“If you did it for money, it would be unwise. You have to be prepared to invest knowing you may not get money back,” Anya said. For the Podburys, it’s the romance of the turf. Anya has loved the Cup since she was a kid watching the race at primary school in Port Fairy. “This is 10-year-old Anya talking now,” she said. “I dreamed of playing for Hawthorn, which in the ’80s and ’90s was not possible, and the other dream was having a runner in the Melbourne Cup. “The people who own Shockletz, we’re normal, average people who work every day, have families and kids. We live a conservative lifestyle, we don’t go overseas; our treat is racing. It absolutely can happen to the average person. That’s the magic of it.” Read more from our racing coverage

World.title: Plane crashes in Nelson, emergency services responding
World.content:
A plane reported missing near Nelson has crashed.

The plane left the city at about 9.10am on Tuesday morning and was reported overdue just before midday.

Two rescue helicopters had been searching at the plane's last-known location north-east of Nelson.

In a statement, police said emergency services were now responding to a plane crash south of Castor Peak.

Police did not say how many people were reported to be on board.

"An update will be provided as soon as we are able," they said.

Flight tracking data on the website FlightRadar24 showed a Cessna Skyhawk taking off from Nelson Airport at 9.10am and flying into the hills near Whangamoa before its tracking data stopped.

World.title: Kāpiti College parents question all-boy head students
World.content:
Parents at a lower North Island school say they're concerned female students won't feel valued by the selection of three boys as head students for 2027.

But Kāpiti College says the school stands by its selection process, and the chosen students should be supported by the community.

In a letter to parents, principal David Lowe wrote that "representation shifts naturally" and reflected how "in 2024 we appointed two female heads of kura, while for 2027 the panel identified three exceptionally strong candidates and appointed three male heads of kura".

Kāpiti College announced the three boys, who are all in the school's first XV rugby team, as heads at its prizegiving last week. The announcement was made alongside a wider student leadership team, mixed between boys and girls.

One parent, who contacted RNZ following the announcement, said she was concerned the message the school was sending with no female head students.

"I'm not trying to take away from those boys, from what I hear they are great, their individual capability is not the question.

"It's about the bigger picture for me, as we all know women are still underrepresented in leadership and CEO positions, and so I think schools just have a responsibility to challenge that, and not inadvertently reinforce it."

The parent said as head students, the three boys were representing a large, diverse school with students from different experiences and backgrounds.

"I just don't feel that is representing everybody."

She was worried younger students who were not sporty or didn't see themselves in their leaders would rule themselves out of going for those positions one day.

"It's all about these young people - what they think leadership looks like and who can be a leader."

She said she had heard multiple parents had written into the school raising concerns, and other students had raised concerns too.

Another parent of a girl at the school, and who also spoke with RNZ, said the boys were outstanding young people but it wasn't fair representation.

"I think it sends a startlingly stark message to any young woman, not only in the college, but across the community, that women are just not valued."

Kāpiti College principal David Lowe. Supplied

RNZ has approached Lowe for comment. In the email to the school community - which RNZ has seen - Lowe said the school was confident its selection process was thorough and collaborative. It had been based on written applications, scenario workshops, pastoral reviews and interviews.

"Appointments are decided by a panel of middle leaders, senior leadership and current head students, who evaluate candidates on their service, living of Parihaka Mai Ai, academic balance and teamwork."

The school decided to retire traditional head boy and girl titles in 2022 to support gender diversity and select leaders on merit rather than quotas.

Lowe said he had heard community concerns about female representation and was grateful for the kōrero shared. He said the school community and student body would have the opportunity to review the head student selection process ahead of 2028, including whether gender-defined roles should be revisited.

Lowe said female students continued to hold more of the positions across the wider senior leadership captaincies, which included te waka rangatahi, Pasifika, sports, academic, service, tech, political advocacy and an all-female hauora team.

World.title: Election 2026: Early voting tips over 1 million mark
World.content:
The number of people who have cast an early vote has tipped over the 1 million mark, with nearly 160,000 voting on Monday.

Early voting is still tracking ahead of 2023, but behind the equivalent 2020 dates.

The Electoral Commission's latest voting statistics show 159,994 people voted on 2 November, with the cumulative number of early votes now at 1,074,416.

At this stage in the 2023 campaign, 860,668 people had cast an early vote. In 2020, 1,282,028 people had cast an early vote by this point.
