World.title: Harrowing seven-hour journey home for wheelchair user after three bus failures
World.content:
A Canterbury woman took seven and a half hours to get home in her motorised wheelchair after three public buses let her down.

Tracy Peters, 60, navigated cycle trails, strong winds and uneven gravel paths as she made her way from Rangiora to Christchurch in a 30-kilometre ordeal.

"Nothing is going to get me on a bus ever again. This is the straw that broke the camel's back. And it's embarrassing that I had to call the fire service to say I'm stuck in a bus in my wheelchair."

In a statement to RNZ, bus company Kinetic said it had apologised to Peters. The Canterbury Regional Council is investigating.

Peters - who has a spinal injury - caught the bus from Christchurch to go to the Labour Day festival at the racecourse in Rangiora since it was a lovely day.

"I use a power chair - that weighs more than 150 kilos - and got on the bus after the driver put the ramp down for me. But when we arrived in Rangiora, he couldn't get the ramp to go out."

People tried to release the ramp as well as the GoBus driver to no avail.

"So I had to stay in the bus, and we went to the main metro bus terminal in Rangiora where they hoped to get the ramp working."

More people at the terminal tried and failed to release the ramp, and there was no way anyone could manoeuvre Peters and her heavy battery-powered chair out of the bus.

"The driver was nice but stressed and rang their depot. I even spoke to the person on the other end of the phone from GoBus while the bus driver worried he would be late for his next stop."

Peters - who is a full-time wheelchair user - rang the fire service and just as a crew arrived, a different bus driver managed to wedge a spoon under the ramp to release it.

By now she was keen to get home and headed to a second bus.

But while the ramp worked at first, it was not flush with the floor when it went back in, meaning she could be tipped out.

By now a third bus was at the terminal.

"The driver of bus number three said to me 'I don't want you on my bus'. He was nice but not particularly articulate so I called the bus info number and was told they couldn't help.

"I explained there were no taxi services available on a public holiday and asked what bus service I could use to return to Christchurch and was told none. The mobility taxi service was also closed.

"I didn't call the police as I didn't feel like it was an emergency. Or an ambulance."

Peters said she chose not to wait for another bus, fearing it could also be unsuitable.

"My power chair has a maximum distance of 20km on its battery and it could be dangerous at night, so I went to McDonald's and they let me charge my battery for about an hour. Someone had earlier suggested I could potentially take the cycleway so that's what I did.

"I rang a friend who would keep in touch every half hour. I didn't want to be a dumb character in a second-grade movie who gets killed. I made friends with pukekos along the tracks that were fascinated by my slow moving powerchair, and cows in the paddocks.

"The wind was utterly brutal. My chair weighs 186 kilos and it was being blown around and that was scary."

Peters believed she was incredibly lucky to have made it home in one piece. "But my wheelchair is quite damaged, and my muscle spasms are worse after bumbling along the cycleway.

"I am angry I was put in this situation. I am also so very disappointed in the bus service that so spectacularly let me down."

Peters was a bus driver in Christchurch for about 20 years and said during her time managers endorsed never leaving any passenger stranded.

"I have the knowledge about how a good bus service works and I don't believe drivers have enough back-up at the moment."

Drivers should also have a small tool kit on board, she said.

Peters followed up her experience with a complaint to Canterbury Regional Council and said she got an apology from customer service.

But she wanted the bus services to acknowledge what had happened and apologise. She did not trust the bus service now.

"I have had previous experiences on buses in Christchurch when the ramp wouldn't work."

The region's public transport network - Metro - is managed by the regional council. Several bus companies contract to the council, including GoBus, which is owned by Australian company Kinetic.

In a statement to RNZ, Kinetic said it had apologised to Peters, saying the bus company understood how upsetting and frustrating her experience must have been.

"We have had an in-depth conversation with the passenger to obtain the details of her experience. Based on this information, we are reviewing the circumstances so that we can improve our processes to avoid similar future situations."

Council public transport general manager Stewart Gibbon said it was taking what happened seriously and that everyone should be able to use public transport with confidence and dignity.

Gibbon said it was investigating what happened and that all buses in the Metro fleet were required to have working accessibility ramps and the ability to kneel.

If a ramp is found to be faulty, the driver is expected to report it so action can be taken. If a customer cannot get on a bus due to accessibility, the driver is expected to contact their control room for support, Gibbon said.

"Based on our review so far, it appears this may not have happened, and we are working with the operator to understand why and what steps are needed to prevent it from happening again."

The New Zealand Spinal Trust is based in Christchurch and spokesman Andrew Hall said there did appear to be a problem with some buses and drivers that needed to be addressed.

"For Tracy it was obviously a distressing situation and disappointing the driver didn't help when she was stuck. Anything out of the ordinary may have stumped them."

Hall said overall the Canterbury bus service was reliable for wheelchair users, but he did hear about failing ramps or wheelchair users not being allowed on board.

World.title: Police involved after alleged assaults on students at Auckland's Lynfield College
World.content:
Police are investigating after a reported assault at an Auckland school.

Authorities were alerted last month to an assault at Lynfield College involving a number of students.

A police spokesperson said the alleged assault happened in late October and was reported to police a week later.

"The matter is currently being assessed by police and all identified lines of inquiry will be followed up," they said.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

As reported by the New Zealand Herald, a mother of a Year 10 student claimed her daughter was attacked by a group of up to 10 girls during lunchtime on 21 October.

She told the Herald her daughter was repeatedly punched and hit with phone pouches - resulting in a cut to her head that required stitches.

"We are very scared to send our kids to school," the mother told the Herald.

"My daughter and my family are suffering right now."

Meanwhile, another mother told the Herald their son was assaulted in a separate incident on 20 October.

The student hadn't been back to school since.

"[My son's] education and wellbeing have been affected, and I do not feel confident sending him back without clear and credible assurances that he will be safe," the boy's mum told the Herald.

"As a mother, I cannot understand how children can continue to face alleged violence and intimidation while families wait for action.

"I understand that incidents must be investigated properly, but I am deeply concerned about our safety."

Lynfield College confirmed it had been working through two incidents of concern that occurred at school two weeks ago.

Principal Cath Knell said they had followed another incident at a community event unrelated to the school, as well as social media concerns.

"We take anything related to the safety and wellbeing of our students very seriously," she said.

"As such we have spent a significant amount of time understanding the background to what happened and the circumstances surrounding these incidents, along with working through our formal processes with a small number of students and their families."

Knell said work was ongoing and they were working closely with police.

"The school has strong pastoral support in place and is providing support where needed as we work with the families and students affected," she said.

"We understand that people may want more information. However, we are still working through this matter and we need to respect the privacy of the young people involved and allow the appropriate processes to continue."

The Ministry of Education told RNZ it was up to schools to address disciplinary matters and keep students safe.

The ministry's director of education for Auckland Central & East, Jason Swann, said they were aware of the situation.

"School leaders take these responsibilities seriously, and we expect schools to follow their established processes and policies," he said.

"The Ministry of Education is available if required."

World.title: Opals veteran opens door to Australian return after WNBA retirement
World.content:
Opals Star Bec Allen has kept the door ajar for a return to Australia's domestic women's basketball competition after ending a glittering 11-year tenure in the WNBA.

The 33-year-old's decision to leave the top women's basketball competition in the world has raised questions about whether she is preparing to finish her career back home in the WNBL.

"It's something that I'm not saying a hard no on. Right now the answer is no, purely because my body just needs rest," Allen told AAP.

Agony and ecstasy for Australian duo in WNBA Finals game seven Australia's Izzy Borlase falls just short of a title as her Atlanta Dream are beaten by Golden State Valkyries in game seven of the WNBA Finals.

"After a year, maybe I'll get a call from Cheryl [Chambers] or a good friend like that, and I'll jump back in and play in Geelong or something like that.

"I just know that I want to be in Melbourne.

"I want to be in Australia and you can't say a hard no to anything."

Allen has a sparkling history in Australia's top domestic league, debuting with the Dandenong Rangers in the 2010-2011 campaign and playing in the competition until 2016.

She claimed the league's Defensive Player of the Year award in 2014, before signing her first WNBA contract with the New York Liberty in 2015.

The WNBL's chief operations officer, Justin Nelson, said he had no doubt some clubs had inquired about securing her signature.

"Bec is an incredible role model, an incredible athlete. She's done so much for girls and women in basketball," he told AAP.

Bec Allen was a member of the Opals squad at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

"All of the fans around Australia would love nothing better than to see her playing in the WNBL, and if the league or I can do anything to help make that happen, we'd love to see Bec playing."

Allen has plans to become a player agent and pursue commentary, but the Tokyo Olympian is currently relishing in some much-deserved rest, having represented the Connecticut Sun, Phoenix Mercury and Chicago Sky before coming back to New York for one final season in 2026.

Reuniting with her past team proved the right move as Allen won the WNBA Commissioner's Cup in June and reached the semi-finals last month.

"My first [WNBA season] was in 2015, and I had impostor syndrome at the beginning, and then I got to realise after years that, hey, I belong here," Allen said.

"I never thought that when I started, I'd play 11 years in the league.

"Body, mind, heart … I've given the game all of myself in those capacities, and so now it's time for the next chapter."

AAP

World.title: Maxwell retires from international cricket but continues franchise T20 career
World.content:
Australian short-form cricket star Glenn Maxwell has retired from the international game.

The 38-year-old retired from one-day international cricket in 2025, but has now hung up his bat and gloves for Australia's Twenty20 team and his state team.

"Post the last one-day game for Victoria, speaking to my teammates and letting them know that was gonna be my last game for the state was probably harder than I thought it was going to be; got a little choked up," Maxwell said on The Final Word.

Maxwell represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka earlier this year and, across his career, played 130 T20 internationals, scoring 2,897 runs at 28.97 and with a strike rate of 154.42.

He also took 51 wickets and claimed 62 catches, with a career-high score of 145 not out against Sri Lanka in 2016.

"I'm grateful for the time I was able to play for my country," he said.

"If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Vic change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.

"I'm extremely grateful to have played that much for my country and to hopefully inspire some kids who want to take the game up, to want to play differently and to be open and vulnerable and to not shy away and be themselves.

"It was pretty incredible when even getting my first Test cap, well and truly before I was probably ready.

"It was pretty exciting, and I'm glad they took a gamble on me, and I'm glad I could, at different stages, repay the faith and be afforded the chance to play as much, for as far, as I did."

Maxwell also played seven Tests for Australia and 149 ODIs, and enjoyed an expansive and productive First Class and List A career with Victoria, too.

He will continue to play Twenty20 franchise cricket, including for the Melbourne Stars in the upcoming Big Bash League.

AAP

World.title: Live: Top trainer explains 'simple mistake' that led to Melbourne Cup scratching
World.content:
Trainer Ciaron Maher has seven chances to win this year's Melbourne Cup (Getty Images)

There are five chances to add to Ireland's four wins in the race — and they're all for the same man.

Joseph O'Brien could become the youngest trainer (at 33) to win a third Melbourne Cup with Sons And Lovers, Trustyourinstinct, Goodie Two Shoes, James J Braddock or Kizlyar.

If he breaks the record, O'Brien would take the place of French trainer Etienne de Mestre, who won five Cups in the 1800s, with his third in 1867 with Tim Whiffler at the age of 35.

There are a number of trainers who could add to England's sole win in the Cup (Charlie Appleby with Cross Counter in 2018).

Roger Varian has Enfjaar, Harry Charlton has Wine Dark Sea, and George Boughey has Hopewell Rock.

Between O'Brien and Ciaron Maher, the pair literally have half the field.

Added to O'Brien's five entries are Maher's septet — Middle Earth, Royal Supremacy, Juja Kibo, Zahrann, Point of Law, Mr Monaco and Shockletz. If any of these come home, it would be Maher's second win after Gold Trip in 2022.

Maher is a leading proponent of the Aussie "imports" strategy for the Cup. Of his seven horses, only Shockletz (NZ-bred) is vaguely local, while the rest are from Britain or Ireland.

Chris Waller no longer has Asterix, but he does have Irish-bred Soul of Spain in the running. If it runs first, Waller would have a second Cup win to add to Verry Elleegant in 2021.

Gai Waterhouse could also add a second victory if (French-bred) Vauban gets up (and a first for co-trainer Adrian Bott). A win would see Waterhouse join Sheila Laxon (Ethereal, Knight's Choice) as the only female trainers to win two Melbourne Cups.

Laxon is going for a third Melbourne Cup — with the same horse as her second as Knight's Choice goes for a second win in three years. Her co-trainer John Symons would win his second.

Then there are the trainers looking to break through and add their names to the honour roll for the first time (aside from those already mentioned).

These are Bjorn Baker with So You Are, Tim Fitzimmons with Onesmoothoperator, Gregory Hickman with Future History, Thomas Carberry with Strictly Business and Grahame Begg with Zakouma.

World.title: Addo-Carr's future in Parramatta's hands as B-sample returns negative
World.content:
Josh Addo-Carr's immediate playing future is in the hands of the Parramatta hierarchy after police advised the winger his second result from a roadside drugs test had come back negative.

Addo-Carr met Eels officials at a board meeting on Monday afternoon to respond to a breach notice after it was widely presumed the former Test and State of Origin star would be sacked.

The Eels released a statement afterwards.

Eels star Addo-Carr allegedly returns positive test for cocaine NRL player Josh Addo-Carr is being investigated by police after allegedly returning a positive test for cocaine.

"Josh and his legal team were given the opportunity to respond to the notice," the Eels said.

"The club will consider their submission and make a decision in due course."

The 31-year-old allegedly tested positive to cocaine at a random roadside test in September.

But police have confirmed to AAP that no further action will be taken, leaving Addo-Carr to potentially earn a stay of execution.

"About 11.10pm on Friday [11 September 2026], officers attached to Inner West Police Area Command were patrolling Enmore Road, Newtown, when they stopped the driver of a vehicle for random testing," a NSW Police spokeswoman said on Monday: "The driver — a 31-year-old man — was subjected to a roadside breath test, which returned a negative result. "The driver underwent a preliminary drug wipe, which allegedly returned a positive indication for cocaine. An oral fluid sample was obtained and sent away for forensic testing. Following the testing the result has returned a negative result. No further police action is expected."

Addo-Carr has scored 27 tries in two seasons with the Parramatta Eels. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Addo-Carr was sacked by Canterbury almost two years ago to the day for testing positive to cocaine.

He declined to talk to media after leaving the club's headquarters at Belmore about 6pm.

But his lawyer, Elias Tabchouri, thanked the club for being "generous with their time".

"The club were able to allow us to express our thoughts in relation to this situation," Tabchouri said.

"We remain positive in relation to the negative finding for the B test, and we remain committed to the club."

Pressed on whether Addo-Carr would remain with the Eels in 2027, after bagging 27 tries in his first two seasons in blue and gold, Tabchouri said: "That's a matter for the club right now. We're waiting for the outcome".

"Josh has always maintained — and still maintains — a commitment to the Parramatta club."

AAP

World.title: Cats' rise well overdue as AFLW finals loom
World.content:
Co-captain Nina Morrison has always felt Geelong had the potential to be among the AFLW's best teams.

And she is not surprised by teammate Georgie Prespakis's rise to super stardom that has helped remove Geelong's underachievers tag and catapult the Cats to new heights.

Geelong has thrived under former Melbourne mentor Mick Stinear this year and will face the Demons in Saturday's qualifying final at Princes Park.

The Cats (11-1) are the highest-scoring regular-season AFLW team of all time and only finished second behind North Melbourne on percentage.

"We've been disappointed the last couple of seasons, to be honest, about where our performance has been," Morrison said.

"I feel like I've always looked at the group that we've had and the list profile and thought that we could be playing better footy.

"So in that sense, I would look at our performance and it doesn't feel like it's come out of the blue.

"We've probably just unlocked a few things that were already there and it's just about being able to do that all together and at the right time."

Georgie Prespakis is one of the superstars of the AFLW. (Getty Images: AFL Photo/Michael Willson)

Explosive midfielder Prespakis, the runner-up in the 2025 AFLW best and fairest, has gone to another level.

The 23-year-old has averaged 30.6 disposals, 8.1 clearances and eight score involvements.

"She's put in a body of work off-field as well to get herself in the right mindset coming into games to be able to perform well," Morrison said.

"She's obviously a star of the competition and I stand back in awe sometimes at the things she's doing on-field.

"She's an amazing player but her ability to bring her teammates into a game has always been a strength, but [she's] riding the ebbs and flows of that a bit better this season.

"To be someone that can do such incredible things but then also be such a great teammate has been her real growth this year."

Saturday will be the first time Stinear leads Geelong against Melbourne.

Tyla Hanks and Melbourne's impressive midfield will pose a tough test for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Wiltshire)

Morrison, who will play her 75th game, played down how much his inside knowledge could help against a star-studded midfield led by Kate Hore, Tyla Hanks and Olivia Purcell.

"We haven't played them, clearly, this year so I'm looking forward to the challenge of going up against one of the best mids in the comp, just seeing how we stack up against them," Morrison said.

"Obviously they're a pretty well-rounded team and Mick will know them pretty well as well.

"I'm sure he'll have some little things that we can draw on but I think a big focus for us over the course of the year has been how we focus on us and do us well. I'm sure that'll be no different this week."

Morrison insisted having to play at Princes Park instead of home ground Kardinia Park — booked out for a dirt bike event — was not on players' minds.

AAP

World.title: Usyk's path to global dominance goes through Gatton
World.content:
Oleksandr Usyk has earned a tongue-in-cheek invite to resume his cruiserweight career in Gatton after the boxing great's plan to return to the division set him on a path for David Nyika.

The Ukrainian (25-0) unified the cruiserweight division before wiping the floor of his heavyweight rivals, beating Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury and Daniel Dubois twice in the last five years.

The 39-year-old now wants to return to the cruiserweight ranks and sweep the belts again in one final act, with the vacant IBF title his first target before a date with current WBO and WBA champion David Benavidez (32-0).

Benavidez will fight Michal Cieslak for the WBC belt next month.

New Zealand Olympian David Nyika, based in the rural Queensland town of Gatton under trainer Noel Thornberry, is the IBF's number one-ranked fighter.

A potential title fight has been put on hold until the organisation's legal dispute with fellow Queensland-based champion Jai Opetaia is resolved.

Opetaia, who brutally knocked out Nyika to retain the IBF and The Ring belts in January last year, had his IBF status stripped when he debuted for rebel league Zuffa Boxing this year.

Jai Opetaia knocked David Nyika out when they met in January, 2025. (AAP Image: Dave Hunt)

Usyk's plans have put a spanner in the works for Opetaia, who is eyeing off a heavyweight cameo against Deontay Wilder next month before a potential unification clash with Benavidez next May.

Opetaia could still win back his IBF strap in the courtroom and earn a date with Usyk he has coveted since they competed at the 2012 London Olympics when the Australian was barely 17.

Opetaia exacts brutal toll in knockout, with heavyweight domination in his sight Jai Opetaia is the only man who can challenge heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk says promoter Eddie Hearn, after the IBF and Ring champion exacted the toll of trying to match it with boxing's best from David Nyika.

But even then Nyika remains the mandatory opponent and would command step-aside money for the Opetaia-Usyk fight to proceed.

"We'd have to sit down and come to an agreement, but we'd enforce his mandatory for sure if we were to stand aside," Thornberry told AAP on Monday.

Thornberry trained and managed former world champion contender Alex Leapai out of his Gatton boxing shed and has regularly held fight nights at the town's Shire Hall.

With Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh backing Usyk, Thornberry joked that he could pencil in an upgrade to the venue as part of the fight contract.

Oleksandr Usyk (right) won the undisputed IBF, IBO, WBA, WBC and WBO world heavyweight titles. (Getty Images: Richard Pelham)

"I've reached out to Usyk's management, they know we're certainly interested," Thornberry said.

"I'm sure they see David as a good way back in, but it's a great opportunity for David and he said he'd take it in a heartbeat.

"And, historically, no-one goes well when they come back in weight."

Oscar De Le Hoya lost to Manny Pacquiao, who went up two classes, when he dropped down in weight for their 2008 clash, while Antonio Tarver got the better of Roy Jones Jnr in a three-fight saga between 2003–2005.

Usyk showed off his slimmed-down physique at Canelo Alvarez's Saudi Arabia win on the weekend, but Thornberry reckons the jury is out.

"They come back down and go, 'Oh shit, this is a different algorithm to what I was accustomed to,'" he said.

"So let's see."

AAP

World.title: Wanderers' chair calls out 'totally unacceptable' fan treatment by police
World.content:
Western Sydney chairman Paul Lederer has slammed the "totally unacceptable" treatment and over-policing of Wanderers' supporters this season and vowed to seek answers from police.

The Red and Black Bloc (RBB), Western Sydney's active supporter group, staged a silent protest against over-policing in the opening 20 minutes of Saturday's goalless draw between the Wanderers and Macarthur at Campbelltown Sports Stadium.

The RBB, who also held banners that read "Stand Up For Fans. Not Police Demands" as a message to the Australian Professional Leagues (APL), said they had been directed by NSW Police to surrender their drums, megaphone and banners two hours before kick-off.

Macarthur coach and former Socceroo Sasa Ognenovski and his Wanderers' counterpart Ufuk Talay backed the fans, and Lederer joined them on Monday, releasing a lengthy statement.

Ufuk Talay (right) and Sasa Ognenovski were both sympathetic to the fans' cause. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

"Since the beginning of the season, we have witnessed repeated issues surrounding the treatment of our supporters. The events of this weekend have brought those frustrations to a tipping point," Lederer said.

"The treatment of our members and fans has been totally unacceptable. Enough is enough.

"The RBB are an integral part of our club which we are extremely proud of. That will never change, and we will continue to stand behind the positive contribution they make to the Wanderers and football in this country.

The fans who care the most The Red and Black Bloc are the most controversial sports fans in Australia, but the game they love is struggling.

"Our supporters should never be made to feel like second-class citizens simply because they choose to support a football club.

"We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for equal treatment and common sense.

"For too long, our supporters have faced excessive policing, policing that you as members and fans pay for."

Lederer pointed to hundreds of fans being withheld from entering the Sydney derby for up to 30 minutes and the presence of up to 20 public order and riot squad officers behind the Wanderers' supporter bays in Campbelltown.

"This only adds to the feeling of intimidation experienced by the families that largely make up our supporter base," he said.

"This level of treatment is neither reasonable nor proportionate, and there is no justification for a riot squad presence at our football matches."

Wanderers' fans, pictured here in round one's Sydney derby, have been backed by their chairman. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Lederer stressed the club did not condone anti-social behaviour, but said most of Western Sydney's fan base were not a problem and should be treated with "the utmost respect".

"As chairman, I have a responsibility to protect the future of the Western Sydney Wanderers. That means standing up for the people who give this club life," he said.

"I will not accept our members and fans being treated as though their passion makes them any less deserving of respect. Neither will this club.

"We will continue to raise our concerns directly with NSW Police, the A-Leagues and relevant stakeholders, seek clear answers and push for fair, consistent and respectful treatment."

Lederer also thanked the Wanderers' fans.

"You have never stopped standing up for this club," he said.

"And as your chairman, I want you to know that we will never stop standing up for you."

AAP has contacted the APL and NSW Police for comment.

AAP

World.title: Big is beautiful as Australia's first UFC champion finally comes home
World.content:
It has taken more than a decade, but Rob Whittaker, Australia's first-ever UFC champion, is finally coming home.

The UFC light-heavyweight has been confirmed for the promotion's next card in Sydney on February 7, where he will face Uzbekistan's Bogdan Guskov in his first hometown fight in over 12 years.

Whittaker can barely recall his last effort in the Harbour City, when he knocked out American Clint Hester in 2014.

It came so early in his career it was closer to his Padstow products days as a Railcorp electrician than a world champion.

"It's hard to remember, to be honest. So much has happened since. I've ridden the rollercoaster," said Whittaker.

Rob Whittaker last fought in Sydney in 2014. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Josh Hedges )

"My friends and family can all be there. They can be a part of the whole journey without having to spend a billion bucks to be there.

"But I hope things settle down. I'm going to have to stop replying (to people asking for tickets).

"It'll be good to be home after so long. You normally have to travel so far to put on a show."

Putting on a show far and wide has been second nature for Whittaker during his long career with the UFC.

Since that night in Sydney, all but one of his UFC losses have come against future or reigning world champions, confirming his status as one of Australia's top combat sport exports.

The 35-year-old snuck in a few fights on home soil, but the last was in 2019 when he lost the middleweight title against Israel Adesanya in Melbourne in front of over 57,000 fans, still the biggest crowd in UFC history.

The crowd won't quite be the same at the Sydney SuperDome for this card, headlined by rising Perth lightweight Quillin Salkilld's bout with Benoit St Denis, but Whittaker — a father of three sons and three daughters — is just happy he can take his kids to work.

Rob Whittaker recently broke a two-fight losing streak. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"Last fight, my two eldest could come. This time it might be my three eldest. They loved it last time, and I loved having them be a part of it," said Whittaker.

"They get to see their old man work for a living. I'm sure half the time they think I'm unemployed.

"I love fighting. I don't think there's a cooler way to earn money if we want to keep it real basic, and I'm good at it as well. I'm earning a trade, and I'm going to keep doing it."

The fight will be Whittaker's second since moving from middleweight (83.91kg) to light-heavyweight (92.99kg).

After a third-round knockout win in his division debut over Nikita Krylov in July, he has plenty of confidence after snapping a two-fight losing streak.

Whittaker was wary of the power difference against bigger fighters, but after a strong start, where he left Krylov with a broken jaw, bigger has become beautiful.

Rob Whittaker has bulked up from middleweight to light-heavyweight. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"I'm definitely more confident in my ability to zip and zag and my ability to land power, to be faster, to have the confidence to shoot when I feel it, to have confidence in my instincts again," said Whittaker.

"I can eat for fuel, I don't need to starve myself, and that makes living — especially with a family and heaps of kids — much more enjoyable.

"But it's a slippery slope, because after a fight I can get really stuck in.

"Light-heavyweight eating is different to middleweight eating, let me tell you."

Guskov has a strong track record with 15 knockouts from his 18 wins, but Whittaker is confident he has the experience to outpoint the 34-year-old.

"He's a big, rangy guy. He hits hard, he's finished a lot of people, but there's nothing he brings to the table that I haven't seen in my years in the game," said Whittaker.

"There's nothing he brings to the table that I think I can't beat."

Tech.title: Apple is ‘not able to predict’ when it’ll have enough iPhone Duos to go around
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple CEO John Ternus doesn’t have a timeline for when iPhone Duo supply constraints could lift. During an interview with Reuters, Ternus said the company is “working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this ​point, we’re not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Apple launched its first foldable last month for $1,999, featuring a 5.4 outer display and 7.6-inch inner screen. Preorders for the iPhone Duo quickly sold out, with some shipments expected to arrive in 2027. Apple also made a limited number of iPhone Duo models available in-store at launch.

In his interview with Reuters, Ternus also addressed reports about cracked screens, saying “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duos were returned for this issue, and that Apple is replacing them.

The company has contended with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs for months now. This resulted in price increases across its product lineup, along with higher iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max starting prices. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” Ternus said during Apple’s Q4 2026 earnings call on Monday. Ternus added that the company expects to see “even higher memory costs” during Apple’s December quarter but notes that this is “partly offset” by recent price increases.

Even without a standard iPhone 18 model, Apple reported record-breaking iPhone revenue at $57.58 billion during its fourth quarter.

Tech.title: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh. In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products. Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027. “We saw higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, and that was partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on non-memory components,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during an interview with CNBC.

Apple reported a 12 percent increase in revenue overall, ballooning to $114.5 billion. Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.

Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks. It made a big push into the smart home space with its first smart home display and a series of video doorbells, security cameras, and door locks, made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Tech.title: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is planning to release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, the company announced today. The last OS update for those devices is planned to be v213, and after that, Meta will continue to ship security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027. Apps that support the Quest 2 or Quest Pro can also be submitted through December 2027, Meta says.

Meta is calling the Quest 3 and 3S “now the baseline for Meta VR gamers.” The company is announcing this shift ahead of the planned release of its new VR Glasses, which are set to launch sometime in spring 2027.

“Quest 2 and Quest Pro laid the foundation for this platform, and millions of people still play on them,” Meta says. “Quest 3 and Quest 3S give your apps more performance headroom and mixed reality built in, and apps built for them carry forward to Meta VR Glasses, which run on the same OS and SDKs.”

Tech.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.

The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

Related Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army

It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”

Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

Tech.title: BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

BMW says that it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow.

The new system can help steer, speed up, and slow down the vehicle on both highways and city streets using its built-in GPS navigation. While driving in town, it can assist with changing lanes, making turns, yielding to other cars, and driving through roundabouts. But as a Level 2 driver assist system, it still requires drivers to keep their eyes on the road and stay ready to take over at any moment. On the highway, BMW will allow drivers to remove their hands from the steering wheel — but on local roads, they’ll need to keep their hands on the wheel.

BMW is the latest automaker to commit to releasing a partially autonomous city driving feature to its customers, as the industry races to keep up with Tesla and its Full Self-Driving (FSD) system. BMW, in particular, recently introduced its next-generation Neue Klasse platform, which includes a driver assist system partly powered by Qualcomm’s technology. And with hands-free highway driving now widely available in many mass-market vehicles, the next frontier is a safe and capable city driving feature that rivals FSD.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Image: BMW

BMW says its system works cooperatively with drivers rather than fighting their control, which means they can steer, brake, or speed up at any point to adjust their driving without shutting the system off. At the same time, the car shows what it sees and what the assistance system is doing right in your line of sight through the heads-up display and in a clear 3D map on the main dashboard screen.

The necessary cameras and sensors already come built into models like BMW’s 3 Series, 7 Series, X5, iX3, and iX4. BMW can activate the feature through an over-the-air software update. The system follows new European safety rules that let cars suggest and make automated driving moves on city streets for the first time. BMW says that outside experts have already road-tested the setup and confirmed it meets the technical standards, with final official government approval expected in early 2027.

With more cars equipped with partial automation hitting the road, safety researchers are growing increasingly worried about driver attention and the potential for these systems to cause crashes. There is compelling evidence that, regardless of the company, most driver-assist systems are less safe than normal human driving. Drivers tend to develop an overreliance on these systems to drive the car for them — even after a short period of use. And when it’s time to take back control of the vehicle, their reaction times are slower than what’s considered safe.

BMW is entering risky territory with the adoption of a Level 2 driving feature. Much like Tesla, the company is emphasizing that drivers remain responsible for the vehicle even while using the partially autonomous system in urban environments. Tesla does the same for its FSD feature, but some customers have successfully argued in court that the company bears some responsibility for crashes when they occur.

Tech.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.

In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”

“We know that trust is earned.” — Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer

The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.

Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.

Previous Next





1 / 4

To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.

It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

Tech.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
Tech.content:
Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure. The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth.

However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear.

When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”

Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.

Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business.

During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory.

“We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.”

Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.”

TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds.

Tech.title: Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them
Tech.content:
In Brief

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.

Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.

According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.

It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.

Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

Tech.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
Tech.content:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.

“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.

On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.

“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.

He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”

As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.

For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”

Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.

“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”

But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

Tech.title: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps
Tech.content:
Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan as its parent company Match Group looks for new ways to get users to pay for dating apps at a time when people are increasingly tired of subscriptions and, in some cases, dating apps altogether.

During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on Monday, Match Group said the new Hinge tier will include features such as additional filters and custom location boundaries, giving users more control over who they see and where they meet people.

“It’s designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users,” said Steve Bailey, chief financial officer of Match Group. “Remember that Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder, around $30. It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.”

Match Group didn’t share how much the new subscription will cost. TechCrunch has reached out to the company for more details.

The move comes as dating apps continue to struggle to convince people to pay for services they’re growing tired of using. Between subscription fatigue, endless swiping, and frustration with the overall dating experience, users are increasingly questioning whether premium dating features are worth the money.

Interestingly, Hinge is making this move despite being one of Match Group’s strongest performers. The app had a much better quarter than Tinder, with global monthly active users growing 12% year over year, direct revenue increasing 19%, and paying users rising 23% to 2.3 million. The app generated $221 million in direct revenue and had 2.3 million paid subscribers as of the end of the quarter. Direct revenue is money earned from subscriptions and in-app purchases.

By comparison, Tinder brought in $480 million in direct revenue but experienced a slight 2% decline year-over-year, although it has 8.9 million paid users, a 4% decline from a year earlier.

The lower-priced subscription could help Hinge build on that momentum by converting more users into paying customers without requiring them to spend as much upfront.

The move also marks a shift in Hinge’s subscription strategy. In 2023, the company experimented with a more expensive tier aimed at users willing to pay extra for features designed to help them get more out of the app. Now, it’s testing whether a more affordable option could appeal to a broader audience.

Still, cheaper subscriptions alone are unlikely to solve the bigger problem facing dating apps: user fatigue. Match Group says it’s seeing some signs of improvement, partly thanks to efforts to make its platforms feel less like traditional dating apps.

Recent initiatives include Group Hangouts and Events, which offer users alternative ways to connect beyond the usual one-on-one matching experience. Match Group plans to ramp up those efforts in the fourth quarter.

Another initiative on the horizon is real-time adaptive recommendations, which the company plans to begin testing in the fourth quarter. Announced during its CEO Connection presentation in September, the feature will allow Tinder to respond to user actions within seconds rather than hours, with the goal of making recommendations more relevant and personalized.

Tech.title: Apple says it’s ‘hard to predict’ when iPhone Duo constraints will improve
Tech.content:
Apple Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan acknowledged the shipping delays plaguing the new iPhone Duo during the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, but offered little clarity on when customers can expect relief.

The delays were just one point of concern during an earnings call filled with questions about the rising costs of memory chips, driven by soaring demand from the AI industry.

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan said.

Customers who didn’t wait in line at an Apple Store or immediately jump on preorders are now seeing ship times stretch into next year. Meanwhile, Verizon has been apologizing to its customers for the delays by offering gift cards.

In an October report from Financial Times, Apple described demand for the Duo as “nothing short of extraordinary,” after the device sold out on the company’s website within hours of going on sale, pushing delivery dates into next year.

The prolonged shipping delays are notable given Apple’s reputation for its highly efficient supply chain. But the company is hardly alone in facing supply pressures. Soaring demand for memory chips from the AI industry has driven up component costs for hardware makers across the board, threatening to push device prices even higher.

Apple, too, has raised prices on a number of products, Khan noted on the call, adding that those decisions were made “reluctantly.”

In another sign of the company’s efforts to meet demand for the Duo, Apple said it’s “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer for supplying materials for the new foldable device.

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during his opening remarks.

Tech.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
Tech.content:
Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.

Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).

Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.

The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.

Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.

With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.

Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.

The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.

Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.

Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. It considers Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, a direct competitor, along with Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, which helps companies build and train their own AI agents.

Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.

Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

Tech.title: Apple’s inventory surges 154% as memory chip costs climb
Tech.content:
Apple’s stockpiling of inventory, particularly computer memory, continued in its fiscal fourth quarter, according to earnings reported Monday. The company reported that its inventory increased significantly in the quarter, growing from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion in Q4, a jump of 31.1%. Year-over-year, inventory grew 154.3% from $5.72 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Apple’s forecast of a 45% to 46% gross margin in the December quarter was largely attributed to the impact of higher memory costs. The company reported a gross margin of 47.9% for the September quarter.

“What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” said Apple CEO John Ternus, speaking to analysts on the call. “As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components.”

He said that the company expected “even higher memory costs” in the December quarter, which would be partially offset by price increases implemented earlier this year on some devices, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhones in September.

Ternus also said that beyond December, Apple expects memory costs “continuing to increase.”

“As we said before, we do believe we’ll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time,” he noted, adding that the company was increasing its purchases of this key component. “As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by 33 billion dollars from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow.”

Apple also brought COO Sabih Khan, who oversees the company’s supply chain and manufacturing, onto the call to address questions about memory. He reiterated the increased purchase obligations but did not rule out future price increases on Apple devices.

The company also blamed supply constraints for weak iPad sales in the quarter. The iPad was one of the only product segments that didn’t grow, even as iPhone and Mac sales beat estimates. iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, below analysts’ expectations of $6.7 billion. The figure was also down 10% from the prior year.

Tech.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
Tech.content:
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.

The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).

RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.

To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.

Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”

When the term RSI became popular earlier this year, many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.

But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):

In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.

However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”

Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.

Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

Tech.title: The Online Right’s Closing Campaign Argument: Fascist Anakin Skywalker Memes
Tech.content:
According to Christian streamer Kangmin Lee, Anakin Skywalker represents the “archetypal disenfranchised chud,” radicalized when he realizes the “political order” he once believed in is “deeply corrupt, hypocritical, and wicked.” Right-wing Substack writer Max Mersault believes that the Anakin posts are “culturally significant” and that you couldn’t “engineer a better anti-progressive memetic virus in [a] lab if you tried.”

Elon Musk himself, after funneling nearly half a billion dollars to Republican candidates this cycle, shared a seemingly AI-generated image of Anakin on a throne, accompanied by his love interest Padmé Amidala, their children Luke Skywalker and Princess Leia, and a bevy of imperial guards and stormtroopers, declaring: “This is what they stole from us.”

Who is “they”? What is “this”? To the MAGA faithful staring down a potential blue wave thanks to inflation, a pointless war in the Middle East, and the president’s historic unpopularity, such details hardly matter. The Anakin memes are all about advertising your fascist worldview, lust for corruptive power, and endless grievances about immigrants or “DEI.” These guys also don’t care that Anakin was groomed to be an evil lackey by a decrepit old wizard and slaughtered children on his orders, since that’s just the price of overthrowing democracy.

But even this may be giving them too much credit. After all, their Anakin trend was preceded by a craze for incel-adjacent “Malfoid” content—a fanfic twist on Harry Potter that introduces a gender-flipped, female version of antagonist Draco Malfoy as a romantic prospect for our main character—and for some reason felt that this slop, too, made good reactionary propaganda. The US Department of Education got in on the meme, later updating it with Anakin imagery.

Likewise signaling the administration’s confusing embrace of fantasy IP, Katie Miller, podcaster and wife of top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, on Sunday posted to X: “I have zero unregretted user seconds spent on Anakin postings.”

The GOP and the tech right aren’t exactly known for their cogent analysis of the stories they hold near and dear, and their identification with a murderous tyrant is no great surprise. What’s somewhat harder to explain is their apparent delusion about this message reaching and resonating with well-adjusted voters outside their esoteric social media feeds. The Anakin stuff, some of them insist, “is not a meme anymore,” constituting a “monumental zeitgeist victory.” Along with the Malfoid posts, they claim, it has reversed “a decade of cultural rot and damage in less than a week.”

Meanwhile, back in reality, this amounts to nothing more consequential than playing with action figures. Wanting to be Darth Vader is the dream of a 10-year-old forced to clean his room and eat his vegetables. Hayden Christensen, who played Anakin Skywalker in the prequels, told Variety in 2023 that depicting his journey to the dark side “humanized him” yet revealed that he was a “pathetic person” and “trapped in this life that perhaps he didn’t really want.”

You might reasonably speculate whether conservative influencers tied to a weakened Trump are in a similar position these days. Just don’t expect them to ever acknowledge this burst of mediated angst as the cringeworthy coping it actually is. However the electoral showdown plays out, they’ll have a new aspirational antihero soon enough—and this time, you won’t dare laugh at their very important posts.

Cases are around $50 apiece, which is the most straightforward way to save, but with dozens of items to choose from, it’s worth browsing what else you might want.

Photograph: Louryn Strampe

Most of Burga’s phone cases use the same material across models. It’s mostly a matter of choosing your favorite printed pattern. You can coordinate or mix and match with Burga’s other accessories. The cases are thin and inflexible—not necessarily rugged but still more protective than going without. Every one I’ve tried has been precisely cut to fit my phone’s buttons and camera bump, and it is easy to install. When you have the option, I recommend picking a MagSafe case since it’ll be compatible with so many accessories.

I also like the brand’s magnetic phone ring holders, which are available in coordinating patterns with the phone cases. They fold down flat and have a slimmer profile than PopSockets or other phone grips you might be familiar with. They stay on well and are comfortable to use if you like ring-style grips.

Tech.title: Best Dyson Vacuum Deals (2026): Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai, Dyson V16 Piston Animal
Tech.content:
I’m asked all too often if investing in a Dyson is worth it. As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum—from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones are worth it, and at what price.

You can often find some kind of Dyson vacuum on sale, though the best time is to wait for an event like Black Friday. While that’s only a few weeks away, a few Dyson vacuums are already on sale. If you’re looking to pick up a new vacuum, here are the best Dyson deals I’ve spotted this week.

The Best Dyson Robot Vacuum Deal Right Now

The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai came out earlier this year but has already been surpassed as Dyson’s top-of-the-line robot vacuum. But I prefer it to the newer Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV I’m currently testing because it’s usually on sale, and the newest model hasn’t blown me away as a better investment. The Spot+Scrub Ai claims to use artificial intelligence to spot places on your floor it needs to scrub, but I didn’t find it obvious whether that was actually working. Still, overall it did a good job, especially for Dyson’s first foray into robot vacuums that also mop. It’s often discounted around this price, but the $400-off sale is a little better than what we saw during Prime Day.

Also on sale: The Dyson R1 Nurovi Dry ($450, usually $550), one of Dyson’s three new robot vacuums it announced this fall, is $100 off. I haven’t tested it, so I can’t say whether it’s worth buying. I’m currently testing the Dyson R3 Nurovi ($1,200), and I’m not super impressed with its vacuuming—I’ve found rice and popcorn left behind on rugs and hard floors—so I’m hesitant to expect the R1 to be better.

The Best Dyson Stick Vacuum Deal Right Now

If you’re going to buy a Dyson vacuum on sale, you might as well go for one of the better ones. The V16 Piston Animal is Dyson’s most powerful stick vacuum, with 315 air watts of power, some nice quality-of-life improvements in the body design, and an option to add the Submarine 2.0 mop head. I really liked this vacuum for the design upgrades and power level, but the price tag can be hard to stomach. It’s on sale fairly regularly, and there are a few different on-sale combos: the base vacuum is $180 off, bundling it with the Submarine head is $200 off, and the option with the charging Floor Dok is also $200 off. I love the Submarine head, but while I haven’t tested the vacuum with the Floor Dok yet, it’s the accessory I want most—having your cordless vacuum fully charged whenever you want it, and somewhere to store it, is really handy.
